excerpt: Binaural recording puts microphones in the ears of a model head to capture 3D sound. Learn how it works and what it means for piano recordings.

title: Bizet's Jeux d'enfants: Twelve Piano Duets From 1871
excerpt: Jeux d'enfants, Op. 22, is a set of twelve piano duets Bizet wrote in 1871, each picturing a children's game. He later orchestrated five of them as a Petite Suite, and the short, vivid pieces are ideal for two players at one piano.

title: What Is Blob Opera? Four AI Blobs Sing in Four-Part Harmony
excerpt: Blob Opera is a machine-learning experiment from Google Arts and Culture in which four blobs sing harmony in real time. Learn how it works, where its limits lie, and how to bring the harmonies you hear to the piano.

title: Blocking Chords Before Practising Arpeggio Figures
excerpt: Before you practise a written arpeggio, play its notes as a blocked chord. That step steadies fingering, harmony and the later rolling figure.

title: Bluegrass for Pianists: Drive, Off-Beat Chop and Fast Tunes
excerpt: What defines bluegrass music, how its off-beat chop, drive and instrument roles work, and how pianists can borrow its rhythm and melodies.

title: Blues Scale Colour on Piano: Blue Notes Without Guesswork
excerpt: How to use a blues scale on piano with clear fingerings, where the blue notes sit, and simple call-and-answer drills that keep the colour intentional.

title: The Blues Scale: Six Notes to Improvise With Your Right Hand
excerpt: The blues scale has six different notes. On C they are C, E♭, F, F♯ (or G♭), G and B♭. Keep your left hand simple and improvise short phrases with your right to build your ear and your feel for the keys.

title: Bluetooth Headphone Latency: Why You Can Feel It on a Digital Piano
excerpt: Wireless headphones are convenient, but the sound reaches your ears a fraction later than the key press. This article explains how latency arises and gives some simple ways to deal with it when practising on a digital piano.

title: Boccherini's Minuet: From String Quintet to Piano
excerpt: This light, elegant minuet comes from a string quintet in E major that Boccherini wrote in 1771. Learn its background and how to keep its lightness when you play it on the piano.

title: Beginner Boogie-Woogie Piano: Left-Hand Patterns and a 12-Bar Plan
excerpt: Start boogie-woogie piano: the 12-bar blues map, four left-hand patterns from easy to hard, swing feel, right-hand riffs and a one-week plan.

title: Borodin's In the Steppes of Central Asia: Two Melodies Meet, 1880
excerpt: In the Steppes of Central Asia is a tone poem Borodin wrote in 1880, in which a caravan crosses the vast steppe. A Russian melody and an Eastern melody sound together before fading into the distance. It is dedicated to Liszt.

title: Borrowed Chords on Piano: Colour From the Parallel Minor
excerpt: Borrowed chords on piano: colour from the parallel minor, flat-side harmony, and short progressions that still resolve to the tonic.

title: Bossa Nova on Piano: Thumb Bass, Soft Syncopation and Rich Chords
excerpt: How bossa nova grew from samba, how its guitar rhythm translates to piano, and which chord colours give the style its relaxed, soft sound.

title: The Bourree on Piano: A Quick Dance That Starts on an Upbeat
excerpt: A bourree is a quick dance, often in two beats, that typically starts on an upbeat. Learn how to feel that pickup and keep the dance clear.

title: Brahms's Hungarian Dance No. 5: The Original Four-Hands Version
excerpt: Brahms wrote 21 Hungarian Dances, WoO 1, first for one piano, four hands. No. 5 was originally in F♯ minor, and its shifting tempo makes it a fine sample of the set.

title: Brahms's Intermezzo in A Major, Op. 118 No. 2: A Gentle Late Piece
excerpt: Brahms's Intermezzo in A major, Op. 118 No. 2, written in 1893 and dedicated to Clara Schumann, is a tender piece in ABA form, with a canon-like B section in F♯ minor.

title: Brahms's Lullaby (Wiegenlied): A Gentle Sway in Three
excerpt: Brahms's Lullaby began as a German art song, Op. 49 No. 4 (1868). On the piano, play the simple triple-time melody like singing, with a steady left hand and a soft touch.

title: Autumn 1853: Young Brahms Knocks on the Schumanns' Door
excerpt: On 30 September 1853, twenty-year-old Brahms visited Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf and played for them. Weeks later Schumann's article "New Paths" introduced him to the public.

title: Brahms's Waltz in A-flat Major: A Gentle Piece From Op. 39
excerpt: Brahms wrote his sixteen waltzes, Op. 39, in 1865 for piano four hands, dedicating them to the critic Hanslick. The gentle fifteenth, in A-flat major, is widely played on its own. Here is its background and how to play it.

title: Brand Playlist Marketing: Show Your Brand's Character in One Playlist
excerpt: Brand playlist marketing means choosing the mood and purpose of a playlist, selecting and ordering tracks, writing the cover and description, updating regularly, and, for music education brands, using playlists to accompany learners.

title: Breath Marks in Piano Music: A Tiny Pause in a Phrase
excerpt: A breath mark is a small comma or tick that asks for a tiny lift, so a phrase can end and the next idea can start cleanly.

title: The Breve: A Note Twice as Long as a Whole Note
excerpt: The breve, or double whole note, is worth two whole notes and fills two bars of 4/4. It is an open oval with a vertical line on each side, and it appears mostly in early music, sacred music and pieces in long metres.

title: Let the Middle Voice Sing: How to Play Inner Voices Well
excerpt: In piano music the melody is not always on top. Sometimes it is hidden in the middle of a chord, and bringing it out while keeping the notes above and below softer takes independent finger weight and careful listening.

title: Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra (1946)
excerpt: Benjamin Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra, Op. 34, was written in 1945 to 1946 for an educational film introducing the instruments of the orchestra.

title: Bu Bu Gao: A Cantonese Music Piece Climbing Step by Step
excerpt: Bu Bu Gao is a famous piece of Cantonese music composed by Lü Wencheng in the 1930s. Its bright melody climbs higher with each phrase, and it is often played at festivals.

title: Tchaikovsky's B♭ Minor Piano Concerto: Premiered in Boston, 1875
excerpt: In late 1874 Nikolai Rubinstein harshly criticised Tchaikovsky's new B♭ minor piano concerto. Tchaikovsky dedicated it to Hans von Bülow, who premiered it in Boston on 25 October 1875 to great success.

title: Burgmüller's Arabesque: The Second Étude of Op. 100
excerpt: Burgmüller's Arabesque is No. 2 of his 25 Easy and Progressive Studies, Op. 100, in A minor and lively in tempo. It trains even sixteenth notes and bringing out the melody.

title: Burgmüller Op. 100: A Skill Map for the 25 Progressive Studies
excerpt: How to use Burgmüller Op. 100: a skill map grouping the 25 studies, a three-week routine for learning one, and common mistakes to avoid.

title: Busking as Market Research: What Street Sets Teach Musicians
excerpt: How a lawful street set can test songs, tempos and openings with real passers-by, and how to turn those observations into release decisions.

title: The Butterfly Lovers Theme: From Violin Concerto to Piano
excerpt: The Butterfly Lovers violin concerto, by He Zhanhao and Chen Gang, premiered in Shanghai in May 1959 with soloist Yu Lina. Its lyrical opening theme has been arranged for piano in many versions.

title: Buying a Second-Hand Acoustic Piano: What to Check First
excerpt: A used acoustic piano can be a good choice if you check it carefully. Learn what to inspect, which questions to ask and why a technician's view helps.

title: Cadences Explained: Four Ways a Musical Phrase Can End
excerpt: A cadence is the chord pair that closes a phrase. Learn the authentic, plagal, half and deceptive endings and how to hear and play each on piano.

title: The Cadential Six-Four: The Tonic-Like Chord Before the Dominant
excerpt: In classical cadences, a special chord often comes before the dominant: it has the tonic's notes, C, E, G in C major, but with the dominant note G in the bass. This is the cadential six-four chord.

title: How to Play a Cadenza: Phrasing and Breathing in Free Passages
excerpt: A cadenza is a passage where the soloist plays freely. Learn where concerto cadenzas come from, how to find the skeleton notes, shape phrases and leave room to breathe.

title: The Cadenza: A Soloist's Moment of Freedom in a Concerto
excerpt: A cadenza is a solo passage where the orchestra stops and the pianist plays freely. Learn its history, how it is built and how to listen for it.

title: The Double Slash in Sheet Music: A Short Pause
excerpt: The two slashes "//" in sheet music, often called train tracks, are known as a caesura: a brief pause that interrupts the beat before the music continues. Unlike a fermata, it stops the sound.

title: Before Playing Caiyun Zhuiyue: Getting to Know the Pentatonic Scale
excerpt: Caiyun Zhuiyue is a well-loved Chinese folk piece often arranged for piano. Built on the pentatonic scale, it sounds soft and airy, so play it with a connected, gentle touch.

title: When a Student Is Nervous: Creating a Safe Piano Lesson
excerpt: Some students get sweaty palms and dare not play out loud in piano lessons. This article shows how teachers can create a reassuring atmosphere through greetings, easier tasks, demonstrations, tone of voice and a gentle ending.

title: Calypso Rhythm: Off-Beat Pulse, Storytelling and Steelpan Roots
excerpt: A guide to calypso from Trinidad and Tobago: storytelling lyrics, the off-beat pulse, its link to the steelpan and how to feel it on piano.

title: Double Neighbour Notes: A Melody Circling Its Target
excerpt: Double neighbour notes, or cambiata, are two non-chord tones above and below a target note: the melody visits one side, leaps to the other, then lands, as in D, B, C.

title: Camera Angles for Online Piano Lessons: Showing Your Hands Clearly
excerpt: In an online piano lesson, a good camera view lets the teacher see hands, posture and the keys. Simple set-ups with a phone or laptop.

title: Camera Hand Tracking for Pianists: What Computer Vision Can See
excerpt: Hand-pose models map finger joints from an ordinary camera. See how they could check piano posture, where they fail and how to film your hands well.

title: Canon at the Octave: The Second Voice Enters an Octave Away
excerpt: In a canon at the octave, the second voice follows the first but enters one octave higher or lower. The outline matches exactly, only later in time and different in height.

title: Canons and Rounds on Piano: One Melody Chasing Itself
excerpt: A canon is a melody that is imitated by another voice starting later. Learn how rounds and canons work and how to play and write simple ones on piano.

title: Cantus Firmus: Polyphony Built on a Single Long-Note Melody
excerpt: Cantus firmus, Latin for "fixed song", is an existing melody a composer uses as a foundation, with new melodies added above and below it. It shaped medieval and Renaissance polyphony and is still used to teach counterpoint.

title: The Canzona: Song Turned Instrumental, Opening Long-Short-Short
excerpt: The canzona was a sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Italian instrumental form, named for the word "song". It began as French polyphonic songs arranged for instruments and often opens with a long-short-short rhythm.

title: The Carillon: Bell Overtones and the Keyboard Played With Fists
excerpt: How a carillon works, why its bells have an unusual minor-third overtone, and what its baton keyboard teaches pianists about harmony and decay.

title: Carl Czerny: Beethoven's Pupil, Liszt's Teacher
excerpt: Carl Czerny (1791-1857) was a Viennese pianist, composer and teacher who studied with Beethoven and later taught the young Liszt. Today he is best known for his many studies, such as Op. 599, Op. 299 and Op. 740.

title: Carmen's 1875 Premiere: The Success Bizet Never Saw
excerpt: Bizet's opera Carmen premiered in Paris on 3 March 1875 to a lukewarm reception. Three months later, on 3 June, Bizet died suddenly at thirty-six, never knowing that Carmen would become one of the most performed operas in the world.

title: Playing Cartoon Themes by Ear Still Needs Reading and a Steady Tempo
excerpt: Working out a cartoon theme by ear is great ear training, but it is easy to speed up and drift. Check the tempo marking, such as Allegro, before you play so that your ears and your reading help each other.

title: Case Study: How a Small Instrument Repair Shop Moved Bookings Online
excerpt: An anonymous small instrument repair shop replaced phone bookings with online booking, then built repeat customers with progress updates and maintenance reminders. This article breaks down the steps and the lessons.

title: Anonymous Case: Turning Long Lesson Videos into Practice Cards
excerpt: A hypothetical anonymous case: an online piano course team finds that learners rarely finish long videos, so they split the content into short practice cards. This article covers the approach, the card design and what to watch for.

title: Anonymous Case: From One-Off Piano Tuning to a Regular Maintenance Plan
excerpt: An anonymous piano tuning service moved from single house calls to a regular maintenance plan. This article sets out the changes in service design, communication and customer experience.

title: Case Study: Setting Up Try-It-Out Sheet Music in a Library Corner
excerpt: A community library corner that offers easy sheet music to browse can make passers-by stop. This generic case covers display, copyright cautions and how to guide visitors.

title: Anonymous Case: How a Small Music Studio Redesigned Its Timetable
excerpt: An anonymous small music studio redesigned its timetable to ease scheduling pressure on teachers and pick-up difficulties for parents. This article sets out its thinking, steps and what others can learn.

title: Anonymous Case: A Small Recording Space and Off-Season Time Packages
excerpt: Small recording spaces often have whole stretches empty in the off-season. This fictional example shows how to turn scattered bookings into time packages, how to explain and schedule them, and what to watch for in pricing, cancellation and neighbours.

title: Anonymous Case: How a Small Studio Keeps Former Students Close
excerpt: When students stop lessons because of a move, school or a job change, does their relationship with the studio end? This fictional small-studio example shows gentle ways to keep in touch, with privacy boundaries.

title: Anonymous Case: A Small Studio Plans Next Term from Enrolment Records
excerpt: How many weekend groups should open next term, and does the weekday evening need another teacher? Using a fictional small piano studio, this article shows how to read patterns in enrolment, enquiry and waitlist records and plan cautiously.

title: Anonymous Case: Turning Parent Feedback into Improvements
excerpt: Using a fictional small music studio, this article shows how to collect parent feedback, turn it into a few clear improvements and tell parents what was done, so feedback is not just collected and left unanswered.

title: Anonymous Case: Using a Waitlist to Handle Popular Time Slots
excerpt: Using a fictional small music studio, this article shows how a waitlist can handle popular lesson slots: how to register people, how to communicate, how to stay fair and how to avoid making parents anxious.

title: Anonymous Case: Turning Quiet Practice Room Hours into Adult Lunchtime Lessons
excerpt: A hypothetical anonymous case: a small piano studio's rooms often sit empty by day, so the team studies nearby office workers' routines, designs short lunchtime lessons and introduces them to new students gently.

title: The 1825 Cast-Iron Frame: Where the Piano's Skeleton Came From
excerpt: In 1825 a Boston piano maker patented a one-piece cast-iron frame, letting pianos take heavier, tighter strings and sound louder and stay in tune longer.

title: The Cavatina: A Short, Songlike Piece or Movement
excerpt: A cavatina is a short, direct, songlike piece with a complete melody and a simpler structure than a grand aria, later also used for instrumental movements.

title: Cellular Automata Music: How Simple Rules Generate Melodies
excerpt: How cellular automata turn tiny rules into evolving patterns, how projects mapped those patterns to notes, and a rule-based game to try on piano.

title: The Chaconne Bass on Piano: Variations Over a Repeating Ground
excerpt: A piano chaconne builds variations over a repeating bass. Keep the ground clear, group the variations, and let upper lines change without losing the bass.

title: Chaconne and Ground Bass on Piano: Variations Over a Repeating Bass
excerpt: What a chaconne and ground bass are, how they differ from the passacaglia, famous examples, and how to write and play your own chaconne on piano.

title: Chaminade's Scarf Dance: A Little Dance from an 1888 Ballet
excerpt: French composer Cécile Chaminade's Scarf Dance comes from her 1888 ballet Callirhoë and became a hugely popular piano solo in Europe and America.

title: The Character Piece: Capturing a Personality or Scene in a Short Work
excerpt: The character piece is a short nineteenth-century piano form with a distinct personality, often a suggestive title, held together by mood, figuration or melody.

title: Buzzing or Rattling in Your Home Piano: Check a Few Things First
excerpt: A sudden buzz or rattle beside the piano on certain notes often comes from objects around it, not the piano itself. This guide shows a few simple checks to try before calling a technician.

title: Put a Mirror Beside the Piano and Check Your Posture
excerpt: While playing, our attention is on the score and keys, so it is hard to notice raised shoulders or a sagging wrist. A mirror beside the piano lets you glance at your posture now and then, then pause and adjust.

title: Let Your Child Decide the Order of Practice Tasks
excerpt: Children's practice is often fully arranged by parents or teachers. A small change is to keep the tasks fixed but let the child choose which to do first and which later, giving a little sense of control.

title: Your Child Plays by Ear and Avoids Reading: How to Guide Them
excerpt: A child who plays by ear and avoids the score has a good ear, but weak reading can become a problem later. Combine ears and eyes: start with short new pieces and slowly bring the eyes back to the page.

title: Let Stuffed Toys Be the Audience: Practising Performing at Home
excerpt: Line up your child's favourite toys as an audience and hold a little concert at home, a pressure-free way to get used to playing while someone listens.

title: Is Your Child Ready for Piano? Signs You Can Look For
excerpt: There is no single right age to start piano. Look at your child's interest, focus, finger control and ability to follow instructions, and try a trial lesson.

title: Cries Over One Wrong Note? Building the Habit of Playing to the End
excerpt: If your child cries over one wrong note, agree to keep playing through mistakes and look back afterwards. Finishing a piece is progress in itself.

title: Your Child Says They Want to Quit Piano: Find the Reason First
excerpt: When a child says they no longer want to learn piano, understand why before deciding. Then adjust together with your child and the teacher.

title: Chinese Tones and Melody: How AI Can Avoid "Flipped Words" in Songs
excerpt: Chinese is a tonal language, so a melody that runs against a word's tone can make listeners hear the wrong word. How songwriters, and AI tools, can handle it.

title: Chiptune: Music Made From Old Video Game Sound Chips
excerpt: Chiptune uses the simple sound chips of early consoles and computers. Learn how a few voices became a creative style and what it teaches about arranging.

title: Chiquinha Gonzaga: Brazilian Composer, Pianist and Conductor
excerpt: Chiquinha Gonzaga, born Francisca Gonzaga, was an important Brazilian composer, pianist and conductor, famous for Ô Abre Alas, written for the 1899 Carnival.

title: Piano Accompaniment in Choir Rehearsal: Breathing Cues and Watching the Conductor
excerpt: Choir accompaniment is more than playing the notes. Learn how the piano can give breathing cues, follow the conductor and control volume in rehearsal.

title: You Don't Have to Match the Fastest Recording: Choose a Tempo You Can Control
excerpt: A pianist's recorded tempo comes from years of training. Choose a tempo you can play steadily, clearly and musically, and raise it gradually as you improve.

title: Choosing a Digital Piano for a Small Room: What to Consider
excerpt: Choosing a digital piano for a small room or dorm? Consider a full 88 keys, weighted keys, a headphone jack, size and weight, and the pedals. Try a few before you decide.

title: Choosing Your First Piano Method Book: Five Criteria
excerpt: Your first method book shapes how learning feels. Here are five criteria for beginners: age fit, pacing, how it teaches note reading, appealing pieces and companion resources.

title: Questions to Ask Before You Choose a Piano Teacher
excerpt: Besides convenient times and location, prepare a few questions to see whether a piano teacher's approach suits you or your child: lesson structure, practice, exams, beginners and a trial lesson.

title: Choosing a Recital Piece: Slightly Below Your Level Is Safer
excerpt: For a student recital, choose a piece slightly easier than your hardest. Also weigh its length, style, preparation time and whether you love it, and talk it over with your teacher.

title: Choosing Piano Exam Pieces Early Enough to Practise Them Properly
excerpt: Choose piano exam pieces early enough to practise them properly. Read the list, test the writing at the keyboard, and leave time for slow work.

title: How to Choose a Student's First Piano Piece
excerpt: Choosing a beginner's first piano piece comes down to difficulty, interest and a sense of achievement. Here is a simple approach for teachers and parents, with no need to rush.

title: Choosing the Next Piano Piece: Signs a Learner Is Ready to Move On
excerpt: Choosing the next piano piece is easier when readiness is visible: a stable pulse, a finished current piece, and a new page that stretches one skill.

title: Choosing Repertoire for Piano Students: Balance Challenge and Joy
excerpt: The right pieces keep students motivated and growing. How teachers choose repertoire by skill, style, length and personal taste across a term.

title: Choosing a Practice Tempo With a Click, Then Moving It
excerpt: Choose a practice tempo where the aim holds under a click, stay for several loops, then move the click in small steps. Know when to wait and when to move.

title: Chopin's Waltz in A Minor (Posthumous): A Short Piece Published in 1955
excerpt: Chopin's Waltz in A minor, often called posthumous, was unpublished in his lifetime and only appeared in print in 1955. Here is its background and tips on the left hand, melody and tempo.

title: Chopin's Barcarolle, Op. 60: Rocking 12/8 in F♯ Major
excerpt: Chopin's Barcarolle, Op. 60, written around 1845 to 1846 in F♯ major and 12/8, is a large-scale piano piece. Here is how to approach its rocking rhythm, layers, pedalling and structure.

title: Chopin's Berceuse, Op. 57: The Ever-Repeating Bass in D♭ Major
excerpt: Chopin's Berceuse, Op. 57, written around 1843 to 1844 in D♭ major, repeats one short bass figure in the left hand while the right hand spins ever more ornamented variations above it.

title: Chopin's Études, Op. 10: Technical Practice Written as Music
excerpt: Chopin's twelve Études, Op. 10, published in 1833 and dedicated to Liszt, each train one technique yet have vivid melody and feeling. They show that technical exercises can be real music.

title: Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu, Op. 66: Written 1834, Published Later
excerpt: Chopin wrote the Fantaisie-Impromptu in C♯ minor in 1834 but never published it. His friend Fontana issued it in 1855 as Op. 66, with a four-against-three rhythm and a D♭ major middle section.

title: February 1832: Chopin's First Concert in Paris
excerpt: Chopin arrived in Paris from Poland in autumn 1831, aged twenty-one. On 26 February 1832 he gave his first concert there, then settled in the city, teaching, composing and playing in salons.

title: Chopin's Polonaise in A-flat, Op. 53: The "Heroic" of 1842
excerpt: Chopin's Polonaise in A♭ major, Op. 53, written in 1842, is nicknamed the "Heroic". Its middle section, with relentless descending octaves in the left hand, is the most famous part.

title: 16 November 1848: Chopin's Last Public Performance in London
excerpt: In 1848 Chopin left Paris for Britain. On 16 November he played at a charity event for Polish exiles at London's Guildhall, his last public performance, and died in Paris the next year.

title: 1830: Chopin Leaves Warsaw on a Journey With No Return
excerpt: On 2 November 1830, twenty-year-old Chopin left Warsaw for Vienna, planning only a few months away. The November Uprising broke out weeks later, and he settled in Paris in autumn 1831, never returning to Poland.

title: Chopin Mazurkas on Piano: Feeling the Accent on Beat Two or Three
excerpt: Why mazurkas stress beat two or three, how they differ from waltzes, and a step-by-step plan to prepare your first Chopin mazurka on piano.

title: Chopin's Military Polonaise, Op. 40 No. 1: A Major Chords and Dotted Rhythms
excerpt: The Military Polonaise is the first of Chopin's two Polonaises, Op. 40, in A major, written in 1838 and published in 1840. Its strong chords and dotted rhythms sound like a marching army.

title: Chopin's "Minute Waltz": The Misunderstanding in the Name
excerpt: Chopin's Waltz in D♭ major, Op. 64 No. 1, published in 1847, is called the "Minute Waltz" or "Little Dog Waltz". Here "minute" means "small", so the aim is lightness and clarity, not speed.

title: Chopin's D-flat Nocturne: The Second of Op. 27
excerpt: Chopin's Nocturne in D♭ major, Op. 27 No. 2, written around 1835, has longer phrases and a more continuous left-hand accompaniment than the famous early E♭ major nocturne.

title: Chopin's Nocturne in E-flat, Op. 9 No. 2: An Early Favourite
excerpt: Chopin's Nocturne in E♭ major, Op. 9 No. 2, written around 1830 to 1832 and published in 1833, is a widely loved early nocturne with an ornate right-hand song over a gently rocking left hand.

title: Rubato in Chopin's Nocturnes: How to Repay Borrowed Time
excerpt: Rubato is not random dragging. Using Chopin's E♭ major nocturne, a four-step way to practise measured freedom: steady left hand, right hand borrows time and pays it back.

title: Chopin's Prelude in E Minor, Op. 28 No. 4: Slowly Changing Chords
excerpt: Chopin's Prelude in E minor, the fourth of the 24 Preludes, Op. 28 (1839), has a slow, simple right-hand melody over repeated left-hand chords that change by only a note or two.

title: Chopin's D♭ Major Prelude, Op. 28 No. 15: The Repeated Note
excerpt: Chopin's Prelude No. 15 in D♭ major, the "Raindrop", repeats an A♭ in the left hand like drops falling from the eaves. Keep the repeated note quiet and even while the melody sings above it.

title: Chopin's "Revolutionary" Étude: News from 1831 and a Storm in the Left Hand
excerpt: In autumn 1831 Chopin heard in Stuttgart that Warsaw had fallen. His C minor Étude, Op. 10 No. 12, is often linked to this and called the "Revolutionary", with a left hand of rushing semiquavers.

title: Chopin's Étude in E Major, Op. 10 No. 3: A Singing Melody Called "Farewell"
excerpt: Chopin's Étude in E major, Op. 10 No. 3, written around 1832 and published in 1833, is slow. It trains you to sing a melody and play the accompaniment in one hand. Its nicknames were not Chopin's.

title: Chopin's "Winter Wind" Étude, Op. 25 No. 11: A Gale After Four Slow Bars
excerpt: The "Winter Wind" is No. 11 of Chopin's Op. 25 Études, in A minor, published in 1837. Four quiet bars give way to a gale of right-hand figures over a marching left hand. The name was not Chopin's.

title: Chorale Prelude: An Organ Piece Born from a Hymn Tune
excerpt: A chorale prelude is an organ piece built on a Lutheran chorale melody. Learn where it comes from, how Bach, Brahms and Busoni used it, and how to play one on piano.

title: Accompanying Songs: Land Your Chord Changes on the Beat
excerpt: When accompanying pop songs, pausing at chord changes breaks the rhythm. Practise the changes themselves: two chords with a metronome, then move early, then add more chords.

title: Chord Inversions: Same Three Notes, a Different Note at the Bottom
excerpt: An inversion rearranges a chord so a note other than the root sits lowest. Using C major as the example, learn root position, first and second inversion, and why inversions help.

title: Chord Inversions on Piano: Move Smoothly Between Chords
excerpt: Inversions rearrange the notes of a chord so your hand moves less. Learn root position, first and second inversion and a short routine to practise them.

title: Finding a Chord's Root: Stack the Three Notes in Thirds
excerpt: A triad is three notes stacked in thirds, and the lowest note of the stack is the root. Learn how to find the root of an inverted chord and use it in accompaniment.

title: Chord Substitution Basics: Using vi in Place of I
excerpt: Chord substitution swaps one chord for another to give the same melody a new colour. The easiest start is replacing I with vi: in C major, Am for C turns bright into soft.

title: Uneven Chords: Getting Every Finger to Land Together
excerpt: When the notes of a chord do not sound together, it comes across like a tiny arpeggio. Shape the chord on the keys first, then let the whole hand drop together with arm weight.

title: Chromatic Five-Finger Warm-Up: A New Key Each Day
excerpt: Place five fingers on five neighbouring white keys, play up and down, then shift the position up a semitone each time. It warms up the fingers in all twelve major keys.

title: Chromatic Mediant Chords: A Colour Shift Beyond the Third
excerpt: Chromatic mediants are chords of the same quality whose roots lie a third apart, such as C and E major. They share one note, and the link feels like a sudden change of light.

title: Chromatic Scale Fingering on Piano: Smooth Semitones Up and Down
excerpt: The chromatic scale plays every semitone in order. Learn the standard fingering, an alternative for speed and drills that keep it smooth and even.

title: Circle of Fifths for Piano: How to Read and Use It
excerpt: The circle of fifths explained for pianists: how to read key signatures, find relative minors, predict common chords, and practice it in ten minutes.

title: Circuit Bending Toy Instruments for Curious Sound Design
excerpt: A careful introduction to circuit bending toy instruments: safety first, musical goals, and how odd timbres can inspire keyboard practice.

title: Clara Schumann: Pianist and Composer of the Nineteenth Century
excerpt: Clara Schumann (1819-1896) was a celebrated German pianist and composer. Learn about her training, her marriage to Robert Schumann, her compositions and her teaching.

title: Classical and Romantic Piano: Two Ways to Shape a Phrase
excerpt: Classical piano music often favours clear, balanced phrases, while Romantic music leans toward flexible timing and rich colour. A listener's guide.

title: Going to a Classical Concert: When to Clap
excerpt: Not sure when to applaud at your first classical concert? Between movements it is usual to stay quiet. Learn the common customs, how to follow the programme, and what changes by occasion.

title: Classical or Pop Songs for Kids Learning Piano? Mix Both
excerpt: Classical or pop does not have to be either-or. Classical pieces build reading and technique, while pop songs keep children motivated. Many teachers combine the two.

title: The Clavichord: A Quiet Keyboard That Can Vibrate
excerpt: How the clavichord makes a quiet tone with a tangent that stays on the string, why the finger can add vibrato, and what pianists can learn from it.

title: The Clavioline: A Small Keyboard That Coloured 1950s Pop
excerpt: The story of the clavioline, an early electronic keyboard that played one note at a time, and what its sound teaches about melody and tone.

title: Keep the Floor Around the Pedals Clear: Safe Feet Help Your Playing
excerpt: Keep the area around the piano pedals free of bags, slippers, cables and clutter. Obstacles can trip you or make you pull your foot back, affecting pedal timing and depth.

title: Clementi's Gradus ad Parnassum: One Hundred Pieces Published from 1817
excerpt: From 1817 Clementi published a large collection of piano studies, Gradus ad Parnassum. By 1826 all three volumes were out, with one hundred pieces: studies, fugues, canons and character pieces.

title: Clementi's Sonatina Op. 36 No. 1: Clear, Light Classical Style
excerpt: The first of Clementi's six sonatinas, Op. 36, is in C major with three short movements. Aim for clear, well-defined tone, steady rhythm, clear dynamic contrast and little pedal.

title: Closely Related Keys: Keys One Accidental Apart
excerpt: When a piece modulates, it most often goes to a closely related key: the relative major or minor, and keys with one more or one fewer sharp or flat. They share many notes, so the change sounds natural.

title: Closing the Lid After Home Practice: A Step That Protects the Action
excerpt: Closing the piano lid after home practice helps protect the action and the keys. Use a simple end-of-sitting routine, and leave repairs to a technician.

title: The Codetta: A Little Full Stop at the End of a Section
excerpt: A coda closes a whole piece, while a codetta is a shorter closing passage at the end of a section. In sonata form it secures the new key; in a fugue it links two entries of the subject.

title: Cohort-Based Adult Piano Courses: Learning Together on a Schedule
excerpt: In a cohort course, a group of adults starts and finishes together. Learn how to design one, set a realistic pace and build a supportive peer group.

title: The "C" in a Time Signature: It Is Not Short for "Common"
excerpt: Many scores open with a symbol like the letter C instead of 4/4. It means the same thing, but it comes from medieval notation, not from the word "common".

title: Common-Tone Modulation: Keep One Note, Change the Surroundings
excerpt: In a common-tone modulation, one note that works in both keys keeps sounding while the harmony around it is rewritten in the new key. Learn how to hear it and play it clearly.

title: Partnering With a Community Centre: Music Workshops Outside the Studio
excerpt: A workshop partnership with a community centre can take music teaching outside the studio. Learn what to agree on before the first session.

title: Case Study: How a Community Music Corner Gets Passersby to Sit Down and Play
excerpt: A public piano in a community centre or shopping mall lets passersby play a tune and gives nearby music schools a chance to meet new people. This article sets out the general approach.

title: Compound Intervals: What Ninths and Tenths Are All About
excerpt: An interval larger than an octave is a compound interval, such as a ninth or tenth. Think of it as an octave plus a simple interval, with the same quality as the simple one.

title: Compound Time on Piano: Feeling 9/8 and 12/8 in Groups of Three
excerpt: Compound metres group eighth notes in threes. Learn to feel 9/8 as three dotted beats and 12/8 as four, without rushing the inner notes.

title: Concerto Grosso: A Small Solo Group Against the Full Orchestra
excerpt: The concerto grosso, a favourite Baroque form, splits the orchestra into a small group of soloists and a full string orchestra that take turns. Corelli's Op. 6 set appeared in 1714.

title: Conducting Beat Patterns: How to Draw Two, Three and Four
excerpt: A conductor's hand traces patterns in the air that correspond to the beat. Learn the two, three and four beat patterns and why they help pianists feel the pulse and bar structure.

title: Conductus: Latin Songs in Matching Rhythm, 12th-13th Century
excerpt: The conductus was a Latin song of the 12th and 13th centuries. Unlike organum, its lowest voice was newly composed, and its voices often moved together in the same rhythm.

title: Consonant and Dissonant Intervals: Which Notes Sound Stable
excerpt: Some note pairs sound stable and blended, others tense. Learn which intervals are traditionally consonant or dissonant, and why dissonance is the source of tension in music.

title: A Content Calendar for a Music School: Planning Posts Around Terms
excerpt: A content calendar helps a music school plan posts, emails and videos around terms, recitals and holidays. How to build one that a small team can keep.

title: The Continuator: The AI That Learned to Improvise Back
excerpt: The Continuator listened to a player and answered in the same style. See how it worked and how to borrow its call-and-response idea at the piano.

title: Contrafactum: Old Melodies, New Words, from Medieval Times to Now
excerpt: A contrafactum keeps a song's melody and replaces its words. The practice goes back to the Middle Ages and the Reformation, and it is still everywhere in folk and pop music today.

title: Contrary Motion Scales: Mirror Practice for Both Hands
excerpt: In contrary motion the hands start on the same note and move apart like a mirror. Learn why it helps fingering and coordination, and how to practise it.

title: Convolution Reverb: Putting a Room Inside Software with Impulse Responses
excerpt: Convolution reverb records how a space responds to a short sound, then gives any sound the echo of that space. This article explains how it works and what it is used for in plain words.

title: 1944: Copland's Appalachian Spring and a Shaker Song
excerpt: In October 1944, Copland's ballet for Martha Graham premiered in Washington, later known as Appalachian Spring. One variation uses the Shaker song "Simple Gifts", and the work won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Music.

title: The Corelli Clash: Suspension and Resolution Overlapping at a Cadence
excerpt: In some Baroque cadences, a dissonance and its resolution briefly sound together, like a gentle bump before closing. Learn how to hear it and how to play it cleanly.

title: Team Music Workshops: A B2B Idea for Music Studios
excerpt: Short group music workshops for companies can open a new income stream for studios. Learn how to design, price and market them clearly and honestly.

title: Count-In and Click Track: Recording Piano Parts in Time
excerpt: A count-in and click track help you start a recording on time and stay steady. Learn how to set them up, choose a tempo and keep music natural.

title: Countermelody: The Second Tune Played Alongside the Melody
excerpt: Beside the melody everyone hums, choral and orchestral music often carries a second tune with its own shape and rhythm. On the piano, this countermelody often hides in the left hand.

title: Count Aloud First, Then Move the Pulse Inside
excerpt: Counting aloud helps piano learners lock in rhythm. Learn when spoken counting helps most, and how to fade it gradually into a steady inner pulse.

title: Counting Sixteenth Notes on Piano: One-e-and-a Made Simple
excerpt: Sixteenth notes divide each beat into four. Learn the one-e-and-a count, common rhythm patterns and practice steps that keep fast notes even.

title: Counting Ties That Cross the Barline at the Piano
excerpt: A tie that crosses the barline can hide the new bar's first beat. Learn to count through the tie and keep the pulse clear in the score.

title: 1716: Couperin Wrote a Book on How to Play the Harpsichord
excerpt: In 1716 François Couperin published a short book in Paris on playing the harpsichord: posture, hand position, fingering and ornaments, with several preludes included.

title: The Courante: The Second Dance in the Baroque Suite
excerpt: In Baroque keyboard suites the courante usually comes second, after the allemande. The French type is stately and shifts between three and two beats; the Italian corrente is light and flowing.

title: Courtesy Accidentals: Those "Unnecessary" Sharps and Flats
excerpt: Under the usual notation rules, an accidental lasts only until the end of the bar. Composers and editors often repeat a sign as a reminder, called a courtesy accidental, to prevent misreading.

title: The Crab Canon: One Melody Forwards, the Other Backwards
excerpt: A crab canon plays a melody forwards in one voice and the same melody backwards in another at the same time. Learn what it is, how it differs from an ordinary canon and how to practise it.

title: Crediting Arrangements on a Studio Recital Programme
excerpt: Credit arrangements clearly on a studio recital programme. Name the arranger, check what the programme should say, and keep the wording consistent.

title: How to Practise Crescendo and Diminuendo as a Smooth Slope
excerpt: Crescendo and diminuendo are gradual changes, not sudden jumps. This article uses a "slope" idea to plan volume, control arm weight and check the result with a recording.

title: Cristofori and the Early Piano: A Keyboard for Soft and Loud
excerpt: The piano is usually credited to the Italian instrument maker Bartolomeo Cristofori, who around 1700 in Florence built a hammer-struck keyboard that responded to the weight of touch.

title: Cross-Staff Notes: A Melody Moving from One Staff to Another
excerpt: Sometimes a beam or a stem stretches from the upper staff to the lower one. This is cross-staff notation, showing a line moving between registers, played by one hand or shared by two.

title: Crossing Hands at the Piano: A Calm Way to Practise
excerpt: When one hand must cross over or under the other, a slow map of the route, a free wrist and a clear landing point keep the motion calm.

title: Crowdfunding an Album: What Amanda Palmer's 2012 Campaign Showed
excerpt: In 2012 Amanda Palmer drew over a million US dollars in fan pledges for an album. How music crowdfunding works and how to plan a fair campaign.

title: Csárdás on Piano: Switching From Slow Lassú to Fast Friss
excerpt: Monti's Csárdás moves from slow lassú to fast friss. Learn how to prepare tempo changes on piano, keep control at speed and land the gear shift cleanly.

title: Cue Notes: What the Small Notes in a Score Mean
excerpt: Small notes printed among normal ones in an accompaniment or chamber part are usually cue notes: what another voice plays, shown to help you come in. Not every small note is a cue, though.

title: Mapping the Customer Journey of a Music Learning Product
excerpt: A customer journey map shows each step from first hearing about a music course to practising every week. Here is how to draw one and act on it.

title: Customer Support Replies for Music Apps: Warm, Short, Useful
excerpt: How a music learning app can write support replies that feel human: greet, answer, offer a next step and respect the user's privacy and time.

title: Cut Time on Piano: Feeling Two Beats in a Bar of Four
excerpt: Cut time, or alla breve, counts two half-note beats per bar instead of four quarter notes. Learn to read it, feel the pulse and keep fast pieces light.

title: Cyclic Form: One Theme Returning Across Several Movements
excerpt: In cyclic form, the same theme or motif returns in different movements of a multi-movement work and ties it together, as in Beethoven's Fifth and Ninth Symphonies and the works of Franck.

title: The Da Capo Aria: Make the Third Section Different
excerpt: The da capo aria, popular in Baroque opera and oratorio, has an ABA structure. When A returns, the singer improvises ornaments to show off skill and musical understanding.

title: DADABOTS and the Endless AI Livestream: Music That Never Stops
excerpt: DADABOTS trained neural networks on recordings and streamed the results nonstop on YouTube. How the project worked and what it says about AI music.

title: Five Minutes of Daily Sight Reading: Build Your New-Score Skills
excerpt: Sight reading means playing a score you have never seen. A simple way to improve is five minutes a day on much easier music, played once or twice before moving on, without stopping.

title: Danny Boy: The Melody of the Londonderry Air
excerpt: The melody of Danny Boy comes from a traditional Irish tune, the Londonderry Air, published in 1855. Weatherly's words were set to it in 1913. On the piano, keep its long phrases connected.

title: Daquin's Le Coucou: A Rondeau in E Minor from 1735
excerpt: In 1735 the French organist Daquin published his first book of harpsichord pieces, including Le Coucou, an E minor rondeau with flowing sixteenth notes and a falling third that imitates the cuckoo.

title: David Cope's EMI: Recombinant Music and Early AI Composition
excerpt: How David Cope's Experiments in Musical Intelligence recombined fragments of existing scores, and what pianists can learn from its patterns.

title: The Daxophone: Making Music From a Strip of Wood
excerpt: How the daxophone turns a bowed strip of wood into voice-like sounds, and what experimental instruments teach about listening and creativity.

title: The Day Before Your Lesson: Sort Out Questions, Don't Cram
excerpt: Instead of cramming the day before a lesson, play through the week's work, note what is solved and what is still stuck, and write down questions for your teacher.

title: Daytime Room Sharing: Music Studios and Co-Working Spaces
excerpt: An idea for small music studios: share quiet daytime hours with local co-working or community rooms, and the practical points to agree first.

title: Debussy's Children's Corner: Six Piano Pieces for His Daughter
excerpt: Children's Corner, finished by Debussy in 1908, is a suite of six piano pieces dedicated to his young daughter, with English titles describing toys, games and an imagined world.

title: How to Play Debussy’s Clair de Lune: A Four-Zone Practice Guide
excerpt: Learn Debussy’s Clair de lune in four zones: counting the 9/8 opening, soft blended chords, flowing arpeggios, pedalling and gentle rubato.

title: Debussy's The Sunken Cathedral: Bells Rising from the Sea
excerpt: Debussy's La cathédrale engloutie is the tenth prelude of Book 1, written in 1909 to 1910 and published in 1910. It comes from a Breton legend of a cathedral that rises from the sea in the morning mist and then sinks back.

title: Debussy's First Arabesque: The Flow of Three Against Two
excerpt: Debussy's Deux Arabesques were written between 1888 and 1891 and published in 1891. The first, in E major, flows in right-hand triplets against even left-hand eighth notes, a three-against-two rhythm.

title: Debussy's The Girl with the Flaxen Hair: A Gentle Prelude
excerpt: The Girl with the Flaxen Hair is the eighth prelude in Debussy's first book, written in 1909-1910 in G-flat major. It is short and tender, and a popular first taste of Debussy.

title: Debussy's La mer: Three Sketches Written Far from the Sea
excerpt: Debussy wrote La mer between 1903 and 1905, beginning it in inland Burgundy, far from the sea. It premiered in Paris in October 1905 to mixed reactions from audiences and critics.

title: Debussy's Rêverie: An Early Piece He Never Valued
excerpt: Rêverie is a gentle F major piano piece Debussy wrote around 1890. He thought little of it, yet it became popular after its publication in 1905.

title: The Deceptive Cadence on Piano: When the Dominant Avoids the Tonic
excerpt: A deceptive cadence moves from dominant to another chord, often vi. Learn the usual move, the part-writing traps, and how to hear the delayed close.

title: Delibes' Flower Duet from Lakmé: Two Parallel Melodies
excerpt: The Flower Duet comes from Act 1 of Delibes' opera Lakmé, premiered in Paris in 1883. Two voices, often a third or sixth apart, sing like two intertwined threads.

title: Delibes' Pizzicati: A Light Dance from the 1876 Ballet Sylvia
excerpt: Pizzicati is a piece from Léo Delibes' ballet Sylvia, which premiered in Paris in 1876. The strings are plucked with the fingers instead of bowed, giving a light, bouncing sound to match the dancer's nimble steps.

title: The Descending Fifths Chord Sequence: Roots Falling by Fifths
excerpt: In a descending fifths sequence, each chord root is a fifth lower than the last, for example in C major: C, F, Bdim, Em, Am, Dm, G, C. It sounds natural and flowing, and is heard in baroque, classical, jazz and pop.

title: Desirable Difficulties: Harder Practice, Longer Memory
excerpt: Playing well at home but badly on another piano is common. Robert Bjork's idea of desirable difficulties suggests that adding moderate variation and difficulty to practice can feel harder now but improve memory and adaptability in the long run.

title: Dett's Juba Dance: A Dance from the 1913 Suite In the Bottoms
excerpt: Juba Dance is a piano piece by the African American composer and pianist R. Nathaniel Dett, from his 1913 suite In the Bottoms. He writes the clapping and stamping tradition of the juba onto the piano as a bright, syncopated pulse.

title: Developing Variation: Letting a Motif Keep Growing
excerpt: Developing variation describes writing in which a small motif grows through continuous change instead of being repeated unchanged, each appearance carrying a trace of the last while moving somewhere new.

title: Diatonic and Chromatic Notes: Inside and Outside the Key
excerpt: In a key, the seven notes of its scale are diatonic notes, and notes outside the key are chromatic notes. Telling them apart helps you read melody and harmony more quickly.

title: Diffusion Models for Music: How AI Turns Noise Into Sound
excerpt: Diffusion models create audio by gradually removing noise, guided by a prompt. A plain guide to how they work and what they mean for musicians.

title: What Is a Digital Audio Workstation? Record, Edit and Mix
excerpt: A digital audio workstation is software for recording, editing and mixing. This article covers its basic parts, common uses, and how piano learners can use it to record their practice.

title: Digital Credits and Liner Notes: The Marketing Value of Names
excerpt: Why full song credits and modern liner notes help musicians get found, hired and trusted, and how to publish them clearly with every release.

title: Digital and Acoustic Piano Action: Why Keys Feel Heavy or Light
excerpt: Piano keys can feel heavy or light because of the action under the keys. Learn how acoustic and digital actions differ, and what a technician can adjust.

title: Checking Yourself with Your Digital Piano's Recorder
excerpt: Many digital pianos have a built-in recorder. Record a short passage, listen back, pick one or two things to improve, then record again and compare: a simple way to check your own playing.

title: Digital Piano Latency: Why Delay Breaks Timing Practice
excerpt: What latency means on a digital piano or keyboard setup, how to hear it, and practical steps to reduce delay so timing practice stays honest.

title: Polyphony on a Digital Piano: What the Voice Count Means
excerpt: Polyphony tells you how many notes a digital piano can sound at once. Here is what the voice count means, when it matters and how pedals use it up.

title: Split and Layer on a Digital Piano: Two Sounds from One Keyboard
excerpt: Split puts a different sound on each half of the keyboard, and layer stacks two sounds on every key. Here is how to use both, how to set them up and what to watch for when practising.

title: Digital Piano in a Storm or Power Cut: Switching Off, Unplugging, Restarting
excerpt: If a storm or power cut hits while you play, switch off and unplug first, then reconnect once the weather settles and power returns. Before restarting, check the volume knob and headphones, and afterwards check your sound and settings.

title: Using a USB Audio Interface With a Digital Piano
excerpt: Why a USB audio interface can improve digital-piano recording and practice monitoring, plus a simple setup checklist for home players.

title: Connecting a Digital Piano to a Computer: USB and MIDI Basics
excerpt: Many digital pianos have USB or MIDI ports for connecting to a computer or tablet. What travels over the cable is playing information, not sound. Check the manual first for the right cable and any driver you need.

title: Digital Piano in an Apartment: Volume and Neighbour Tips
excerpt: Lower the volume, use headphones, add a vibration pad and avoid early and late hours to keep a digital piano neighbour-friendly. Key and pedal thumps can still travel through floors.

title: Digital Skill Certificates for Music Learners: A New Course Product
excerpt: Digital skill certificates record specific music abilities a learner has shown. How studios and apps can design, verify and offer them responsibly.

title: Digital or Acoustic Piano as a First Instrument: What to Weigh
excerpt: Digital or acoustic first? Weigh your home, budget, practice times and goals. Digital pianos suit apartments and headphone practice; acoustic pianos reward those who value touch and tone.

title: Diminished Seventh Arpeggios: Symmetrical Chords of Minor Thirds
excerpt: A diminished seventh chord is built entirely from minor thirds, such as B, D, F, A♭, so it is perfectly symmetrical on the keyboard. Its tense sound made it a Romantic favourite.

title: Diminished Seventh Chords on Piano: Four Notes, Many Resolutions
excerpt: A diminished seventh chord stacks three minor thirds. Learn the shape, the enharmonic spellings, and how each note can resolve in a different direction.

title: Direct Modulation: Changing Key in One Step, No Pivot Chord
excerpt: Direct modulation skips the pivot chord: one phrase ends in the old key and the next begins in the new one, with no transition. The effect is bold and striking.

title: Direct-to-Fan Sale Days: What Fee-Free Fridays Taught Indie Music
excerpt: When a music store waived its fees on set days, fans rushed to buy directly from artists. What direct-to-fan sales teach musicians about loyalty.

title: Do-Re-Mi: A Song Built from Solfege Syllables
excerpt: Do-Re-Mi comes from the 1959 musical The Sound of Music, with music by Rodgers and lyrics by Hammerstein. In the show, the governess uses it to teach the children the solfege syllables, giving each one a memorable line.

title: Dolce, Cantabile, Grazioso: Reading Character Words on a Score
excerpt: What character words like dolce, cantabile, grazioso and espressivo ask from a pianist, and practical ways to turn each word into sound.

title: Domenico Scarlatti and His 555 Keyboard Sonatas
excerpt: Domenico Scarlatti (1685-1757) was born in Naples, the same year as Bach and Handel. He spent the second half of his life mainly on the Iberian Peninsula and left about 555 keyboard sonatas, mostly short one-movement pieces.

title: The Dominant Ninth Chord: Adding Another Third to V7
excerpt: Stack one more third on a dominant seventh chord and add A, and you get a dominant ninth. The extra ninth gives richer colour and more tension, and the chord is common in Romantic, jazz and pop music.

title: Dominant Seventh Arpeggios: Practising the Four-Note Broken Chord
excerpt: A dominant seventh has four notes, such as G, B, D, F in C major. Played one after another across octaves, they form the arpeggio, which has a different hand shape and fingering from a triad arpeggio.

title: How the Dominant Seventh Chord Resolves to the Tonic
excerpt: The V7 chord wants to go home to the tonic. Two notes matter: the leading note rises a semitone and the seventh falls a semitone, which makes V7 to I sound smooth and natural.

title: Dominant Thirteenth Chords on Piano: Colour Tones Without the Clutter
excerpt: A dominant thirteenth adds the sixth above the root on a dominant seventh. Learn which notes to keep, which to drop, and how the chord resolves.

title: The Dorian Mode on Piano: Minor With a Brighter Sixth
excerpt: The Dorian mode is a minor scale with a raised sixth step. Find it on the white keys, compare it with natural minor and improvise with it.

title: Dotted Rhythms on Piano: Counting the Long-Short Pattern Precisely
excerpt: Dotted rhythms pair a long note with a short one, and many learners blur them. Learn what the dot means, how to count it and drills for crisp rhythm.

title: Double-Dotted Notes: Two Dots Make a Note Even Longer
excerpt: A single dot adds half a note's value; a double dot adds half, then half of that again. A double-dotted crotchet equals seven semiquavers, and is usually followed by a very short note.

title: The Double Escapement of 1821: Making Fast Repeated Notes Possible
excerpt: In 1821 a French piano workshop patented a "double escapement" action. A key now only had to rise part of the way to sound the same note again, which made fast repeated notes and trills far easier. Modern grand piano actions still use the principle.

title: The Double Exposition: Two Openings in a Classical Concerto
excerpt: In a classical concerto's first movement, the orchestra states the main material first, then the soloist joins and states it again, often with new or more brilliant passages. The two expositions are not a simple repeat.

title: Double Sharps and Double Flats: Raised Twice, Lowered Twice
excerpt: The double sharp, written like a small "×", raises a note by two semitones, a whole tone. The double flat, written as two flats, lowers it by two semitones. F double sharp sounds as G, and B double flat as A.

title: Double Sharps and Double Flats: When a Note Moves Twice
excerpt: A double sharp raises a note by two semitones and a double flat lowers it by two; here is how to read the signs and find the keys.

title: Double Thirds: Legato Practice with Two Fingers Moving Together
excerpt: Double thirds means playing two notes a third apart in one hand, group after group. Practise each line separately, then slowly together with at least one voice legato, keeping the hand relaxed.

title: Double Thirds on Piano: Fingering Two Notes a Third Apart
excerpt: Double thirds ask two fingers to play a pair of notes a third apart, often in a scale. Learn a calm fingering method and a slow way to join the pairs.

title: Dowland's Lachrimae: Seven Pavans of Tears, Published in 1604
excerpt: John Dowland's song "Flow, My Tears" opens with a falling melody that sounds like tears. In 1604 he used it for seven solemn pavans in Lachrimae, scored for five viols and a lute.

title: Draw the Phrase: Feel a Melody's Rise and Fall with a Line
excerpt: Drawing a line above the music that follows a melody's contour is a simple way to understand phrase shape. Draw first, then play, and your fingers will know where the phrase starts, peaks and ends.

title: Drop-2 Voicings on Piano: Opening Up Close Chords
excerpt: A drop-2 voicing lowers the second-highest note of a close chord by an octave. Learn how to build these open, warm shapes and use them in progressions.

title: Drum Machines: How Programmed Rhythm Changed Music
excerpt: How drum machines grew from simple rhythm boxes into programmable grooves, and what their steady patterns can teach pianists about time and feel.

title: Wipe the Keys Before You Practise: A Dry-Cloth Habit
excerpt: Before practising, wipe the keys gently from back to front with a clean, dry, soft cloth. It takes seconds, clears dust and skin oil, and helps you switch into practice mode.

title: Dual Coding: Memorise Music Better with Words and Images
excerpt: Psychologist Allan Paivio's dual coding theory says information stored as both words and images is easier to recall. This article turns it into five concrete ways to memorise piano music.

title: Duplets in Compound Time: Two Even Notes in a Beat of Three
excerpt: In compound time such as 6/8, a duplet fits two even notes into a beat that normally holds three quavers. It is marked with a "2" and is the mirror image of the triplet.

title: The Double-Keyboard Piano: An Invention That Made Octaves Easier
excerpt: In the early twentieth century a double-keyboard piano appeared with an upper manual an octave above the lower, making wide stretches easier. This article covers its design, strengths and weaknesses, and what it teaches us today.

title: Dust Covers and Keyboard Care in a Piano Studio
excerpt: Dust covers and simple keyboard care help a studio piano stay ready for lessons. Cover the keys when the room is idle, and keep liquids off the instrument.

title: Dvořák's Humoresque: The Light Dotted Rhythm in G-flat Major
excerpt: Dvořák's Humoresque is a familiar piano piece with a bouncy dotted rhythm. It is the seventh of the eight Humoresques, Op. 101, written in the summer of 1894 and set in G-flat major.

title: December 1893: Dvořák's New World Symphony Premieres in New York
excerpt: In 1892 the Czech composer Dvořák came to New York to direct a conservatory. There he wrote his Ninth Symphony, "From the New World", which premiered on 16 December 1893 to a warm welcome.

title: Dvořák's Slavonic Dances, Op. 46: Eight Piano Duets from 1878
excerpt: Dvořák's Slavonic Dances, Op. 46, are a set of eight dances written in 1878, first as piano duets and the same year as an orchestral version. Brahms recommended him to a publisher, and the success of the set carried Dvořák's name across Europe.

title: A Dynamics Ladder for Beginners: Soft, Medium and Loud
excerpt: Beginners can explore volume with a three-step ladder from soft to loud. A simple way to practise dynamics on piano with listening and good control.

title: How to Practise the E♭ Major Scale: Three Flats and Fingering
excerpt: E♭ major has three flats. This article covers the key signature, common fingering and how the hands work together, to help you play this scale steadily.

title: Ear Training Starts with Echo Games: Listen, Sing, Find Intervals
excerpt: How do you start ear training? Use "listen, sing, find" echo exercises in three stages, then learn common intervals from the major second to the perfect octave, with a one-week plan.

title: Train Your Ears with Melodies from Everyday Life: Hum, Then Find the Notes
excerpt: Songs on the radio, music from a street vendor's cart and TV theme tunes all make good ear-training material. Hum the melody, decide whether it goes up or down, then find each note on the piano and try it in a different key.

title: Ear Training for Beginners: High and Low First, Then Long and Short
excerpt: Ear training is a foundation of learning music. Starting with the simplest ideas, high and low and long and short, this article offers a few games to play at home that help beginners sharpen their ears step by step.

title: Warm Up Your Ears Before Practice: Sing and Hear Today's Key
excerpt: Finger warm-ups ready the hands, and the ears need preparing too. Spend two or three minutes before practice singing the opening, playing the tonic and tonic chord, and hearing the tempo and tone in your head.

title: The Forgetting Curve and Practice: Why Spaced Review Sticks Better
excerpt: Forgetting a well-practised piece within days is common among adult learners. The forgetting curve shows that forgetting is fastest right after learning, so spacing reviews apart often works better than one long session.

title: Echo Dynamics: Play a Phrase Loud, Then Soft When It Repeats
excerpt: When a short phrase is repeated, play the first time louder and the second softer, like an echo in a valley. Bach even titled the last movement of his 1735 French Overture "Echo".

title: The Ecossaise on Piano: A Light, Quick Dance in Two Beats
excerpt: An ecossaise is a light, quick piano dance in two beats. Learn the usual metre, the bright character, and a method that keeps the pulse steady.

title: "Edelweiss": A Waltz-Time Song from the 1959 Musical
excerpt: "Edelweiss" was written by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein for the 1959 Broadway musical The Sound of Music. Many people think it is an Austrian folk song, but it was written for the stage.

title: Elbows Slightly Away from the Body: Give Your Arms Room to Move
excerpt: Elbow position is often overlooked at the piano. Keeping the elbows slightly away from the body, with a little space between arm and body, lets the arms move freely from side to side.

title: The Electric Piano Story: Tines, Reeds and a New Keyboard Voice
excerpt: Electric pianos used struck metal tines or reeds and pickups to create a new sound. Learn how they worked and why their tone still shapes music today.

title: The Electric Piano: How Tines and Reeds Make Its Tone
excerpt: How classic electric pianos use hammers, metal tines or reeds and pickups to make a warm, bell-like tone, and how to play that sound well today.

title: Electronic Tuning Devices: How Piano Tuners Use Technology
excerpt: How electronic tuning devices and apps help piano tuners measure pitch, account for string stretch and keep records, and why the trained ear still matters.

title: 11th and 13th Chords: Stacking Higher Than the Seventh Chord
excerpt: Keep stacking thirds above a seventh chord and you get 9th, 11th and 13th chords. These extensions are common in jazz and pop, and in practice some notes are usually left out.

title: Elgar's Enigma Variations: Friends Hidden in the Music
excerpt: One evening in October 1898 Elgar improvised a melody at the piano, and his wife Alice liked it. He turned it into a theme and fourteen variations, each portraying a friend: the Enigma Variations, premiered in London in 1899.

title: Elgar's Salut d'Amour: An Engagement Gift from 1888
excerpt: Elgar wrote Salut d'Amour in 1888 as an engagement gift for his fiancée Caroline Alice Roberts. Published in 1889 under a French title, it exists in versions for solo piano, violin and piano, and more.

title: Ellmenreich's Spinning Song: A Fast Repeated Figure from Student Albums
excerpt: Ellmenreich's Spinning Song (Spinnlied) is a nineteenth-century piano piece found in many student albums. Its light, even repeated figures in the right hand are excellent for practising relaxed, clear touch.

title: Email Newsletters for Music Studios: Useful Updates People Open
excerpt: A simple monthly email can keep music students and families informed and engaged. Learn what to include, how often to send and how to respect consent.

title: Empfindsamer Stil: C.P.E. Bach and His 1753 Keyboard Treatise
excerpt: The "sensitive style" (empfindsamer Stil) was a mid-eighteenth-century North German style of delicate, sincere and changeable feeling. Its leading figure was C.P.E. Bach, who published his keyboard treatise in 1753.

title: Ending a Piano Practice Session on a Calm, Good Note
excerpt: How you finish a practice session shapes how you feel next time. Try a simple three-step closing routine that leaves you calm and ready to return.

title: End Your Practice Session with Music You Play Well
excerpt: How a practice session ends often shapes how you feel the next time you sit down to play. Save the last few minutes for music you play well, and you will look forward to next time.

title: Same Piano Key, Different Note Name: Enharmonic Equivalents
excerpt: Understand enharmonic equivalents, compare C-sharp with D-flat, and learn why musical notation uses different names for the same piano key.

title: Enharmonic Modulation: Same Chord, New Spelling, Distant Key
excerpt: On the piano, F♯ and G♭ are the same key, so a chord can be respelled and heard anew. This is enharmonic modulation, and it can carry the music to a distant key.

title: Enharmonic Notes on Piano: Same Key, Different Names
excerpt: F-sharp and G-flat are the same piano key with different names. Learn why spelling matters, how keys and chords decide the name, and how to read faster.

title: Equal Temperament and Older Tunings: Why Keys Once Sounded Different
excerpt: Modern pianos use equal temperament, but earlier keyboards used tunings that gave each key its own colour. Learn how they differ and why it matters.

title: Erquan Yingyue: Abing's Erhu Piece and Its Piano Arrangements
excerpt: Erquan Yingyue is an erhu solo by Wuxi folk musician Hua Yanjun, known as Abing, recorded in 1950. Its deep, gentle melody now lives on in piano arrangements too.

title: Escape Tones: Step Away, Then Leap to a Chord Tone
excerpt: An escape tone (échappée) is a non-chord tone that steps away from a chord tone, then leaps the other way to the next chord tone. Knowing it explains some "extra" notes in a melody.

title: Collecting Student Testimonials with Consent and Care
excerpt: Testimonials help families trust a music studio, but they must be honest and collected with consent. A practical, privacy-aware process for teachers.

title: Piano Études: Short Pieces That Train One Skill
excerpt: An étude is a short piece built around one technical idea. Learn what études are for and how to practise them in a calm, musical way.

title: Evaded Cadences on Piano: Delaying a Close So the Phrase Can Continue
excerpt: An evaded cadence starts like a close, then slips aside so the phrase can continue. Learn how it differs from a deceptive cadence and how to play it.

title: Piano Exam Day: A Checklist to Run Through Before You Leave
excerpt: On piano exam day, small details can affect your mood as much as the pieces. A checklist helps: entry details, music, clothes, water and an early start. Always follow the exam board's official notice.

title: In Your Piano Exam, Think About the Music, Not the Examiner
excerpt: If you keep wondering how the examiner will mark you, your attention drifts from the music and mistakes become more likely. Focus on phrasing, steady tempo and clear sound instead.

excerpt: A made-up example of how a piano teacher might fit a lesson plan on one card: warm-up, focus skill, new piece and a home note. A format to adapt.

excerpt: An illustrative scenario of a small music studio creating a bursary for families who need help with lesson fees, with fair rules and privacy.

title: Example Scenario: Refreshing a Studio Brand Without Losing Recognition
excerpt: An illustrative scenario of a music studio updating its dated logo, colours and tone to look modern while keeping what loyal families recognise.

title: Explain Your Piece to Your Family: If You Can Say It, You Can Play It
excerpt: Before playing a piece for family or friends, spend two or three minutes explaining it to them: its sections, its climax, its key changes and its mood. Explaining forces you to understand the piece, and it makes memorising more secure.

title: Explainable AI Feedback for Piano Learners: Showing the Why
excerpt: Practice tools that explain their feedback help learners improve and trust the result. Learn what explainable feedback looks like and why it matters.

title: Expressionism in Music: Pierrot Lunaire (1912) and Intense Inner Feeling
excerpt: Expressionism was an early twentieth-century movement in Germany and Austria that sought to express intense inner emotion directly. In music it is tied to Schoenberg, Berg and Webern, with sharp harmonies and leaping melodies.

title: Fado Listening Guide: Portugal's Song of Longing
excerpt: A listening guide to fado: saudade, the Portuguese guitar, flexible rhythm and how pianists can borrow its expressive, speech-like phrasing.

title: Running a Fair Studio Waitlist: Clear Rules for Music Teachers
excerpt: When a studio is full, a clear waitlist keeps families informed and treats them fairly. Learn how to set rules, communicate and offer interim options.

title: Falla's Ritual Fire Dance: A Midnight Dance from a 1915 Stage Work
excerpt: In 1915 Manuel de Falla staged El amor brujo in Madrid. Its Ritual Fire Dance has a heroine dancing round a fire at midnight, with a repeating bass figure and trills like flickering flames.

title: Family Music Games Everyone Can Play
excerpt: Simple music games at home, such as name that tune, find the key and rhythm echo, make learning the piano more fun and train listening, rhythm and reaction. No special props are needed.

title: Family Lesson Plans: Bundles for Siblings and Parent-Child Learners
excerpt: Many families have several members who want to learn music. This article explains how music schools can design family lesson bundles, covering structure, pricing communication, scheduling and fairness.

title: Family Music Time: Small Habits for Singing and Playing Together
excerpt: A weekly family music time lets children and adults enjoy music together. This article shares simple activity ideas and things to keep in mind. The content is general information.

title: Fan-Voted Setlists: Letting the Audience Shape a Concert
excerpt: When fans vote on part of a setlist, they arrive invested in the show. How musicians and music schools can run setlist votes that stay fair and fun.

title: Fanny Hensel and Das Jahr, Her 1841 Piano Cycle
excerpt: Fanny Hensel (1805-1847), sister of Felix Mendelssohn, completed the piano cycle Das Jahr in 1841: twelve pieces for the twelve months, plus a postlude. Most of her music went unpublished in her lifetime.

title: The Fantasia: A Keyboard Genre as Free as Improvisation
excerpt: The fantasia has no fixed form, and its tempo, key and mood can change at any moment, so it often sounds like improvisation. Bach, Mozart and Schubert all wrote famous examples.

title: Short-Burst Practice for Fast Passages: Play a Small Group, Then Stop
excerpt: Split a fast passage into small groups, play each group in a quick burst near target tempo, then stop on the next note to relax. Join the groups up gradually until the whole passage flows.

title: Fauré's Après un rêve, Op. 7 No. 1: Dream and Waking in a French Song
excerpt: Après un rêve is an early art song by Gabriel Fauré, Op. 7 No. 1, written in the late 1870s. A dreamer meets a loved one, wakes alone and calls the dream back, over gentle piano chords.

title: Fauré's Dolly Suite: Piano Duets Written for a Little Girl in the 1890s
excerpt: Fauré's Dolly Suite, Op. 56, is a set of six piano duets written between about 1893 and 1896 and published in 1897. "Dolly" was the nickname of a friend's little daughter, who received a new piece each birthday or New Year.

title: Fauré's Pavane: A Slow Processional Dance from 1887
excerpt: In 1887 Fauré wrote Pavane, Op. 50, in F♯ minor. Plucked strings open it, and a flute plays an elegant, slightly wistful melody above, like a procession walking slowly. In 1888 he added an optional chorus.

title: Fauxbourdon: Writing Two Parts and Singing Three in the 15th Century
excerpt: Fauxbourdon was a fifteenth-century church music technique: only two parts were written, a chant melody above and a lower part moving in parallel sixths, while singers improvised a middle part a fourth below the top, giving parallel 6-3 chords.

title: The Fenaroli Schema: A Little Loop Where Bass and Melody Swap Places
excerpt: The Fenaroli schema is named after the Neapolitan teacher Fedele Fenaroli and was identified by modern scholars of eighteenth-century galant style. Melody (4-3-7-1) and bass (7-1-2-3) move in opposite directions, usually twice.

title: Fengyang Flower Drum: Drumbeats and Song in an Anhui Folk Tune
excerpt: "Let's talk of Fengyang" opens the Anhui folk song Fengyang Flower Drum. On the piano, let the left hand play clear "drumbeats" and the right hand sing the bouncy melody.

title: Meeting a Fermata: How Long to Hold Depends on the Music
excerpt: A fermata, drawn over a note or rest like a half-open eye, lets it last longer than written. How long depends on the tempo and mood of the piece; in slow pieces the hold is often more relaxed.

title: What Is Figured Bass? Reading the Little Numbers in Baroque Scores
excerpt: Baroque scores often put numbers such as 6, 7 and 4-3 under the bass to tell keyboard players which harmonies to play. Learn to read them and try a simple accompaniment exercise.

title: Figured Bass on Piano: Reading the Numbers Under a Bass Line
excerpt: Figured bass writes numbers under a bass line to show which intervals to add. Learn common figures and how to realise them clearly on the piano.

title: Piano in Film Scores: Telling a Story with a Single Motif
excerpt: Many film scores run a simple piano motif through the whole film. See how a motif changes with the story, and turn a short melody into different moods in three steps.

title: Finding a Comfortable Key for the Singer
excerpt: When you accompany a singer, the written key may be too high or too low for them. Ask them to sing the top and bottom lines, then move the key until singing feels easy.

title: Find a Song's Key by Ear
excerpt: To play a song you have heard, first work out its key, even without sheet music. Find the final note, judge major or minor by feel, then check with the scale on the piano.

title: Find the Centre First: Steady One Core Thing at a Time
excerpt: Potters first centre the clay on the wheel, and shaping gets easier. Practice works the same way: steady the core rhythm and hand shape first, then add speed and expression step by step.

title: Stubborn Fingers? Five Finger Independence Drills
excerpt: Finger independence means one finger plays while the rest relax. Here are five drills, a weekly plan and the most common mistakes to avoid.

title: Finger Independence on Piano: Held-Note Drills That Stay Calm
excerpt: How to train finger independence on piano with held-note drills: keep one finger quiet, move its neighbours, and build control without forcing speed.

title: Legato Without the Pedal: Passing the Note Between Fingers
excerpt: Finger legato connects one note smoothly to the next using the fingers alone. The key is the handover: no gap between notes, and no long overlap either.

title: Finger Numbers on Piano: How to Read the Tiny Digits
excerpt: The small numbers above or below notes tell you which finger to use. Learn the numbering system and how good fingering helps you play evenly.

title: Finger Pad vs Fingertip: Changing Tone with Different Parts of the Finger
excerpt: The same note sounds a little different played with the fingertip or the finger pad. The fingertip tends to sound crisp and focused, the pad soft and rounded.

title: Finger Pedaling: Connecting Sounds Without the Pedal
excerpt: Finger pedaling means holding some notes down longer than written so they keep sounding, giving a pedal-like connection. It is especially useful in Baroque and Classical works.

title: Finger Substitution on Piano: Keep Legato Lines Truly Connected
excerpt: Changing fingers on a held key lets you keep a melody connected when fingering runs out. When to use finger substitution and how to practise it.

title: How Long Should Your Fingernails Be for Piano?
excerpt: For piano, trim your nails so they do not touch the keys when the finger pad meets the key. Check weekly, cut them short and file the edges smooth.

title: Collapsing Fingertip Joints: How to Keep Your Fingers Standing Firm on the Keys
excerpt: When the first joint of a fingertip folds inward, the tone turns thin and speed stalls. This article explains common causes and offers a step-by-step fix, from single fingers to full phrases.

title: First and Second Endings: Taking the Right Repeat Path
excerpt: Bracketed first and second endings tell you which bars to play the first time through a repeat, and which bars to play the second time.

title: The First Piano Lesson After Switching Teachers
excerpt: Changing piano teachers can feel unsettling. What teachers and families can do so the first lesson with someone new feels safe, clear and welcoming.

title: The First Read and the Practised Run: Two Different Jobs at the Piano
excerpt: A first read and a practised run are different jobs at the piano. Learn how to keep the first meeting honest, and how to use a later run as a clear check.

title: First and Second Endings: Don't Get Lost in the Repeat Maze
