excerpt: First and second endings are common repeat markings. Play the first ending, return to the repeat start, then skip it the second time and go straight to the second ending. Mark your route in the score.

title: First-Species Counterpoint: Writing Note Against Note on Piano
excerpt: First-species counterpoint pairs one note against one note over a fixed melody. Learn the core intervals, motion types and how to try it at the piano.

title: Learning the Sustain Pedal: Steady Hands First, Then Add the Foot
excerpt: When first learning the sustain pedal, get your hands steady first, then add the foot. Change the pedal after the new chord is played: key down, pedal up, pedal down again at once. Practise hands and feet separately, then together.

title: First-Week Orientation for New Piano Learners and Families
excerpt: A first-week orientation helps new piano learners and families start well. Cover the room, the practice plan, and how to bring scores and questions.

title: Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk: A Guzheng Classic's Evening Return
excerpt: Fishing Boats Sing at Dusk is a widely loved guzheng piece picturing boats returning full at sunset as fishermen sing. It begins in a lilting slow tempo, speeds up, and ends in joyful celebration.

title: Four Against Five: Four Notes in One Hand, Five in the Other
excerpt: Four against five divides one span of time into four in one hand and five in the other, meeting only at the start of each group. Make each hand even first, then layer them.

title: 5/4 Time: The Asymmetrical Pulse of Five Beats to a Bar
excerpt: 5/4 has five quarter notes per bar, usually felt as three plus two or two plus three. It gives a slightly lopsided, forward-driving pulse, unlike the evenness of 4/4.

title: Five Minutes at the Piano After a Busy Day: A Quiet Time for Yourself
excerpt: Too tired to practise a whole piece after work? Try a relaxed five-minute routine of slow scales, long chords and a familiar tune to make playing a quiet part of your day.

title: A Five-Minute Quiet Listening Break in a Busy Day
excerpt: A short listening break with one calm piece of music can be a pleasant pause in a busy day. General ideas for choosing music and keeping the habit simple.

title: A Five-Minute Sight-Reading Routine for Every Piano Lesson
excerpt: Short, regular sight-reading in each lesson builds fluent readers. A five-minute routine teachers can use, with material ideas and feedback tips.

title: The Five Common Types of Seventh Chords at a Glance
excerpt: How major seventh, dominant seventh, minor seventh, half-diminished and diminished seventh chords are built, how they sound and how to find them on the piano.

title: Fix the First Mistake First: Solve Problems One at a Time
excerpt: A piece often has several trouble spots, and playing straight through just repeats the errors. Find the first mistake, fix it, then move on to the next, since later errors can stem from earlier ones.

title: Fixed Do vs Movable Do: Is Do Always C, or Does It Follow the Key?
excerpt: Solfège syllables can be used in two ways. In fixed Do, Do is always C. In movable Do, Do follows the key: C in C major, G in G major. Each method has its own strengths.

title: Flamenco Compás on Piano: Feeling the Twelve-Beat Cycle
excerpt: Flamenco compás groups twelve beats with accents on 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Learn to count it, clap it and play the Andalusian cadence on piano.

title: Flight of the Bumblebee: A Fast Chromatic Run From a Fairy-Tale Opera
excerpt: Flight of the Bumblebee is by the Russian composer Rimsky-Korsakov, first an orchestral interlude in an opera of 1899-1900. Fast chromatic scales imitate the buzzing of the bee, and many virtuoso arrangements followed.

title: Florence Price: A Symphony Found in an Old House
excerpt: In 1933 the Chicago Symphony Orchestra premiered Price's Symphony in E minor, and in 2009 manuscripts resurfaced in an old house. Her story and what it offers piano learners.

title: FM Synthesis Explained: The Bell-Like Keys of 1980s Pop
excerpt: What FM synthesis is, how carriers and modulators create bright bell-like tones, and why the sound shaped 1980s electric piano parts.

title: How to Adjust Your Piano Practice During Exam Week
excerpt: In the week of a big school exam, shorten your practice to ten or fifteen focused minutes of familiar pieces, then ease back to your usual routine afterwards.

title: folk-rnn: What an AI Folk Tune Generator Teaches Pianists
excerpt: folk-rnn learned tens of thousands of folk tunes written in ABC notation. Its output reveals the AABB patterns that make tunes easy to learn at the piano.

title: Fonte and Monte: Falling and Rising Sequences in 18th-Century Music
excerpt: In the mid-18th century a German theorist gave vivid names to common progressions: Fonte ("fountain") steps down, Monte ("mountain") climbs up. Both are everywhere in Haydn and Mozart.

title: Tapping Your Foot While Playing: When It Helps and When to Stop
excerpt: Foot tapping can help you feel a steady beat when learning rhythms or playing groovy music, but it causes problems with the pedal, in free-tempo music and in formal performance.

title: What to Wear on Your Feet for Piano: Getting the Feel of the Pedal
excerpt: Pedalling needs a clear feel for how far the pedal is down, so thin-soled, flat, close-fitting shoes or bare socks work best. Thick soles, heels, slippers and boots dull the feel.

title: Forearm Rotation on Piano: Tremolos and Broken Octaves Without Strain
excerpt: Small forearm rotations let the arm help the fingers in tremolos, broken octaves and Alberti figures. A clear step-by-step guide for learners.

title: The Fortepiano and the Modern Piano: One Family, Different Sounds
excerpt: The modern piano and the instrument played in the 18th and early 19th centuries belong to one family but differ clearly in sound and touch. Early fortepianos had lighter hammers, thinner strings, quicker decay and often a narrower range.

title: Fortspinnung: How Baroque Phrases Spin a Motif Forward
excerpt: In many Baroque works a short motif is spun on and on, the same figure moved higher or lower or slightly altered, yet always sounding as if it is moving forward. This writing is often called Fortspinnung, or spinning out.

title: Four Against Three: Four Notes in One Hand, Three in the Other
excerpt: After three against two, four against three can tie your fingers in knots. One hand plays four even notes while the other plays three, and they align only at the start. Splitting it into twelve small cells makes it less mysterious.

title: Four-Chord Songs on Piano: Play Pop Hits with I–V–vi–IV
excerpt: Learn the I–V–vi–IV four-chord progression on piano, four accompaniment patterns from easy to groovy, and how to turn it into a song of your own.

title: Rushing in Piano Duets? Agree on the Tempo Before You Start
excerpt: Rushing in four-hand duets usually means the two players hear different tempos. Agree on a speed, count a bar in together, and let the melody player lead while the other listens.

title: Four Kinds of Musical Memory: Memorise Piano Pieces More Securely
excerpt: Aural, visual, kinaesthetic and analytical memory support each other. How to build all four so a memorised piano piece holds up under pressure.

title: Melody Notes on Fingers 4 and 5: Give the Outer Fingers Support
excerpt: When the right-hand melody falls on fingers 4 and 5, let the palm and arm support them: tilt the hand slightly outward so the weight reaches the outer fingers and the melody sings.

title: fp and rfz: Loud Then Soft, and a Sudden Push
excerpt: Besides f and p, scores use fp (loud, then immediately soft) and rfz (rinforzando, a sudden reinforcement). Both are about emphasis, but they work differently at the piano.

title: 435 Hz: A Reference Pitch Used in 19th-Century France
excerpt: In the mid-19th century France fixed a reference pitch at 435 Hz, giving orchestras, theatres and instrument makers a shared point of reference. It was neither the first such standard nor the last.

title: The French Overture: Dotted Rhythms and a Quick Fugue
excerpt: The French overture is a Baroque form with a slow, stately opening full of dotted rhythms, followed by a faster, fugue-like section.

title: Fugue Basics: Subject, Answer and Countersubject Explained
excerpt: A fugue builds a piece from one short theme that enters in several voices. Learn what subject, answer and countersubject mean and how to follow them.

title: Funiculì, Funiculà: The Song Written for a Vesuvius Cable Car
excerpt: Funiculì, Funiculà is a cheerful Neapolitan song of 1880 written to celebrate the first funicular on Mount Vesuvius, later quoted by Richard Strauss.

title: Playing the Opening of Für Elise: The Alternating Hands
excerpt: Beethoven's Für Elise opens with a melody rocking between E and D♯, then alternating arpeggios in both hands. Here is how to play those first bars.

title: The Opening of Für Elise: A Rocking Pair of Notes
excerpt: The opening of Für Elise rocks between two neighbouring notes before the melody opens out. A calm guide to the pattern, the hands and slow practice.

title: The Furiant: A Czech Dance Where Twos and Threes Interlock
excerpt: The furiant is a rhythmic device linked to Czech folk dances, in which the stresses seem to switch between groups of two and three within a short span.

title: Furusato (1914): A Triple-Time Song of Homesickness from Japan
excerpt: Furusato entered a Japanese sixth-grade singing textbook in 1914, with words by Tatsuyuki Takano and music by Teiichi Okano. It is a gentle triple-time song using only five notes.

title: Species Counterpoint: Fux's Five Steps of 1725
excerpt: Species counterpoint, a classic way to learn counterpoint, comes from Fux's Latin treatise of 1725. It builds from note against note to florid counterpoint in five steps, and Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven studied it.

title: The Galliard: A Leaping Triple-Time Dance of the Renaissance
excerpt: The galliard was a lively triple-time dance of sixteenth-century Europe, full of leaps, often paired with the slow duple-time pavane. Arbeau's 1589 manual describes its steps.

title: Gamelan Sounds on Piano: Exploring Slendro and Pelog Colours
excerpt: An introduction to gamelan music from Java and Bali, its slendro and pelog scales, interlocking parts, and how pianists can explore its colours.

title: Streaks, Levels and Badges: Using Gamification in Piano Practice
excerpt: How streaks, levels and badges can keep piano practice going, where they backfire, and how to set up game-like goals that build real skill.

title: The Gavotte on Piano: A Courtly Dance That Starts Mid-Bar
excerpt: The gavotte is a moderate Baroque dance that begins halfway through the bar. Learn its rhythm, its place in suites and how to play it with poise.

title: Generated Sight-Reading Exercises: Endless New Music to Read
excerpt: Software can generate fresh sight-reading exercises matched to a learner's level. How generators work, what makes a good exercise and their limits.

title: Generative Accompaniment: How Software Plays Along With You
excerpt: Generative accompaniment that follows a pianist: MIDI or audio input, practice formats, and how to keep musical control.

title: Evolving Melodies: Genetic Algorithms in Music Composition
excerpt: Genetic algorithms breed and mutate melodies over many generations, keeping the fittest. Learn how they work and why judging music is the hard part.

title: Music and Winding Down at Night: A Gentle Listening Habit
excerpt: Listening to quiet music before bed is a small habit for many people. This article shares general listening practices on choosing pieces, volume, timing and surroundings, and is not medical advice.

title: Rhapsody in Blue: What Piano Learners Can Borrow From Gershwin
excerpt: Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue mixed jazz rhythm with concert form in 1924. Learn its story and practise syncopation, blue notes and its lyrical theme.

title: Ginastera's Danza de la moza donosa: Danzas argentinas No. 2
excerpt: The slow, singing middle dance of Alberto Ginastera's Danzas argentinas, Op. 2 (1937): a long melody and slightly bitter harmony, played as one complete phrase.

title: Give the Piece a Story: Using Images to Shape Your Playing
excerpt: When the notes are right but the expression is missing, invent a simple story or picture for the piece, and let it guide your tone, tempo and dynamics.

title: Glenn Gould and His 1955 Goldberg Variations Recording
excerpt: In June 1955 the 22-year-old Canadian pianist Glenn Gould recorded Bach's Goldberg Variations in New York, and the 1956 release made a great impression.

title: The Glissando: Sliding Your Fingers Across the Keys
excerpt: A glissando, often abbreviated gliss., is a quick slide from one note to another across all the white or black keys in between. Mind your hand angle and force.

title: Golden Snake Dance: Nie Er's 1934 Folk Ensemble Piece
excerpt: Golden Snake Dance is a lively folk ensemble piece that Nie Er arranged in 1934 from the folk tune Dao Ba Ban, with a middle section of ever-shortening phrases.

title: Gongche Notation: Old Chinese Music Written in Characters
excerpt: Gongche notation is a traditional Chinese system that writes pitches with characters such as He, Si, Shang, Chi and Gong, with beats marked by ban and yan.

title: Gospel Piano Basics: Passing Chords, Fills and Call-and-Response
excerpt: A listening and playing guide to gospel piano: call-and-response, passing chords, right-hand fills and the rhythmic drive behind the style.

title: Gossec's Gavotte: A Little Dance from an 1786 Opera
excerpt: Gossec's Gavotte, familiar to many young violin and piano students, comes from his 1786 opera Rosine, which is hardly ever staged today.

title: Gounod's Funeral March of a Marionette: A Humorous Piece of 1872
excerpt: Gounod's Funeral March of a Marionette is a humorous piano piece of 1872 in D minor, with a stiff, swaying rhythm like a puppet's walk, later orchestrated in 1879.

title: Before Your Grade Exam, Fix the Hand Shape for Every Scale
excerpt: Before a grade exam, rather than simply speeding up your scales, first settle the hand shape and fingering for each key. It gives you a familiar routine to lean on when nerves strike.

title: Granados' Andaluza: No. 5 of the Twelve Spanish Dances
excerpt: Andaluza, also known as Playera, is the fifth of Enrique Granados' Twelve Spanish Dances for piano. It is a minor-key piece with a singing melody over a gently swaying accompaniment.

title: Granados' Goyescas: The 1911 Piano Suite Born from Paintings
excerpt: Goyescas is a piano suite Enrique Granados completed in 1911, inspired by the paintings of Goya. Its best-known piece, The Maiden and the Nightingale, ends with a nightingale-like cadenza, and the music later became an opera premiered in New York in 1916.

title: The Grand Staff Brace: Why Two Staves Are Read Together
excerpt: The grand staff joins a treble staff and a bass staff with a brace. The top line is usually played by the right hand and the bottom by the left, and notes lined up vertically sound together.

title: The Grand Staff: How Two Clefs Make One Page of Piano Music
excerpt: Piano music uses two staves joined by a brace. This guide shows how the treble and bass clefs share middle C and how to read across the page.

title: Grandma's Penghu Bay: Sea and Sunshine in a 1979 Campus Folk Song
excerpt: Grandma's Penghu Bay, written by Ye Jiaxiu and first sung by Pan Anbang in 1979, is a classic of Taiwan's campus folk era. Its bright, lilting tune suits the piano well for practising light rhythms and broken-chord accompaniment.

title: Granular Synthesis: Cutting Sound into Grains and Recombining It
excerpt: Granular synthesis slices a sound into many tiny fragments, then rearranges, layers and reshapes them to create cloud-like textures. This article explains the idea with everyday analogies, the main parameters and how it is used in music.

title: Graphic Notation: When the Five-Line Staff Is Not Enough
excerpt: When the sound a composer wants cannot be written accurately in notes and beats, lines, shapes and timelines can be used instead. This article covers common graphic symbols, how to read them and how to play with them in class.

title: Green Tours: How the Live Music Industry Can Lighten Its Footprint
excerpt: Large tours need a lot of transport, power and materials. This article looks at environmental ideas in energy, transport, stage materials and audience involvement, and what small music events can do too.

title: Greensleeves: The Minor-Key Melody of an Old English Folk Song
excerpt: Greensleeves is a traditional English song first recorded in the late 16th century and mentioned by Shakespeare. Its minor-key melody sways gently in triple time or 6/8.

title: Gregorian Chant: One Ancient Melody and the First Neumes
excerpt: Gregorian chant is the Latin liturgical singing of the Western church: a single melody, no harmony, no fixed beat. Scholars think most chants took shape in the 8th and 9th centuries.

title: Grieg's Lyric Pieces Begin with Arietta, Op. 12 No. 1
excerpt: Grieg wrote 66 Lyric Pieces in 10 books between 1867 and 1901. Book 1 (Op. 12) opens with Arietta in E-flat major, and the last book brings its melody back as a waltz.

title: Grieg's Morning Mood: The Sunrise Music from Peer Gynt
excerpt: Grieg's Morning Mood opens with a flute phrase answered by an oboe, as if the sun were slowly rising. Written for Ibsen's Peer Gynt and premiered in 1876, it became the first piece of Suite No. 1.

title: Grieg's Notturno, Op. 54 No. 4: Birdsong on a Nordic Summer Night
excerpt: Grieg's Notturno is the fourth piece of Lyric Pieces Book 5, Op. 54, published in 1891. In C major, it pairs a gentle melody with trills that are often heard as night birds.

title: Summer 1868: Twenty-Four-Year-Old Grieg Writes His A Minor Piano Concerto
excerpt: In the summer of 1868, Grieg wrote his Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16, in the Danish countryside at the age of twenty-four. It premiered in Copenhagen the following spring to great success.

title: Grieg's To Spring: No. 6 of the Lyric Pieces, Op. 43
excerpt: To Spring is the sixth of Edvard Grieg's Lyric Pieces, Op. 43. Short but bright, it has an open right-hand melody over a flowing left hand, capturing the feeling of spring arriving.

title: Grieg's Wedding Day at Troldhaugen: A Piece for a Silver Wedding
excerpt: In June 1892, Grieg and his wife Nina marked their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary, and he wrote a piano piece for it: Wedding Day at Troldhaugen, Op. 65 No. 6. It moves from a cheerful arrival of guests to a tender middle section.

title: Voice Models and Consent: Grimes and the Open AI Voice Experiment
excerpt: In 2023 Grimes invited fans to release songs using an AI model of her voice and share earnings. What the experiment shows about consent and credit.

title: Fast Runs in Groups of Four: Breaking a Long String into Chunks
excerpt: A long run of fast sixteenth notes is easy to get lost in. Grouping them in fours, with a slightly clearer first note in each group, turns the run into small chunks that hands and mind can handle.

title: Managing a Piano Group Class: Keep Every Student Busy
excerpt: Piano group classes have many students at different levels, so they can easily become chaotic. This article shares ways to plan seating, turns, tiered tasks and the pace of the lesson.

title: Guide-Tone Lines on Piano: Thirds and Sevenths That Connect
excerpt: Guide tones are the thirds and sevenths that define each chord. Learn to trace them through progressions to voice chords smoothly and improvise.

title: The Habanera Rhythm on Piano: Dotted Bass and a Swaying Pulse
excerpt: How the habanera rhythm works on piano: the dotted left-hand pattern, how to count it, how to balance the melody and simple ways to practise it.

title: The Half Cadence Is Like a Question: A Phrase Ending on the Dominant
excerpt: A half cadence is a phrase that ends on the dominant chord. It sounds like a question, not fully finished, and leaves you waiting for the answer that follows.

title: Half-Diminished Chords on Piano: The m7-flat-5 Sound
excerpt: A half-diminished chord is a diminished triad plus a minor seventh. Learn the m7-flat-5 shape, where it sits in a key, and how to resolve it cleanly.

title: Half Pedal: Press Only Part Way for a Less Full Sound
excerpt: Half pedalling means pressing the sustain pedal only part of the way down, so the dampers lift just slightly from the strings. The sound lingers a little without keeping every note, which helps in fast runs and thick bass passages.

title: Half Steps and Whole Steps: The Shortest Distance on the Keyboard
excerpt: On the piano keyboard, the distance between two neighbouring keys is a half step, and two half steps make a whole step. Understanding them is the basis for scales, key signatures and chords.

title: Once a Week, Play the Whole Piece at Half Tempo
excerpt: Once a week, play a well-learned piece from start to finish at about half speed. Slowing down reveals problems that speed hides, and stops the piece from getting faster and messier.

title: Half-Time Feel: Why a Groove Can Feel Slower at the Same Tempo
excerpt: What half-time and double-time feel mean, how drums and bass create them without changing tempo, and how to play both feels on the piano.

title: Handel and Bach: Born in 1685, Yet They Never Met
excerpt: Handel and Bach were both born in 1685 in central Germany, but took very different paths: Handel to Italy and London, Bach staying in Germany. Bach twice tried to meet Handel and never did.

title: Handel's Harmonious Blacksmith: A Later Name and Five Variations
excerpt: The last movement of Handel's Suite in E major, published in London in 1720, is a theme with five variations. Its famous nickname and the blacksmith story both came long after his death.

title: 1742: Handel's Messiah Premieres in Dublin
excerpt: Handel's oratorio Messiah was first performed not in London but in Dublin, on 13 April 1742, at a charity concert so crowded that ladies were asked to leave their hoops at home and gentlemen their swords.

title: Handel's Sarabande in D Minor, HWV 437: A Stately Slow Triple Metre
excerpt: The sarabande from Handel's Suite in D minor, HWV 437, has a solemn melody and rich harmony. This guide covers what makes a sarabande and how to play it on the piano.

title: Hands-Free Practice: Voice Commands and Foot Controls at the Piano
excerpt: Voice commands and foot controls let pianists start a metronome, turn pages or replay a passage without lifting their hands. How these tools work.

title: After a Mistake, Put Your Hands on Your Knees: A Simple Reset
excerpt: When mistakes pile up and you start rushing, stop, rest your hands on your knees and count slowly to five. This simple reset breaks the cycle of tension and helps you restart with a clear idea.

title: Hands Separately, Then Together: Combining Hands in a New Piece
excerpt: Practising each hand alone, then combining them in small steps, builds secure pieces. Learn when to separate the hands and how to put them back together.

title: Hands Separately, Then Together: A Clear Practice Order
excerpt: Practising each hand alone before combining them makes new piano pieces calmer. Follow this step-by-step order to bring both hands together smoothly.

title: Hanon's The Virtuoso Pianist: 60 Exercises from 1873
excerpt: French piano teacher Charles-Louis Hanon published The Virtuoso Pianist in 1873, with 60 finger exercises meant to build independence, strength and evenness.

title: Happy Birthday on Piano: Three Arrangement Levels That Grow
excerpt: How to play Happy Birthday on piano in three levels: melody alone, simple left-hand chords, then a fuller accompaniment you can use at real celebrations.

title: Haptic Metronomes for Piano: Feeling the Beat on Skin
excerpt: How haptic metronomes help piano practice: wrist or clip pulse, quieter rooms, and steady time without a loud click.

title: Harmonic and Melodic Intervals: Together or One After the Other
excerpt: The distance between two notes is an interval. Played together it is harmonic; played one after the other it is melodic. Same name, but they sound different.

title: Harmonic Minor on Piano: The Raised Seventh and Its Pull
excerpt: How the harmonic minor scale works on piano: why the seventh is raised, how the V chord gains pull, and simple drills to use the colour in melodies.

title: Harmonic Reduction: Turn a Complex Passage into a Few Chords
excerpt: Dense passages often rest on just a few simple chords. Harmonic reduction, playing each beat or bar as a block chord, makes reading and memorising easier.

title: Harmonic Rhythm: How Often Do the Chords Change?
excerpt: Harmonic rhythm is how quickly the chords change. It differs from melodic rhythm, and noticing it helps you understand a piece, use the pedal and accompany well.

title: What Is the Harmonic Series? The Many Notes Hidden in One Note
excerpt: A single note is really many overtones layered together. This article uses what you can hear at the piano to explain the harmonic series, how it relates to tone colour, and how to discover it by ear.

title: The Harmonium: A Hand-Pumped Reed Keyboard Explained
excerpt: How the harmonium uses bellows and free reeds to make a sustained keyboard tone, and what it teaches pianists about breath, phrasing and drones.

title: Harmonise a Melody Yourself: Try It with Three Chords
excerpt: You do not need much theory to add chords to a familiar melody. Start with the three main chords of a key, such as C, F and G in C major, and let your ear decide which one fits.

title: How the Harpsichord Makes Sound: Plucked Strings vs Struck Strings
excerpt: The harpsichord sounds by plucking its strings with plectra, while the piano strikes them with hammers. This article compares how the two keyboard instruments make sound and what that means for touch and tone.

title: From Harpsichord to Piano: How Keyboards Learned Soft and Loud
excerpt: How Cristofori turned the plucked harpsichord into the hammer-driven piano around 1700, and what that history means when you play Bach today.

title: Haydn's Farewell Symphony: Musicians Snuff Out Their Candles and Leave
excerpt: In 1772 Haydn wrote a symphony in F sharp minor whose final movement has the players stop one by one, snuff out their candles and walk off, until only two violinists remain.

title: Haydn's Gypsy Rondo: The Finale of a 1795 London Piano Trio
excerpt: Haydn published a set of piano trios in 1795 during his second stay in London. The finale of the G major trio, marked in the Hungarian style, became known as the Gypsy Rondo.

title: Haydn's Surprise Symphony: One Loud Chord in London, 1792
excerpt: Haydn's Symphony No. 94, the Surprise, premiered in London on 23 March 1792. A sudden loud chord after a quiet melody in the second movement gave it its name.

title: Haydn's The Creation: The 1798 Oratorio and Its Moment of Light
excerpt: The Creation is an oratorio by Haydn, written between 1796 and 1798 and premiered in Vienna in 1798. Its famous moment is the loud C major chord at the word light.

title: Hazel Scott: The Pianist Who Played Classical and Jazz Together
excerpt: Hazel Scott was a pianist known for blending classical and jazz. In 1950 she hosted a television show under her own name, often giving classical pieces a swing rhythm.

title: He Luting's Shepherd Boy's Piccolo: A Chinese-Flavoured Piano Piece from 1934
excerpt: Shepherd Boy's Piccolo is a piano piece composed in 1934 by the Chinese composer He Luting. It won the top prize in a competition for Chinese-style piano music started by Alexander Tcherepnin in Shanghai.

title: Headphone Piano Practice: Silent Systems in Shared Spaces
excerpt: How silent piano systems and headphone outputs let you practise without filling a room, what the sensors capture, and what the ear still has to check.

title: Hearing the Four Triads: Telling Major, Minor, Diminished and Augmented Apart
excerpt: Major, minor, diminished and augmented triads each have their own sound colour. With vivid images, piano comparisons and a daily listening game, this article helps you tell the four triads apart by ear.

title: Listen to the Original Song Before You Play the Piano Arrangement
excerpt: Many piano pieces are arrangements of songs, symphonies or film scores. Listening to the original first shows you the melody, accompaniment, tempo and mood, so your playing carries the right flavour.

title: Follow the Bass: Training Your Ear to Hear Root Movement
excerpt: Learn to recognise rising, falling and repeated bass notes through short listening exercises that build chord awareness.

title: Heiligenstadt, 1802: The Long Letter Beethoven Wrote
excerpt: In the summer of 1802, a thirty-one-year-old Beethoven lived in Heiligenstadt, near Vienna, afraid of losing his hearing. That October he wrote a long letter to his brothers, never sent, now called the Heiligenstadt Testament.

title: Hemiola in Piano Repertoire: Three Beats in the Time of Two
excerpt: A hemiola places three beats in the time of two. Find the grouping in a piano score, count it aloud, and practise the bars so the new pulse is audible.

title: Hemiola on Piano: When Three Beats Feel Like Two
excerpt: A hemiola briefly makes two groups of three beats feel like three groups of two. Learn how to hear it, count it and play it steadily on piano.

title: Hemiola Explained: When Two Bars of Three Feel Like Three of Two
excerpt: Hemiola regroups beats so two bars of triple time sound like three bars of duple time. Learn to hear it, count it and play it cleanly on piano.

title: Heterophony: Different Versions of One Melody at Once
excerpt: In heterophony, several players perform the same melody at the same time, each with a slightly different version. It is common in Chinese folk ensembles and many other traditions.

title: High Mountains, Flowing Water: The Story of Boya and Zhong Ziqi
excerpt: High Mountains, Flowing Water comes from an ancient story of the zither player Boya and his listener Zhong Ziqi, which gave Chinese the word for a kindred spirit.

title: Hildegard of Bingen: Songs by a 12th-Century Abbess
excerpt: Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179) was a German nun and abbess who wrote poetry, theology and more than seventy monophonic chants, plus the musical morality play Ordo Virtutum.

title: What Is Hocket? Two Players Share One Melody
excerpt: In hocket, a melody is split into pieces that different players perform in turn. This article covers where it comes from and offers relay exercises for piano families and classes.

title: A Relaxed Holiday Plan for Piano Practice
excerpt: School holidays bring more free time, but routines can slip. Make a relaxed practice plan with your child: a fixed daily slot, one or two goals, and days left free for trips and rest.

title: Holiday Music Marketing: Warm Ideas for New Year and Seasonal Events
excerpt: How a music school can market itself over New Year and the holidays: themed concerts, parent-child activities, gift lessons and warm content, without heavy promotion, so the brand stays sincere.

title: Holst's The Planets: Musical Portraits of Seven Planets
excerpt: Between 1914 and 1916 the English composer Holst wrote the orchestral suite The Planets, seven movements from Mars to Neptune, each portraying a planet's character. His inspiration came from astrology, not astronomy.

title: Home on the Range: A Pioneer Folk Song from 1870s Kansas
excerpt: Home on the Range is an American Western folk song. Its words come from a poem by the Kansas pioneer Brewster Higley, set to music by his friend Daniel Kelley in the 1870s. It became the Kansas state song in 1947.

title: Caring for a Piano at Home: Humidity, Dust and Clean Keys
excerpt: A piano stays in tune longer and plays better with simple care. Learn how humidity, placement and cleaning affect it, and what to leave to a technician.

title: Home Piano Recording With Contact Mics: Clear Tone, Less Room
excerpt: How contact microphones help home piano recording, where to place them carefully, and how learners can review tone without capturing every room noise.

title: Home! Sweet Home!: A Song From an 1823 Opera
excerpt: "Home! Sweet Home!" comes from the opera Clari, first staged in London in 1823, with music by Henry Bishop and words by John Howard Payne. It sings of a simple home that no palace can match.

title: Homework and Piano Practice: Order and Time Blocks
excerpt: Children often do not know whether to do homework or practise first. A practical way is to divide the afternoon into time blocks, keep a roughly fixed routine and protect one uninterrupted block for practice.

title: Honest Claims in Music Education Ads: A Plain-Language Checklist
excerpt: Music education ads earn trust when every claim is specific, provable and kind. A practical checklist for copy, visuals, offers and learner stories.

title: Honest Trial Lessons: What a First Piano Session Should Show
excerpt: A trial lesson helps a family and teacher decide whether they fit. Learn how to plan an honest first session and follow up without pressure.

title: Horn Fifths: A Special Kind of Part-Writing in Classical Style
excerpt: Horn fifths are a two-part motion common in the Classical period: they sound like parallel fifths but were accepted in the style. They come from the limits of the natural horn and are not a licence for parallel fifths.

title: The Hornpipe: A British Dance From 3/2 Time to the Sailors' Dance
excerpt: The hornpipe is a British dance named after an old reed instrument. In the 17th and 18th centuries it was often in 3/2 time with syncopation; later it became a lively sailors' dance in duple or quadruple time.

title: House Concerts for Piano Students: Music in a Living Room
excerpt: A house concert brings a small audience into a home to hear students play. Learn how to plan one, choose a programme and make guests feel welcome.

title: How Fans Find Concerts: Follow Buttons, Tour Alerts and Local Reach
excerpt: Concert-alert services tell fans when an artist they follow plays nearby. How tour discovery works and how musicians can fill rooms with it.

title: How Long Until You See Progress at Piano? Look for the Visible Signs
excerpt: There is no fixed timetable for piano progress. Instead of expecting big changes quickly, watch the small things: faster note reading, a smoother tricky spot, a more relaxed posture and hand shape.

title: How Music Recommendation Works: From Listening Habits to Playlists
excerpt: Recommendation systems learn from what millions of people play and skip. See the main methods, their blind spots and what musicians can learn from them.

title: How Researchers Evaluate AI-Generated Music
excerpt: Judging AI-made music is hard. See how researchers mix listening tests, statistics and expert reviews, and what each method can and cannot show.

title: How to Listen to Piano Recordings: Listen with One Question in Mind
excerpt: Listening to fine piano recordings is a great supplement to lessons, but as background music it gives little. Listen with one specific question each time, then compare with the score or your own playing.

title: Before You Play, Sing the First Phrase in Your Head
excerpt: Many pieces start unsteadily because the hands move before the mind has decided on tempo and sound. Sing the first phrase in your head first, then place your hands on the keys.

title: Humanizing MIDI: Timing and Velocity That Sound Played
excerpt: Why perfectly quantised MIDI can sound stiff, how small timing and velocity changes add life, and what this teaches about expressive piano playing.

title: Practising in Humid Rainy Weather: Caring for Piano, Music and Hands
excerpt: In the humid rainy season the piano, the sheet music and your playing hands are all affected. A hygrometer, moderate dehumidifying, dry storage for scores and dry hands make practice smoother.

title: The Humoresque: Wit, Whimsy and Mood Swings at the Piano
excerpt: A humoresque is a character piece with changing moods, from playful to tender. Learn what the title meant to composers and how to play its contrasts.

title: The Hungarian Minor Scale: A Minor With Raised 4th and 7th
excerpt: The Hungarian minor scale is a seven-note scale made by raising both the fourth and seventh degrees of the natural minor. This creates a sharp, colourful augmented second in the middle of the scale.

title: The Hurdy-Gurdy: A Wheel, a Keyboard and a Constant Drone
excerpt: How the hurdy-gurdy uses a cranked wheel, wooden keys and drone strings, and what its sound teaches keyboard players about drones and rhythm.

title: Hybrid Lesson Models: Blending App Practice and Studio Time
excerpt: A hybrid model combines guided practice at home with time in a studio or live lesson. Explore how music businesses can design and explain it clearly.

title: Hybrid Lesson Models: Combining Studio Visits With App Practice
excerpt: Hybrid models mix in-person music lessons with app-guided practice between visits. How studios can design, price and explain them clearly.

title: The Hydraulis: How an Ancient Water Organ Shaped the Keyboard
excerpt: The hydraulis used water pressure to steady the air in its pipes. Meet the ancient invention that gave the world one of its first keyboards.

title: Hypermeter: Bars Grouped Into a Larger Beat
excerpt: Just as a bar has strong and weak beats, groups of bars can feel strong or weak too. This is called hypermeter. The most common grouping is four bars, as in Beethoven's Ninth Symphony scherzo.

title: The Idée Fixe: The Leading Melody of Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique
excerpt: The idée fixe is the melody that returns throughout Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique of 1830, changing character in each movement. It stands for the beloved person the work tells of, and recalls the later leitmotif.

title: The ii–V–I Progression on Piano: A Clear Beginner Guide
excerpt: What the ii–V–I progression is, why it sounds like coming home, and a step-by-step way to play it on piano in C and then in all 12 keys.

title: The Illiac Suite: The 1957 Computer Score That Started AI Music
excerpt: In 1957 Lejaren Hiller and Leonard Isaacson used the ILLIAC I computer to compose a string quartet. The story and what it teaches about musical rules.

title: Imagine a Listener While You Practise: Give the Music Direction
excerpt: Picture a specific listener while you practise, such as a family member or friend, and your playing gains direction. Music goes from getting the notes right to saying what you mean, and expression usually follows.

title: Imagine an Orchestra at the Piano: Find an Instrument for Each Voice
excerpt: The piano can play melody, bass and harmony at once, like a small orchestra. Imagining which instrument plays each voice helps you find richer tone colours and clearer layers.

title: Imitating Nature's Sounds on the Piano: Simple Improvisation
excerpt: Imitating rain, birdsong, wind or waves on the piano is a simple and fun improvisation exercise. No score is needed: listen to the sounds around you, then try to express them on the keys.

title: "If... Then...": Plan Daily Practice with Implementation Intentions
excerpt: A goal like "I will practise every day" often fails through tiredness or distraction. Implementation intentions link the goal to a specific situation, written as "If..., then...".

title: Impressionism in Music: A Name Borrowed from an 1874 Art Show
excerpt: The name "Impressionism" began in painting: in 1874 a critic seeing Monet's Impression, Sunrise mocked the painters as "Impressionists". The word was later borrowed for the music of Debussy and Ravel.

title: The Impromptu: Piano Pieces That Sound Spoken, Not Planned
excerpt: An impromptu is a piano piece that sounds spoken or improvised, yet is usually written with a clear shape. Learn what to listen for in practice.

title: Improvise an Ending with the IV, V and I Chords
excerpt: A simple, reliable way to end an improvisation is to play the IV, V and I chords, which are F, G and C in C major, and land your right-hand melody on C.

title: Writing Down a Mood Through Improvisation
excerpt: When a feeling is hard to put into words, a few notes on the piano can express it. A general introduction to improvising your mood, with points to keep in mind. For reference only.

title: Start Improvising with Just Two Chords
excerpt: You don't need a complicated chord progression to improvise. Loop Am and G in your left hand, play short phrases on the white keys with your right, and build from two or three notes.

title: Making Variations on a Familiar Tune
excerpt: Variation is a classic musical device. Take a familiar nursery tune and change one thing each time, such as the rhythm, the passing notes or the key, so the theme stays recognisable.

title: How to Use IMSLP for Piano: Find, Choose and Practise Free Scores
excerpt: A practical IMSLP guide for pianists: check copyright for your country, choose the right edition, make old scans readable and plan your practice.

title: Indian Raga: More Than a Scale, with Set Paths and Moods
excerpt: The raga is a core idea of Indian classical music. It is more than a scale: it sets the notes, the paths up and down, the emphasised notes, typical phrases and a mood, often tied to a time of day or season.

title: Sing the Phrase First: Inner Hearing Before You Play
excerpt: Singing a short phrase before you play it trains inner hearing. A simple habit for beginners and returning adult players who want to hear music first.

title: Inquiry Replies for Music Studios: Fast, Clear Answers to New Messages
excerpt: A short inquiry reply helps a music studio answer new messages clearly. Learn a simple structure for timing, fees, and next steps.

title: Bundling Instruments, Lessons and Apps: When Packages Help Buyers
excerpt: Bundles can make starting music easier, or more confusing. How music sellers and studios can design honest packages that buyers understand.

title: Instrument Rental Trial Periods: Lowering the Bar for Parents
excerpt: When a child is just starting piano, parents often hesitate to buy an instrument straight away. This article looks at how rental trial periods work as a business design, and what shops and families should each watch for.

title: The Intermezzo on Piano: A Character Piece Between Larger Works
excerpt: An intermezzo is often a short character piece that can stand on its own. Learn what to listen for, how to shape a modest form, and how to keep the mood.

title: Learn Intervals from Song Openings: A Handy Ear-Training Trick
excerpt: The distance between two notes is an interval. A practical way to recognise intervals by ear is to link each one to a familiar song and remember the first two notes of that song.

title: Interval Inversion: The Numbers Always Add Up to Nine
excerpt: To invert an interval, move the lower note up an octave or the upper note down. The two numbers always add up to nine, and the quality swaps: major becomes minor, augmented becomes diminished, perfect stays perfect.

title: Interval Quality: Major, Minor, Perfect, Augmented, Diminished
excerpt: An interval has two parts: its number and its quality. The number counts note names, the quality counts semitones. Perfect, major, minor, augmented and diminished are explained here with examples from C.

title: Reading Music by Interval: Read Faster Without Naming Every Note
excerpt: Naming every note is slow. Reading by interval means judging whether notes move by step, skip or repeat, so your eyes read direction and distance.

title: Interval Homework: Link Each Interval to a Familiar Melody
excerpt: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in numbers, such as C to E being a third. When doing interval homework, play and sing each interval so your ear remembers its sound.

title: Upper Pedal Point: A Sustained Note in a Higher Voice
excerpt: A pedal point is usually pictured in the bass, but the held note can also sit in a high or middle voice while the chords change beneath it. This is the upper, or inverted, pedal point.

title: Invertible Counterpoint at the Piano: Two Lines That Can Swap Places
excerpt: Invertible counterpoint lets two piano lines swap places and still make sense. Learn each line alone, practise the swap, and keep both parts audible.

title: Isorhythm: The Medieval Trick of Repeating Patterns
excerpt: Isorhythm repeats a rhythm pattern and a pitch pattern of different lengths so they shift against each other. See how it works and try it at the piano.

title: Italian at the Top of the Score: Piano Tempo Terms Explained
excerpt: What do Largo, Adagio, Andante, Allegro and Presto mean? Tempo terms from slow to fast, modifiers such as molto and poco, and markings such as rit. and a tempo, all in one place.

title: Italian Tempo Words: Allegro, Andante and Friends
excerpt: Allegro, andante, adagio: what common Italian tempo words mean in plain English, how they relate to a metronome, and how to use them when practising.

title: Janáček's On an Overgrown Path: A Set of Memories Published in 1911
excerpt: On an Overgrown Path is a set of piano pieces by the Czech composer Leoš Janáček. The first book has ten pieces, published in 1911, recalling his Moravian homeland and the daughter he lost in 1903.

title: Jasmine Flower: Four Pentatonic Left-Hand Accompaniment Layers
excerpt: For Jasmine Flower, use fewer triads and more open fifths and seconds. Using the C major pentatonic scale, four layers build from sustained open fifths to bass lines.

title: Origins of Jianpu: French Number Notation to Chinese School Songs
excerpt: Jianpu writes notes as the numbers 1 to 7. It was not invented in China: Rousseau proposed number notation in Paris in 1742, and French teachers later turned it into a singing method.

title: Jianzipu: Guqin Notation That Shows How to Play, Not Which Note
excerpt: Jianzipu is notation made just for the guqin. Its symbols are simplified Chinese characters that record the playing technique rather than the pitch, and it is said to have been compiled in the Tang dynasty.

title: Jingle Bells: A Bright, Rhythmic Winter Song for Beginners
excerpt: Jingle Bells was written by James Lord Pierpont and first published in 1857. Its lively rhythm, catchy tune and plenty of repeated notes in the chorus make it a good piece for beginners.

title: Cage's 4'33": The Famous Silent Premiere of 1952
excerpt: On 29 August 1952 in Woodstock, New York, David Tudor premiered John Cage's 4'33" without playing a note. The piece made many people rethink what music and silence really are.

title: John Field's Nocturnes: A New Kind of Piano Piece, Published in 1812
excerpt: Dublin-born John Field (1782-1837) published the first piano pieces called nocturnes in 1812: a singing right-hand melody over wide broken chords in the left hand, with the pedal.

title: Joplin's The Easy Winners: A Ragtime Piece from 1901
excerpt: The Easy Winners is a ragtime piano piece Scott Joplin published in 1901: a steady left-hand pulse under a syncopated right-hand melody, with an unhurried, confident character.

title: Joplin's Solace: A Slower Ragtime Piece from 1909
excerpt: Solace, published by Scott Joplin in 1909 with the subtitle "A Mexican Serenade", is slower than his quick, bouncy rags, with a more singing melody and a gently swaying accompaniment.

title: Joplin's The Entertainer: A Ragtime Piece from 1902
excerpt: The Entertainer is a ragtime piano piece published by Scott Joplin in 1902, in 2/4 time with a bouncing left hand and a syncopated right-hand melody. A 1970s film made it famous again.

title: Josquin des Prez, the Renaissance "Master of the Notes"
excerpt: Josquin des Prez, born in what is now northern France and Belgium, worked for years in Italy and wrote masses and motets. In 1502 a Venetian printer published a book of his masses alone.

title: Just Intonation: Pure Intervals from Simple Frequency Ratios
excerpt: Just intonation sets pitches with simple whole-number frequency ratios, so its chords sound very pure, with almost no beating. But instruments tuned this way are hard to transpose.

title: Kabalevsky's 30 Pieces for Children, Op. 27
excerpt: Op. 27 is a set of thirty short piano pieces written by Dmitry Kabalevsky in 1937-38. Each piece practises one technique or expresses one mood, and the lively Toccatina is a favourite with young pianists.

title: Kalimba and Mbira: Thumb Pianos for Keyboard Players
excerpt: What kalimba and mbira are, how their metal tines and zig-zag note layout work, and what a pianist can learn from playing a thumb piano.

title: Playing "Kangding Love Song" on Piano: The Hill Where Horses Run
excerpt: "Kangding Love Song" comes from Kangding in Sichuan and has a bright, relaxed, playful tune. At the piano, the key is to catch its light step and the speech-like feel of a folk song.

title: Katyusha: The 1938 Soviet Song of the Girl on the Riverbank
excerpt: Katyusha is a Soviet song of 1938 by Matvey Blanter and Mikhail Isakovsky, about a girl singing on a blossoming riverbank and thinking of her sweetheart far away. Its melody is bright yet touched with sadness.

title: Keep a Reference Recordings List for Every Piece
excerpt: Listening to recordings helps you learn a new piece, but picking any version at random can confuse you. Choose two or three good ones for each piece, note who plays them, and keep listening to those.

title: When Your Child Loses Interest in Piano, Change How Practice Starts
excerpt: When a child loses interest in piano, try changing how practice begins, with a favourite piece or one very small task, so they feel "I did it" as soon as they sit down.

title: Wrong Note in a Performance? Let the Music Keep Going
excerpt: Playing a wrong note or missing a beat in a performance or exam is common. The best response is to keep the music moving, and to practise "carrying on after a mistake" and mark places where you can rejoin.

title: Stop at Every Wrong Note? Practise Playing Straight Through
excerpt: Starting over after every mistake makes the opening of a piece ever more familiar and the ending ever shakier. This article explains how to practise "not stopping" and when to use it.

title: Always Have One Piece Ready to Play: Keep a "Reserve Piece"
excerpt: When a friend says "play something" or guests want to hear the piano, learners often find their current pieces unfinished and old ones forgotten. Keeping one well-learned piece ready solves this.

title: Keep Your Piano Out of Direct Sunlight: Placement Basics
excerpt: Many families put the piano by a window, but long hours of direct sun can heat the wood, fade the finish and affect the strings. A little attention to where the sun falls keeps a piano in better condition.

title: Practising Under a Fan: Keeping Your Score from Blowing About
excerpt: Music pages that flip or lift in the breeze of a fan or air conditioner are a common nuisance. Clips, fan direction, and transparent sleeves can all keep the score steady so your attention stays on the music.

title: Sheet Music Curling or Creased? Simple Ways to Protect Your Scores
excerpt: Curled, creased or loose pages make it hard to find your place and turn pages. Storing scores flat, taping page corners and using binders keeps them flat and easy to read on the music stand.

title: Key Changes in Songs: How Modulation Lifts the Music
excerpt: A key change moves a song to a new tonal centre. Learn the common types of modulation, how to hear them and how to play them smoothly on piano.

title: Silent Key Presses: Feeling the Depth of the Keys
excerpt: Silent key presses mean pressing a key slowly to the bottom without making a sound, or only a very quiet one. It helps you feel the key's travel and resistance and find where the sound begins.

title: Key Signature Changes Mid-Piece: Prepare at the Double Barline
excerpt: When the key signature changes mid-piece, the new one is written after a double barline. Marking it in advance and knowing the new scale helps your hands and eyes get ready.

title: Reading Key Signatures Fast: Sharps, Flats and the Circle of Fifths
excerpt: Learn the order of sharps (FCGDAEB) and flats (BEADGCF) plus two simple rules to name any key signature, with the circle of fifths, relative minors and a daily flashcard drill.

title: Finding the Keys Without Looking: Building Keyboard Geography
excerpt: Looking down for keys pulls your eyes off the score. Learn to find them by feel, starting with the groups of black keys, and read and sight-read more smoothly.

title: Playing Keyboard in a Band: Play Less, Listen More
excerpt: In a band you are not alone in covering harmony and rhythm. Play less bass, keep chords in the middle and upper register, use simple rhythms and listen to the drums and bass.

title: Setting Up a Keyboard Stand: Height, Stability and Posture
excerpt: The height and stability of your keyboard stand directly affect your posture and hands. Aim for a level forearm and relaxed wrists on a steady stand, adjusting the stand or the chair.

title: Moving from a Keyboard to an Upright Piano: Your First Week
excerpt: Keys feeling heavy and the sound hard to control in the first week on an upright piano is common. Adapt with slow playing and familiar hand shapes before new pieces.

title: Khachaturian's Sabre Dance: A Breathless Number from Gayane
excerpt: The Sabre Dance comes from Aram Khachaturian's 1942 ballet Gayane. It was reportedly added just before the premiere, with a driving rhythm, a relentless xylophone figure and roaring brass.

title: Piano Practice for Kids at Home: A Parent's Guide to AI Apps
excerpt: How parents can support a child's piano practice at home with an AI piano teaching app: routines, praise that works, privacy tips and when to add a tutor.

title: Kitchen-Timer Practice: One Musical Ingredient at a Time
excerpt: Set a short timer and focus on just one musical ingredient: rhythm, notes or dynamics. A practical way to make piano practice clearer and less tiring.

title: Klangfarbenmelodie: One Melody Passed Between Instruments
excerpt: Klangfarbenmelodie, or tone-colour melody, is Schoenberg's 1911 idea that a series of timbres might form a melody. It later came to mean passing a melody between instruments, changing colour with each one.

title: Klezmer Colours on Piano: Freygish Mode and Ornaments
excerpt: Klezmer music uses expressive modes and vocal-style ornaments. Learn the freygish scale, common accompaniment patterns and ornament ideas on piano.

title: Kodály Hand Signs: Linking Solfa, Singing and Piano Keys
excerpt: Curwen hand signs, used in the Kodály approach, give each scale degree a shape. Learn the seven signs and pair them with the keyboard for sharper ears.

title: Kreisler's "Old Composers": A Musical Joke Revealed in 1935
excerpt: For decades Fritz Kreisler played short pieces he said were found manuscripts by eighteenth-century composers. In 1935 he admitted he had written them himself in the old styles.

title: Kuhlau's Sonatinas Op. 20: Three Familiar Pieces on the Learning Path
excerpt: Kuhlau's Sonatinas Op. 20 are three short, clearly structured piano sonatinas published around 1820, popular with intermediate students. Kuhlau lost an eye as a boy yet became a prolific composer.

title: L’istesso tempo: When the Time Signature Changes but the Beat Doesn’t
excerpt: When the time signature changes mid-piece, the Italian term l’istesso tempo means "the same speed": the length of each beat stays the same, for example when 2/4 becomes 6/8.

title: Labelling Sections A, B, C in Your Score for Tidier Practice
excerpt: Marking a new piece in pencil with section letters A, B and C, and A′ for varied repeats, makes practice, lessons and memorising more organised.

title: Labelling AI-Generated Music: Disclosure, Credits and Listener Trust
excerpt: As AI tools spread, platforms, artists and educators are deciding how to label AI-generated or AI-assisted music. Options, challenges and good practice.

title: The Lament Bass: Four Notes Descending from Tonic to Dominant
excerpt: Baroque composers often expressed grief with a bass line falling four notes from tonic to dominant, such as D, C, B♭, A in D minor, sometimes filled in chromatically.

title: The Landini Cadence: Stepping Down Before the Final Note
excerpt: The Landini cadence, common in 14th and 15th century polyphony, has the top voice step down from the leading note to the sixth degree before leaping up a third to the tonic.

title: The Ländler: Austria’s Country Dance in Three Before the Waltz
excerpt: The Ländler is a slow three-beat country dance from Austria and southern Germany and one forerunner of the waltz. Schubert wrote many for piano, often improvised at gatherings of friends.

title: For Adult and Older Learners: Make Your Sheet Music Bigger
excerpt: Many adult and older piano learners find the notes on the page too small and crowded. Enlarging the score, brightening the light and adjusting the music stand can make reading easier and practice more pleasant.

title: Largo: How to Play a Broad, Slow Tempo Well
excerpt: Largo is an Italian tempo marking meaning very slow and broad. It stresses fullness and dignity of sound, so playing it well takes more than simply slowing down.

title: "The Last Rose of Summer": An Irish Air and Its Variations
excerpt: Thomas Moore wrote the poem in 1805 to an old Irish folk tune, later published in his Irish Melodies. Flotow used it in his opera Martha, and Beethoven and Mendelssohn arranged it.

title: Late Arrival Policies for Music Studios: Starting the Clock Fairly
excerpt: A late-arrival policy says how a music studio starts the clock when a learner is late. Learn what to write, and how to apply the same rule fairly.

title: Layered Practice: Get It Even First, Then Add One Layer at a Time
excerpt: Trying to play a new piece fast and complete all at once leaves uneven spots. Like painting a wall, play the passage evenly and slowly first, then add speed, dynamics and expression layer by layer.

title: Learning a Pop Song? Start with the Chorus
excerpt: Learning a pop song from bar one means waiting a long time to reach the part everyone knows. Starting with the chorus gets you playing something recognisable straight away, and keeps you motivated.

title: Watching Piano Masterclass Videos: How to Get the Most from Them
excerpt: Masterclass videos show how problems are found and solved. Watch with a specific question, take notes, and then try the advice at the piano, so that someone else's lesson becomes your own gain.

title: Sometimes Start with the Left Hand: More Time for Accompaniment and Bass
excerpt: Many learners practise the right-hand melody first and neglect the left. Sometimes start with the left hand: get the bass and chords steady, then add the right hand, especially in complex pieces.

title: How to Learn a Movie Theme on Piano: A Step-by-Step Method
excerpt: A practical method to learn a movie theme on piano: choose the right arrangement, map the music, build three levels of difficulty and add expression.

title: Learn a New Piano Piece in Four-Bar Chunks
excerpt: Learning a whole piece at once feels heavy. Splitting it into four-bar chunks gives learners small, clear goals and steady progress. A simple method.

title: Learn a New Piano Piece in Chunks: Phrases, Patterns and Joins
excerpt: Splitting a piece into musical chunks speeds learning and reduces errors. How to choose chunk sizes, practise the joins and rebuild the whole.

title: Listen to a New Piece a Few Times Before You Learn It
excerpt: Listening to a recording a few times before practising shows you a new piece’s tempo, character and structure, so reading is quicker and you know where each passage is heading.

title: Learn Piano Online with an AI App: Your First 30 Days
excerpt: A week-by-week plan for your first month learning piano online with an AI piano teaching app: setup, daily routine, simple checkpoints and FAQs.

title: Play the Scale of a New Piece Before You Learn It
excerpt: Check the key signature of a new piece and play its scale and tonic chord a few times first, so your hands and ears know the key and you are less likely to miss sharps or flats.

title: Learning to Play Your School Song: From Melody to Chord Accompaniment
excerpt: To play a school song at the piano, learn the melody with your right hand, add chords with your left, and choose a tempo and key that let everyone sing along comfortably.

title: A Family Member Asks for a Song: Turning It into a Version You Can Play
excerpt: When a family member requests a song, find its main melody, pick a comfortable key, add simple left-hand chords, and make a version you can play all the way through.

title: Learner Testimonials With Consent: Honest Proof for Music Brands
excerpt: Testimonials can reassure new learners, but only when they are real, approved and fair. How music brands can collect and share them responsibly.

title: Learning Piano With Small Hands: Fingering and Voicing Tips
excerpt: Ways to play piano with small hands: smart fingering, rolled and shared chords, relaxed stretches and editions that suit your reach.

title: Lecuona's Malagueña: A Cuban Composer's Spanish Dance
excerpt: Malagueña is one of the pieces from Ernesto Lecuona's Andalucía suite most often played on its own, bringing southern Spanish dance colour to the piano with a repeated bass and Phrygian flavour.

title: Ledger Lines on Piano: Read Notes Above and Below the Staff Faster
excerpt: Ledger lines extend the staff for very high and low notes. Learn anchor patterns, octave tricks and short drills to read them without counting.

title: The Left-Hand "1-5-10" Broken Chord for a Wider Accompaniment
excerpt: A broken chord within one octave sounds clear but a little thin. The wider 1-5-10 pattern, with the root, fifth and a tenth above, gives lyrical songs a fuller left-hand accompaniment.

title: Left Hand Can't Keep Up? Four Symptoms and a 7-Day Plan
excerpt: Uneven rhythm, slow jumps, too loud, or dragged along by the right hand? Find the cause by symptom, then steady your left hand with a seven-day plan and track progress with TIGA ALPHA.

title: Left-Hand Pinky Bass Notes: Making the Lowest Note Stand Firm
excerpt: In many accompaniment patterns the left-hand pinky plays the lowest note of each chord. Let the weight of your forearm flow down to the fingertip, and practise the bass alone first, so the music sounds grounded.

title: When the Melody Moves to the Left Hand: Let the Bass Sing
excerpt: Sometimes the composer hands the melody to the left hand. Balance the two hands so the melody is heard: full and connected on the left, lighter accompaniment on the right, and a warm tone in the low register.

title: Left-Hand Octave Bass: Giving Your Accompaniment More Weight
excerpt: To give a pop-song or hymn accompaniment a weightier bass, play it in octaves with thumb and pinky, keeping the wrist and arm relaxed. Smaller hands can start with single notes or play octaves only on key beats.

title: Leggiero, Con Brio, Maestoso: Terms for the Character of Music
excerpt: Besides tempo and dynamic terms, scores use Italian words for character. Leggiero means light, con brio means with spirit, and maestoso means majestic, telling the player how the music should feel.

title: The Leitmotif: One Melody for One Character or Thing
excerpt: A leitmotif is a short melody or harmony that stands for a character, object, place or idea in an opera or large work. Wagner used it extensively and systematically, especially in the Ring cycle.

title: Anderson's The Typewriter: Office Sounds in a 1950 Orchestra Piece
excerpt: The Typewriter is a short 1950 orchestral piece by Leroy Anderson in which a percussionist plays a real typewriter. It lasts just over a minute and is full of humour.

title: The Teacher With No Method: Leschetizky and Personal Piano Lessons
excerpt: Theodor Leschetizky taught famous pianists yet said he had no method. What his student-by-student approach can teach learners using AI apps today.

title: Lesson Pack Pricing: Clear Bundles for Music Studios
excerpt: How a music studio can describe lesson packs in plain words: what is included, how long a pack lasts and how families compare choices calmly.

title: Lesson Packages or Monthly Plans? Pricing Models for Music Teachers
excerpt: Music teachers can charge per lesson, sell packages or use monthly plans. Compare the models, their trade-offs and how to explain prices clearly.

title: Lesson Reminder Messages: Timing and Tone for Music Studios
excerpt: Lesson reminders help families arrive ready without feeling nagged. How to choose timing, keep messages short and respect opt-outs and privacy.

title: "Let Us Row the Boat": A Children's Song About Rowing on a Lake
excerpt: A much-loved Chinese children's song from a 1955 film, with words by Qiao Yu and music by Liu Chi. Its flowing, bright melody and rocking accompaniment are good for practising a singing line on the piano.

title: Li Huanzhi's Spring Festival Overture: Gongs, Drums and Yangge Dance
excerpt: An orchestral work written by Li Huanzhi in 1955-56, the first movement of his Spring Festival Suite, with lively gongs and drums, a lyrical middle section and a joyful return.

title: Li Yinghai's "Flutes and Drums at Sunset": An Old Melody Written for Piano
excerpt: A piano arrangement by Li Yinghai of a famous Chinese instrumental piece, often played on the pipa, depicting drums, flutes and a quietening river at dusk. Learn it through sparse and dense passages and contrasting touch.

title: Liadov's Musical Snuffbox: A Music-Box Miniature from 1893
excerpt: Anatoly Liadov's Musical Snuffbox, Op. 32 (1893), is a tiny piano piece that sounds like a mechanical music box being opened. Practise it for even touch and a steady beat.

title: Lifetime Value and Acquisition Cost: Unit Economics for Music Courses
excerpt: How music course providers can compare what it costs to win a learner with what that learner brings over time, using simple, honest numbers.

title: Tidying Your Room to Light Music: A Relaxed Link Between Music and Daily Life
excerpt: Listening to light music while tidying up is a small habit in many homes. This article covers choosing pieces and setting the volume, as general life tips and not medical advice.

title: Playing Mozart and Haydn Sonatas: Use the Pedal Lightly and Sparingly
excerpt: In Mozart and Haydn sonatas, pedal lightly, sparingly and change it often, so every note stays clear and phrases keep their shape, because instruments of that time sounded lighter and shorter.

title: Light-Up Key Keyboards: How Guided Lighting Helps and Hinders
excerpt: Light-up keyboards show which key to press next. Learn how the systems work, where they help beginners, and how to avoid relying on lights alone.

title: Lighting for Practice: Key Points for Reading Music Without Eye Strain
excerpt: Poor light or glare tires the eyes quickly when reading music. Use soft daylight, avoid direct sun on the page, and light the music stand from above and to the side in the evening.

title: Meet Lili Boulanger, First Woman to Win the Prix de Rome
excerpt: Lili Boulanger was a French composer of the early twentieth century. In 1913 she became the first woman to win the Prix de Rome, for her cantata Faust et Hélène. Her career was short, but she left much worth hearing.

title: Hearing Pitch Rise and Fall Through the Tones of Language
excerpt: Mandarin has four tones plus a neutral tone, and Thai has five. You can borrow that sensitivity to feel melodies going up, down or staying put: hum a phrase like speech, then listen for where it rises and falls.

title: Learn Phrasing from Singers: Let the Piano Breathe
excerpt: Singers must breathe, so their phrases naturally have a beginning, an end and a shape. The piano needs no breath, so phrases easily run on. Try singing a melody first and leave a little space at the same spots on the piano.

title: Listening Practice on Your Commute
excerpt: Your commute can become piano listening time: replay the piece you are learning, compare performers, tell melody from accompaniment, or count the beat in your head. None of it needs a piano.

title: Listening Tests for Music AI: How People Judge Generated Sound
excerpt: Numbers alone cannot say whether generated music sounds good. Learn how listening tests are designed, what they measure and where they can mislead.

title: Rests Are Music Too: Learning to Listen to the Quiet Parts
excerpt: A rest marks a stretch of silence, but it is part of the music, not a gap. Count rests as carefully as notes and keep feeling the beat so the quiet has direction.

title: Liszt and the Piano Recital: One Pianist Carrying a Whole Concert
excerpt: Today one pianist playing a whole concert is normal, but in the early 1800s concerts featured several performers. Liszt helped shape the recital, notably in London in 1840.

title: Liszt's Consolation No. 3 in D-flat: A Quiet Song
excerpt: Liszt's six Consolations were written between 1844 and 1850. The third, in D♭ major, has a calm, gentle melody over flowing broken chords and is often compared to a Chopin nocturne.

title: 1832: Liszt Hears Paganini in Paris
excerpt: In April 1832, twenty-year-old Liszt heard Paganini play in Paris and resolved to reach the same heights on the piano. The experience led to his Paganini studies.

title: Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2: Lassan and Friska
excerpt: Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 (written 1847, published 1851, C♯ minor) pairs a slow, solemn lassan with a fiery friska that keeps getting faster.

title: Liszt's La campanella: Paganini's Little Bell on the Piano
excerpt: La campanella is the third of Liszt's Paganini Etudes. The version usually played today was published in 1851, and its theme imitates a little bell in a Paganini violin concerto.

title: Liszt's Liebesträume No. 3: The Melody in the Middle Voice
excerpt: Liszt's Liebesträume are three piano pieces published in 1850, adapted from his own songs. In No. 3 the melody often sits in the middle voice, shared between the hands.

title: The 1837 Paris Piano Duel: Liszt Against Thalberg
excerpt: In March 1837 Liszt and Thalberg played in turn at a charity concert in a Paris salon, and the hostess's clever remark spared both men's pride.

title: Liszt's Transcendental Études: Three Versions, Finalised in 1852
excerpt: Liszt's Transcendental Études are a set of twelve piano studies, usually played today in the final 1852 edition. They went through three versions: a simple set in 1826, a fiendish one in 1837 and the titled version of 1852.

title: Liszt's Un sospiro: Alternating Hands in a D-flat Concert Study
excerpt: Un sospiro is the third of Liszt's Three Concert Studies, published in 1849 in D-flat major. Flowing arpeggios pass between the hands while the melody is handed back and forth, sometimes with the left hand crossing over the right.

title: Liszt's Waldesrauschen: A Concert Study Evoking the Rustle of Leaves
excerpt: Waldesrauschen is a concert study by Franz Liszt that uses fast, light figuration to evoke the continuous rustle of wind through a forest. It is often denser than similar pieces, and its layers must stay clear over long stretches.

title: Lisztomania: The Name the Poet Heine Gave a Craze in 1844
excerpt: In the 1840s, audiences across Europe were wild about Liszt. In 1844 the German poet Heine gave the craze a name, "Lisztomania", and wrote about it with a hint of irony.

title: Liu Tianhua's Liangxiao: An Erhu Piece Written on New Year's Eve 1928
excerpt: Liangxiao was written by Liu Tianhua on New Year's Eve, 22 January 1928, as an erhu piece originally called Little Song for New Year's Eve. It is short, warm and flowing, and has since been arranged for piano.

title: Live Group Practice Sessions: An Online Business Model
excerpt: Live practice sessions let students practise together at a set time while the teacher demonstrates and prompts online. This article looks at lesson design, pricing, technical setup and running the model.

title: Live Looping: Layering Many Parts Alone
excerpt: Live looping lets a performer record a short passage, play it back on repeat and layer new parts on top. This article covers the basic process, why exact start and end points matter, and common beginner problems.

title: Safe Ways to Promote Together with a Local Music Store
excerpt: Studios and local music stores should first align goals and set clear boundaries: trial playing, restrained referral wording, transparent benefits and a review afterwards.

title: Local Listings for Music Studios: Keeping Details Accurate
excerpt: Map and directory listings are often the first place families find a music studio. How to keep hours, address, photos and descriptions accurate and honest.

title: Local Search Profiles for Music Studios: Help Nearby Learners Find You
excerpt: A complete local search profile helps nearby families find a music studio. What to include, how to keep it accurate and how to handle reviews honestly.

title: Localising Music App Marketing for Thai, English and Mandarin
excerpt: Translation is only the start. How to localise music app messages, examples, visuals and support for Thai, English and Mandarin-speaking learners.

title: Loco After an Ottava Sign: Returning to the Written Pitch
excerpt: An 8va sign with a dotted line means the notes beneath it sound an octave higher than written. Where the line ends, loco may appear, meaning return to the written pitch. Move your hand back to where the score actually places the notes.

title: Locrian Mode on Piano: The Scale That Never Feels Home
excerpt: Locrian is the mode built on B using only white keys. Its flat second and flat fifth make home sound unstable. Here is how to hear, build and use it.

title: Lo-Fi Hip Hop Listening Guide: Dusty Beats and Mellow Keys
excerpt: Why lo-fi hip hop sounds warm and relaxed: swung drums, soft jazz chords, crackle and filtering. A listening guide with ideas to try on piano.

title: London Bridge Is Falling Down: An Old English Rhyme and Arch Game
excerpt: London Bridge Is Falling Down is an old English nursery rhyme, with similar words recorded in the seventeenth century. The verses try wood, bricks and iron to mend the bridge, and each one seems to have a problem.

title: Long, Long Ago: A Nostalgic Song Written by Bayly in the 1830s
excerpt: Long, Long Ago is a song written in the 1830s by the English poet and songwriter Thomas Haynes Bayly, words and music both. It asks for the old songs and old stories again, and recalls days spent with a loved one.

title: Look at the Ending First When Learning a New Piece
excerpt: When you get a new piece, turn to the last page first and see how it ends: the final chord, changes of tempo and dynamics, any ritardando or fermata. Knowing the destination makes the whole piece easier to understand.

title: A Lost Property Box for Your Music Studio: Simple Routine
excerpt: Pencils, scarves and music books get left behind in every studio. A small lost property box and a clear routine keep things tidy and families happy.

title: Ten Minutes of Piano at Lunch: A Quiet Listening Habit for Workers
excerpt: Spending a lunch break of ten minutes listening closely to a piano piece can add a quiet moment to a busy day. This article covers how to choose pieces, how to listen, and tips for keeping the habit going.

title: Lupin Flower: A 1989 Taiwanese Film Theme and the Tea-Garden Bloom
excerpt: Lupin Flower is the theme song of a 1989 Taiwanese film of the same name, composed by Chen Yang with words by Yao Qian. Its gentle, heartfelt melody is lovely on the piano for practising singing lines and soft accompaniment.

title: Lydian Dominant on Piano: Bright Colour With a Flat Seventh
excerpt: How the Lydian dominant scale works on piano: raised fourth, flat seventh, left-hand shells and short bright phrases.

title: The Lydian Mode on Piano: How One Raised Note Creates a Floating Sound
excerpt: The Lydian mode is a major scale with a raised fourth. Learn its formula, find it in any key and try three keyboard experiments to hear its colour.

title: Lyric Videos and Visualisers: Low-Cost Visuals for a New Release
excerpt: Lyric videos and audio visualisers give a song a video presence without a film crew. How to plan, design and publish them clearly and legally.

title: Let the Left Hand Accompany Softly: Melody and Accompaniment Balance
excerpt: In lyrical pieces the left-hand accompaniment often covers the right-hand melody without you noticing. Think of a singer and accompanist: step back while the melody speaks, and come forward only when it pauses for breath.

title: MacDowell's To a Wild Rose: The Opening of Woodland Sketches, 1896
excerpt: To a Wild Rose is the first piece of Edward MacDowell's 1896 suite Woodland Sketches, Op. 51. Short, slow and in F major, it tests control of touch: soft sound, connected phrases and no sudden heaviness.

title: Machaut's Messe de Nostre Dame: A Poet-Composer's Four-Voice Mass
excerpt: Guillaume de Machaut wrote his Messe de Nostre Dame in the 1360s for four voices. It is one of the earliest surviving Masses set complete by a single known composer.

title: Made-Up Lyrics: Teaching Piano Phrasing Through Words
excerpt: Adding playful words to instrumental melodies helps piano learners feel phrase shape, stress and breathing points. How teachers can use it well.

title: Borrowing Hunter's Lesson Design: The Stages of a Piano Lesson
excerpt: Educator Madeline Hunter's lesson design is often summed up as a handful of stages. Piano teachers can borrow the idea to plan a lesson around one clear goal.

title: The Madrigal: Part-Songs Sung at Home in the Renaissance
excerpt: The madrigal was a secular vocal form that arose in sixteenth-century Italy, for four to six voices, one singer to a part, setting love poetry. It later spread to England.

title: Munich, 1910: Mahler's Eighth Symphony Premieres with 1,000+ Performers
excerpt: Mahler's Eighth Symphony premiered in Munich on 12 September 1910 under his own baton, with over a thousand performers recorded on stage. It earned the nickname "Symphony of a Thousand".

title: The Major Scale Secret: Whole, Whole, Half, Whole, Whole, Whole, Half
excerpt: Every major scale follows one pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Learn it and you can find a major scale from any note and see why key signatures have sharps or flats.

title: The Mannheim School: The Orchestra Famous for Its Crescendo
excerpt: In the mid-1700s the Mannheim orchestra under Johann Stamitz became famous across Europe for its precision, its long crescendo and the rising "Mannheim rocket", and its composers became the Mannheim School.

title: March Character on Piano: A Steady Walk With Clear Downbeats
excerpt: A piano march needs a steady walk and clear downbeats. Build the left-hand step, keep the tune above it, and finish the last cadence on the beat.

title: Maria Szymanowska: An Early Professional Woman Pianist
excerpt: Maria Szymanowska (1789-1831) was a Polish pianist and composer, one of the first women to tour Europe as a professional performer, who wrote etudes, nocturnes, mazurkas and polonaises, some before Chopin's.

title: Mark Identical and Nearly Identical Bars Before Learning a New Piece
excerpt: Before learning a new piece, spend a few minutes marking bars that are identical or nearly identical. You will find less truly new material than you expected, and the nearly identical bars are the traps.

title: Mark the Pages You Practise with Bookmarks and Tabs
