excerpt: Bookmarks, coloured tabs or sticky notes let you open your music straight to the pages you are practising, and colours can show what each piece is for.

title: Marking Phrase Ends in a Piano Score Before You Play
excerpt: Mark phrase ends in a piano score before you play so cadence and breath are planned. Learn simple marks, how to play to them, and when to erase them.

title: Markov-Chain Melodies: How Simple Probability Writes Tunes
excerpt: A Markov chain picks each note based on the note before it. Learn how this simple model generates melodies, where it succeeds and why it wanders.

title: Mary Had a Little Lamb: An 1830 Rhyme and a Three-Note Tune
excerpt: Mary Had a Little Lamb is an American nursery rhyme by Sarah Josepha Hale, published in Boston in 1830. Edison recited it in 1877 while testing the phonograph.

title: Massenet's Méditation: A Violin Solo from the Opera Thaïs
excerpt: In March 1894, Massenet's opera Thaïs premiered in Paris. Between two scenes of Act II, a violin solo over gentle harp arpeggios became the famous Méditation.

title: Matching Tone Across Repeated Chords on Piano
excerpt: Repeated chords at the piano often change tone without a musical reason. Learn how to match weight, voicing and spacing so the set stays even.

title: Meantone Temperament: Pure Thirds at the Cost of a Fifth
excerpt: Before equal temperament, keyboards often used meantone tuning, narrowing the fifths to make major thirds pure. It sounds sweet in simple keys but leaves a harsh wolf fifth.

title: Practice Goals Children Can Measure: Clean Repetitions, Not Minutes
excerpt: Replacing 'practise for 20 minutes' with clear, countable goals helps children focus. Practical goal types, examples and tips for parents.

title: Measure Practice by What You Finish, Not Just How Long You Play
excerpt: Practice goals are often set in minutes, but time at the piano does not guarantee you practised what needed practice. Measuring by tasks, such as which bars to play accurately today, gives practice real results.

title: The iii Chord in a Major Key: The Often Overlooked Mediant
excerpt: Among the seven triads of a major key, I, IV and V are the stars and vi and ii often appear, but iii is rare. In C major it is E minor (E, G, B), sharing two notes each with the tonic and the dominant.

title: The Mellotron: A Keyboard That Played Tape Recordings
excerpt: Each key on a Mellotron started a strip of recorded tape. Discover how it worked, why it sounded unique and what it teaches about sampling.

title: Melodic Dictation: Writing Down What You Hear
excerpt: Melodic dictation means hearing a short melody and writing it as notation. Start with three or four notes: direction first, then the first note and intervals, then rhythm, and check your answer afterwards.

title: Melodic Inversion: Turning a Melody Upside Down
excerpt: Melodic inversion flips a melody's direction: rising intervals fall and falling ones rise, so C, D, E becomes C, B, A. Bach used it widely, and twelve-tone music treats it as a basic technique.

title: The Melodic Minor Scale: Different Going Up and Down
excerpt: The melodic minor scale raises two notes on the way up and returns to the natural minor on the way down. Here is why, with a simple way to practise.

title: Melodic Minor: Why It Goes Up and Down Differently
excerpt: In the melodic minor scale, the sixth and seventh notes are raised a semitone going up and return to natural minor coming down. In A minor it rises through F♯ and G♯.

title: Melodic Sequence on Piano: How Patterns Climb and Fall
excerpt: What a melodic sequence is on piano, how to spot rising and falling copies of a motif, and how to practise sequencing without tension or muddle.

title: What Is a Melodica? A Keyboard Instrument Played with Breath
excerpt: The melodica is part piano, part wind instrument: fingers choose the note and breath sounds the reed. Learn how it works, mouthpiece versus tube, breath and tonguing, and how it pairs with piano study.

title: Play the Melody as a Song First, Then Add the Accompaniment
excerpt: Learn the melody alone first, as if it were a song: find where each phrase starts, ends and breathes. Then add a much quieter accompaniment so the tune floats clearly on top.

title: Make Your Melody Breathe: Phrase Arcs with Twinkle, Twinkle
excerpt: Does your melody sound flat? Using Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star, find the peak, draw the arc, close the phrase softly and leave room to breathe, so the tune sounds like speech.

title: Membership Music: How Monthly Fan Support Became a Business Model
excerpt: Membership platforms let fans support musicians monthly in return for extras. How tiers work, what to offer and how teachers can use the model.

title: Memorise the Left Hand Separately for More Secure Memory
excerpt: Many people memorise the right-hand melody and let the left hand follow along. Practising the left hand alone from memory builds a steady foundation that helps you recover quickly if the right hand slips.

title: Memorising Music More Securely: Structure, Ear and Touch Memory
excerpt: Memorising by finger repetition alone often fails under nerves. This article covers structural, aural and muscle memory, plus tests you can do at home.

title: Blank on Page Two? Give Your Memory Several Starting Points
excerpt: A blank on page two usually means memory relies on finger habit alone. Mark several starting points and practise from each, so you can rejoin at the next familiar spot.

title: 1829: Mendelssohn's First Notes on a Scottish Island
excerpt: In summer 1829, twenty-year-old Mendelssohn toured Scotland and wrote a few bars of melody in a letter home. They became the opening of The Hebrides overture, also called Fingal's Cave.

title: Mendelssohn at Seventeen and the Midsummer Night's Dream Overture
excerpt: In 1826, aged seventeen, Mendelssohn wrote an overture to Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, first as a piano duet. In 1843 he added the full incidental music, including the Wedding March.

title: Mendelssohn's Rondo Capriccioso, Op. 14: A Song, Then a Sprint
excerpt: Mendelssohn's Rondo Capriccioso, Op. 14, opens with a quiet E major song without words, then dashes off into a sprightly E minor presto full of light staccato.

title: Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words: Make the Piano Sing
excerpt: Play Songs Without Words so the melody sings like a voice: sing the shape first, practise two dynamics in one hand, then link long phrases with finger changes.

title: Mendelssohn's Spinning Song: No. 4 of Songs Without Words, Op. 67
excerpt: The Spinning Song is No. 4 of Mendelssohn's Songs Without Words, Op. 67, sometimes called "The Bees' Wedding". Fast, even figures hint at a spinning wheel, with a singing line hidden inside.

title: Mendelssohn's Spring Song: A Bright A Major Gem
excerpt: Spring Song, Op. 62 No. 6, is one of the most-played Songs Without Words: a bright A major piece with a light, singing right-hand melody over a gently flowing left hand.

title: 1829: Mendelssohn Brings the St Matthew Passion Back to Life
excerpt: On 11 March 1829, the 20-year-old Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St Matthew Passion in Berlin, a work that had hardly been performed complete since Bach's death in 1750.

title: Meno mosso and più mosso: Slower and Faster on the Page
excerpt: Meno mosso and più mosso are two Italian terms meaning a little slower and a little faster. Here is what they mean and how to handle them when you play.

title: Mensuration Canon: One Melody at Different Speeds at Once
excerpt: A mensuration canon sets the same melody going at different speeds at the same time, for instance one voice at the original speed and another with every note doubled in length.

title: Mental Practice: Learning Music Away from the Keyboard
excerpt: Mental practice means studying a piece in your head, with the score, singing and silent finger movements. Here is a gentle routine for any day.

title: Practising Away from the Piano: Mental Practice
excerpt: Even away from the piano you can practise in your head: look at the score, imagine playing, hear the sound inwardly and feel the fingering. It is a useful supplement to practice at the keyboard.

title: Modes of Limited Transposition: Messiaen's Special Scales
excerpt: Modes of limited transposition are a set of scales organised and often used by Olivier Messiaen: transpose them by semitones and the same notes soon return, so few distinct versions exist.

title: Premiere in a POW Camp, 1941: Messiaen's Quartet for the End of Time
excerpt: In 1940 Messiaen was taken prisoner and held in a German camp, where he wrote the Quartet for the End of Time for four fellow prisoners, premiered on 15 January 1941.

title: Metric Modulation: Changing Tempo Through One Note Value
excerpt: Metric modulation changes tempo by making one note value in the old tempo equal a different note value in the new one, usually shown on the score as a note-equals-note marking.

title: Setting the Metronome to Click Only on Beats Two and Four
excerpt: In pop, jazz and dance styles, beats two and four are the accented ones. Set the metronome to half speed so it clicks on 2 and 4, and feel beats 1 and 3 yourself.

title: The Metronome's Evolution: From Mechanical Pendulum to Phone App
excerpt: From a mechanical pendulum over two hundred years ago to electronic metronomes and phone apps: the story of its invention, what M.M. means on a score, and the new features of modern metronomes.

title: Using a Metronome for the First Time: Listen to a Few Beats First
excerpt: The first time you use a metronome, listen to a few beats and nod or clap along before you play. Set it slower than usual, play one note per beat, and speed up only when your hands match the clicks.

title: "♩=100" on a Score: How to Read Metronome Markings
excerpt: Besides an Italian tempo term, many scores carry a marking like "♩=100", meaning one hundred quarter notes per minute. This guide explains M.M., compound time and how to use the number.

title: One Metronome Click per Bar: Building Your Inner Beat
excerpt: Instead of a click on every beat, set the metronome to sound once per bar and count the other beats yourself. The metronome becomes a checkpoint, and you keep the rhythm.

title: Metronome Subdivisions: Click More Often to Steady Fast Notes
excerpt: When tempos are very slow or beats hold many fast notes, let the metronome click on subdivisions. It places every note accurately; then thin the clicks out until you play steadily without it.

title: How to Use a Metronome: A Five-Step Tempo Ladder for Steady Rhythm
excerpt: Rushing the beat at the piano? Use a five-step tempo ladder, from slow to fast, moving up only after three correct runs, and log your daily tempo in the TIGA ALPHA app.

title: Working With Micro-Creators: Honest Partnerships for Music Products
excerpt: Small, focused creators can introduce music products to engaged audiences. How to choose partners, brief them fairly and keep disclosures clear.

title: Microtonal Keyboards: Splitting the Semitone
excerpt: Why some keyboards split the semitone into smaller steps, how retuning works in practice, and how to explore microtones without confusion.

title: Clef Changes Mid-Piece: When the Left Hand Suddenly Reads Treble
excerpt: Clefs change mid-piece to avoid ledger lines and keep the score clear. Scan ahead, mark each change, and you will read faster and more steadily. Includes practice ideas and FAQ.

title: Middle C and C4: How Piano Octaves Are Numbered
excerpt: A piano has many Cs, so how do you say which one? Octaves are numbered. In scientific pitch notation, middle C is C4, the lowest C is C1, the highest is C8, and A4 is the tuning note.

title: MIDI 2.0 and Your Digital Piano: What Learners Should Know
excerpt: What MIDI sends, how MIDI 2.0 (adopted 2020) improves touch detail, and a checklist for connecting a digital piano to a learning app.

title: MIDI Continuous Controllers: Expression Beyond Note On and Off
excerpt: What MIDI continuous controllers are, how they shape dynamics and timbre on digital pianos, and which practice uses help learners play more expressively.

title: Minimalist Music: Starting with Riley's In C (1964)
excerpt: Minimalist music emerged in 1960s America, using little material, repetition and slow change. In 1964 Terry Riley wrote In C, with 53 short phrases for any number of players.

title: How to Listen to Minimalist Music: Small Changes in Repetition
excerpt: Minimalist music repeats simple patterns and changes them bit by bit. This article covers its common techniques, ways to listen, and small exercises on the piano.

title: Minuet and Trio: The Elegant Dance Inside Classical Music
excerpt: The minuet and trio is a three-part dance form in triple time: minuet, contrasting trio, minuet again. Learn its shape, its sound and how to play one.

title: Mixed Meter on Piano: How to Count 5/4, 7/8 and Changing Bars
excerpt: Play 5/4, 7/8 and bars that change length by counting groups of twos and threes. A four-stage practice sequence for odd meters on piano.

title: The Mixolydian Mode on Piano: Major With a Flattened Seventh
excerpt: The Mixolydian mode is a major scale with a lowered seventh step. Find it on the white keys from G, hear its relaxed sound and use it in grooves.

title: Perform It at Home First: How to Practise with Mock Performances
excerpt: Before a recital or exam, run mock performances at home: play straight through without stopping, as if an audience were listening, then review what needs work.

title: Modelled or Sampled? Two Ways to Make a Digital Piano Tone
excerpt: Digital pianos make sound by playing recordings or by calculating vibration in real time. Here is how sampling and modelling differ and why it matters.

title: molto, poco, non troppo: Adding Degree to Musical Terms
excerpt: Small words before or after terms in a score show degree. Molto means very, poco means a little, and non troppo means not too much, as in Allegro molto, poco rit. and Allegro ma non troppo.

title: Mompou's Cançó i Dansa No. 1: Sing a Line, Then Dance Lightly
excerpt: Federico Mompou's Cançó i Dansa No. 1, written in 1928, is a short piano piece in two parts, a quiet song followed by a light dance, with a very economical texture where every note counts.

title: Monteverdi's Orfeo: A Myth Told in Music in 1607
excerpt: Orfeo is an opera by Monteverdi, first performed in Mantua in 1607 to a libretto by Alessandro Striggio. It tells the Greek myth of the singer Orpheus and is still often staged today.

title: The Moonlight Sonata's Name: Beethoven Did Not Choose It
excerpt: The famous Moonlight Sonata is Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, Op. 27 No. 2, written in 1801. Beethoven himself called it Sonata quasi una fantasia.

title: Morendo and Smorzando in the Score: Sound Slowly Fading Away
excerpt: Morendo and smorzando are Italian terms for a sound that gradually dies away, usually at the end of a phrase or piece. The change should be smooth and the last note soft but clear.

title: Moscow Nights: A Lyrical Song of a Summer Night by the River
excerpt: Moscow Nights, composed by Vasily Solovyov-Sedoy to words by Mikhail Matusovsky, was written in 1955-56 for a documentary. It paints a quiet summer night by the river.

title: The Motet: A Choral Form from the Middle Ages to Bach
excerpt: The motet is a choral form with a long history. It began in thirteenth-century France with different texts in each voice, and became Latin sacred polyphony in the Renaissance.

title: Motif Development: How a Few Notes Grow Into a Whole Piece
excerpt: A motif is a short musical idea that composers repeat and transform. Learn the main development techniques and how to hear and use them at the piano.

title: How to Handle Your Piano When Moving House
excerpt: When moving, have experienced professional movers carry the piano. In the new home, choose a spot away from sun, vents and damp walls, wait a while, then book a tuning.

title: Rome, 1770: Fourteen-Year-Old Mozart and the Miserere
excerpt: In spring 1770, the fourteen-year-old Mozart heard Allegri's Miserere in Rome. According to his father's letter, he wrote it down from memory. This article looks at the story and its details.

title: Mozart and Salieri: A Misunderstanding Told for 200 Years
excerpt: Antonio Salieri was a leading composer in late eighteenth-century Vienna. After Mozart died in 1791, a rumour spread that Salieri had harmed him out of envy, but historians find no evidence.

title: Prague, 1787: The Legend of Mozart's Don Giovanni Overture
excerpt: Mozart's opera Don Giovanni premiered in Prague on 29 October 1787. A famous story says he wrote the overture only the night before. This article looks at the legend and the music.

title: Mozart's Eine kleine Nachtmusik, K.525: Four Movements of 1787
excerpt: On 10 August 1787, Mozart entered a new work in his catalogue in Vienna, titled "a little serenade". Today it is the familiar Eine kleine Nachtmusik, K.525, in G major, written while he was busy with Don Giovanni. Four movements survive, though he recorded five.

title: Mozart's Unfinished Requiem of 1791: His Last Work
excerpt: In summer 1791 Mozart received an anonymous commission for a requiem. He died in Vienna on 5 December, aged thirty-five, with the work only partly finished. His student Süssmayr later completed it from the manuscripts and sketches.

title: Mozart's Sonata in C major, K.545: A Sonata "for Beginners"
excerpt: Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K.545, was entered in his catalogue in June 1788 as "a little sonata for beginners". It has three movements. The notes look easy, but playing them clean, even and singing is not, which makes it ideal for learning Classical touch and phrasing.

title: Mozart's Turkish March: Starting in A Minor, Ending in A Major
excerpt: The Turkish March is the third movement of Mozart's Piano Sonata in A major, K.331, marked "Alla turca", probably written around 1783. It opens in A minor with lively sixteenth-note ornamental figures, then moves to A major with drum-like broken chords.

title: Mozart's Twinkle Variations K.265: Twelve Takes on a French Song
excerpt: The tune of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star comes from an eighteenth-century French song. Around 1781 to 1782 in Vienna, Mozart wrote twelve piano variations on it, catalogued as K.265.

title: mp vs mf: Using Speaking Volume to Build Dynamic Levels
excerpt: mp and mf are both medium dynamics, and the difference lies in how fast the key travels down. Learn six dynamic levels through speaking volume, with four practice exercises and a recording check.

title: Eight Bars of Rest in Ensemble Playing: How to Count Multi-Bar Rests
excerpt: In ensemble or orchestral playing, piano parts often show multi-bar rests: a thick horizontal line with the number of bars to rest above it. Keep counting and listen to the other instruments for cues so you can come in on time.

title: Counting Beats in a Multilingual Home: Which Language Works Best?
excerpt: In a multilingual home there is no single right language for counting beats. Letting your child choose the most natural one usually keeps the pulse steadier; what matters is even counting that lines up with the music.

title: Musette in D Major: A Little Piece from the Anna Magdalena Notebook
excerpt: The Musette in D major is found in the 1725 Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach, catalogued as BWV Anh. 126, and its composer is still not entirely certain. It imitates a bagpipe drone, with the left hand leaping between two Ds an octave apart.

title: Licensing Datasets for Music AI: Permission, Scope and Credit
excerpt: Licensing a music-AI dataset means agreeing who may use which recordings, for what purpose, and with what credit. Learn questions a studio should raise.

title: How Music AI Reads Notes: Tokens, Events and Representations
excerpt: Before a model can learn music, notes must be turned into tokens. Learn the main ways music is represented and why the choice shapes what AI produces.

title: Reading Music App Retention with Cohorts: A Beginner's Guide to the Chart
excerpt: A cohort chart looks at retention by group of users who started in the same period. Learn to read its rows and columns, then propose gentle, testable changes for early or mid-stage drop-off.

title: Naming Music App Features: Make Every Button Clear at a Glance
excerpt: A feature can be excellent, but if its name is unclear, users may never tap it. This article covers naming features in a music learning app: use learners' language, keep consistent rules, allow for several languages, and test that users really understand.

title: Writing In-App Messages for a Music App: Reminders, Encouragement and Balance
excerpt: In-app messages shape how learners feel about a music app. This article covers how to write reminders, encouragement and update notices, and how to balance frequency, timing and tone.

title: Music App Onboarding: Designing the First Seven Days

excerpt: Once you own a lot of sheet music, it ends up scattered across piano stools, shelves, phones and computers. This article suggests sorting by learning status, with consistent folders and file names for paper and digital scores.

title: Organum: Adding a Second Voice Beside the Chant
excerpt: Organum is early medieval polyphony in which one or more voices are added to an existing chant melody. Over time, the added voices grew freer and more ornate.

title: The Orphica: A Little Piano You Could Carry, from the 1790s
excerpt: Around the 1790s a small keyboard instrument called the orphica appeared. Lighter and narrower than a square piano, it was a movable piano that could leave the fixed drawing room.

title: Ossia: The "Alternative Way to Play It" in the Score
excerpt: Ossia is an Italian word meaning "or". It marks a passage with an alternative way of playing, which can be simpler or more showy, written by the composer or an editor.

title: Ostinato on Piano: Building Energy From a Repeating Figure
excerpt: What an ostinato is on piano, how to design a short repeating figure, and how to layer melody and harmony above it without losing the pulse.

title: Overdotting: A Baroque Habit of Lengthening the Long Note a Little More
excerpt: In some Baroque performance habits, a written dotted rhythm is sharpened: the long note is held a little longer and the short note is shorter and lighter than the notation suggests.

title: Pachelbel's Canon Chords: Eight Bass Notes on Repeat
excerpt: Pachelbel's Canon in D was written for three violins and continuo. Its eight-note bass repeats again and again while the upper parts build on it. Learn the chords and how to approach the piano arrangement.

title: Paderewski's Minuet in G (1887): A Little Piece "Like Mozart"
excerpt: Paderewski's Minuet in G, written in 1887 and included in his Humoresques de concert, imitates the elegant minuet style of Mozart's day, with a flashy Romantic second half. Learn the story and how to play it.

title: Paganini's Caprice No. 24: Many Variations from One Theme
excerpt: Paganini wrote twenty-four caprices for solo violin, published in Milan in 1820 as his Op. 1. The 24th, in A minor, has a short theme, eleven variations and a finale, and has inspired many composers.

title: Page Turns Keep Interrupting the Music? Plan Where to Turn Ahead of Time
excerpt: Music often breaks off at a page turn because the turn happens at the last moment. Plan each turn ahead, turn at a rest, long note or one-handed passage, and memorise the start of the next page.

title: Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass: The Legend That "Saved Polyphony"
excerpt: A popular story says Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass convinced the Council of Trent that polyphony could stay in church. Historians think the tale is mostly a later embellishment.

title: Pandiatonicism: Diatonic Notes Without Traditional Function
excerpt: Pandiatonicism is a twentieth-century idea of writing with notes mostly from one diatonic collection, combined without necessarily following traditional dominant-to-tonic function.

title: Paper Scores or Tablet Scores: The Pros and Cons of Each
excerpt: Paper scores are easy to mark and need no charging; tablet scores are light and hold many pieces. Neither is simply better, and many players use both.

title: Paradies's Toccata in A Major: A Fast-Running Keyboard Finale
excerpt: Paradies's Toccata in A major comes from a keyboard sonata and is often played on its own: a bright right-hand stream of notes over steady left-hand support.

title: Parallel Fifths on Piano: When Styles Disagree
excerpt: Why classical textbooks flag parallel fifths, how to spot them at the piano, and when modern styles keep that colour.

title: Parallel Major and Minor: One Starting Point, Two Colours
excerpt: Parallel major and minor keys share a tonic but differ in mode, like C major and C minor. The lowered third gives a different colour, and many pieces switch between the two.

title: Parents Learning Too: Learning Alongside Your Child
excerpt: Some parents start learning a little piano while their child learns. It helps them understand the child's difficulties, but progress should not be compared and the relationship should stay relaxed.

title: Parent Orientation Sessions: Starting a Studio Year Together
excerpt: A short orientation for new families explains how lessons, practice and communication work. Learn how to plan the session and what to cover.

title: What to Say When Practising with Your Child: Observe, Don't Rush
excerpt: What parents say during practice affects a child's mood. Here are gentle phrases: observations instead of pushing, and questions instead of commands, to help children stay interested.

title: You Can Support Practice Without Playing: A 15-Minute Weekend Review
excerpt: Parents who cannot read staff notation can still support a review: three questions, one specific piece of praise and one goal for next week, with a 15-minute script to follow.

title: Parent Workshops: Making Piano Families Long-Term Brand Partners
excerpt: How a music school can run parent workshops: choosing topics, planning the session, interactive exercises and follow-up materials that build lasting trust and word of mouth.

title: Pärt's Für Alina (1976): Bells on Two Pages of Music
excerpt: Arvo Pärt wrote Für Alina in 1976, on just two pages. It marks the start of his bell-like tintinnabuli style: one voice moves by step, the other plays only the tonic triad.

title: The Passacaglia Ground on Piano: A Repeating Bass Under Changing Lines
excerpt: A passacaglia places changing lines over a repeating bass. Learn the cycle first, keep it even under later variations, and group the changes for practice.

title: The Passepied: A Light, Quick French Dance in Triple Time
excerpt: The passepied is a fast French dance from Brittany that found its way into many Baroque suites. It feels like 3/8, often starts on an upbeat and moves like quick, light steps.

title: The Passing Six-Four Chord: A Bridge Between Two Chords
excerpt: A six-four chord is the second inversion of a triad, with the fifth in the bass. The passing six-four sits between two chords while the bass moves by step, like climbing stairs, to link them.

title: Passing Tones and Neighbour Notes: Decorating a Piano Melody
excerpt: Passing tones and neighbour notes decorate a piano melody around main tones. Find them in the score, keep main notes clear, and play the ornaments in time.

title: Passing and Neighbour Tones: Notes That Colour a Melody
excerpt: Passing tones and neighbour tones are extra notes that sit between or beside chord tones, giving a melody a smoother or more decorated path.

title: Before a Hard Spot, Pause: Stop, Prepare, Then Play
excerpt: Hard spots often go wrong because the hand isn't ready in time. Pause on the note before the spot, plan the notes and fingering, then play on, shortening the pause until it is no longer needed.

title: Pause on the Thumb Notes in Fast Runs
excerpt: In fast scales and runs the thumb is often the unsteady spot. Pausing on each thumb note lets you check that your hand is ready for the next group, so the run becomes steadier.

title: Pedalling in Bach: Use It Sparingly, but Don't Rule It Out
excerpt: Bach's keyboards had no sustain pedal, so teachers advise using it sparingly. Sparingly does not mean never: a short, shallow pedal, changed with the harmony, can warm slow passages.

title: Reading Pedal Markings: Ped., the Asterisk and the Pedal Line
excerpt: Pedal markings come in two styles: the traditional ornate "Ped." with an asterisk-like ✻ for release, and a line beneath the bass staff that dips, notches and lifts. Here is how to read both.

title: Pedal Point on Piano: Holding a Bass While Harmony Moves
excerpt: What a pedal point is on piano, how tonic and dominant pedals work, and how to practise a held bass under changing chords without muddying the sound.

title: The Pedal Six-Four Chord: Bass Holds Still, Upper Voices Sway
excerpt: The pedal six-four, also called the neighbour six-four, keeps the bass still while the upper voices step up and return, giving music a gentle sway on one stable note.

title: Left Hand and Pedal First: Getting Pedal and Bass Working Together
excerpt: When hands and feet start together, something slips and the sound turns muddy. Practise the left hand with the pedal first, then add the right hand for a much clearer sound.

title: Pencil Markings on a Piano Score: A Simple Colour Code
excerpt: A light, consistent system for marking a piano score with pencil and colour, so reminders help practice instead of cluttering the page.

title: Pentatonic Scales on Piano: Five Notes for Easy Improvising
excerpt: Learn major and minor pentatonic scales on piano, why five-note scales sound good in any order, and a five-minute routine for your first improvisations.

title: Perfect and Imperfect Authentic Cadences: How Final Is the Ending?
excerpt: Both authentic cadences move from dominant to tonic, but one sounds like a full stop and the other leaves a little room. The difference lies in whether bass and top note both land on the tonic.

title: Period and Sentence: Two Common Ways to Build a Classical Theme
excerpt: Two common ways to organise a classical theme are the period and the sentence. A period is like question and answer; a sentence states a short idea, develops it, then closes.

title: Petrucci and the Odhecaton: A Polyphonic Collection Printed in 1501
excerpt: In 1501 Ottaviano Petrucci printed Harmonice Musices Odhecaton in Venice, one of the earliest surviving polyphonic collections printed with movable type, making part-music easier to copy uniformly.

title: The Petrushka Chord: Two Major Triads a Tritone Apart
excerpt: The Petrushka chord stacks two major triads a tritone apart, most often C major and F♯ major sounding together. It takes its name from Stravinsky's 1911 ballet Petrushka.

title: Cats and Dogs at Home: Small Ways to Protect Your Piano
excerpt: With cats and dogs at home, you can protect the piano: close the lid, keep food and drinks off it, clear pet hair, and give pets their own place to rest and play.

title: Where to Keep Your Phone While Practising: Fewer Interruptions
excerpt: Keep your phone out of reach, switch on Do Not Disturb and fetch it only for the metronome or a recording. Each glance at a message breaks a smooth practice session into fragments.

title: Photo Consent at Music Studios: A Clear Social Media Policy
excerpt: Photos of lessons and recitals can warm up a studio's social pages, but only with clear consent. A plain guide to asking, recording and respecting choices.

title: Photograph Your Score After Lessons: Keep Your Teacher's Markings
excerpt: After a lesson, photograph the pages your teacher has marked and save them by date. It gives you a backup, a record of each lesson, and the markings if you forget your score.

title: Phrases and Breathing: Finding Where the Music Takes a Breath
excerpt: Phrases in piano playing are like breathing in swimming: music needs small gaps between phrases. Pause lightly in the right places and the music sounds more natural and unhurried.

title: Phrase Elision: When One Phrase's Ending Is the Next One's Beginning
excerpt: Normally one phrase ends and the next begins after a small pause. In an elision, the last note of one phrase is also the first note of the next, so the music flows on without a break.

title: Finish Your Phrases Well: The Last Note Matters as Much as the First
excerpt: The end of a phrase is often overlooked, and many players let go as soon as they reach the last note. A good ending is like the final tie on a zongzi: it gently closes the phrase and lets it land securely.

title: Phrase Extension: Why Some Phrases Are Not Four Bars Long
excerpt: Many Classical phrases come in groups of four or eight bars, but some run to five, six or more. Composers stretch them through repetition, sequence or delayed cadences to create surprise and expectation.

title: The Phrygian Half Cadence on Piano: A Minor-Mode Close on the Dominant
excerpt: A Phrygian half cadence in minor ends on the dominant after a falling bass step. Find the close, voice it clearly, and arrive without rushing.

title: Phrygian Mode on Piano: Dark Colour From a Lowered Second
excerpt: How the Phrygian mode works on piano: the lowered second degree, dark colour, simple left-hand drones and short melodies you can build in one sitting.

title: Physical Modelling: How Software Simulates Piano Strings
excerpt: How physical modelling simulates piano strings, hammers and a soundboard, how that differs from sample playback, and where a model still needs care.

title: Accompanying Singers on Piano: Balance, Breath and Flexible Pulse
excerpt: Accompanying a singer on piano means sharing pulse, leaving space for breath, and keeping the piano under the voice. Learn a practical rehearsal method.

title: When Piano Clashes With Other Activities: How to Schedule
excerpt: When a child does piano and other activities, times often clash. List the week together, keep practice short and fixed, adjust on busy days, and check in on how your child feels.

title: Piano Arpeggios Across Octaves: Fingering, Crossings and Flow
excerpt: Arpeggios play chord notes one after another across the keyboard. Learn standard fingerings, smooth thumb crossings and drills for flowing arpeggios.

title: The Piano Ballade: Telling a Long Story Through Sound
excerpt: The ballade began as a story-telling poem or song. Chopin gave the name to solo piano works, writing four large-scale ballades that, without words, tell a long story with a beginning, a climax and an ending.

title: Piano Bench Height and Distance: Setting a Place for Free Arms
excerpt: Set piano bench height and distance so the arms can move freely. Use a simple home check, adjust one setting first, and review the setup as needed.

title: Entering a Piano Competition: Treat It as a Learning Experience
excerpt: A piano competition can bring goals, performing experience and a chance to hear others play, but also pressure. A healthy attitude treats it as a learning experience, not a final verdict on you.

title: Setting Up a Piano Corner at Home: Position, Lighting and Storage
excerpt: When setting up a piano corner at home, think about where the piano goes, where the light comes from, and where music and supplies are kept, so sitting down to practise is easy.

title: How the Sustain Pedal Came to the Piano
excerpt: Today's sustain pedal is the most-used foot in piano playing. Early pianos often used knee levers to lift the dampers, and the foot pedal only gradually became the usual way, from the 18th to the early 19th century.

title: Piano Duets: How to Balance and Listen to Your Partner
excerpt: The key to piano duets is not just playing the right notes but hearing your partner. From telling melody from accompaniment to adjusting dynamics and breathing together, build a balanced, in-tune duo step by step.

title: Why Pianos Usually Have 88 Keys
excerpt: Most pianos have 88 keys, from A to C: seven octaves plus a minor third. Early pianos had a much narrower range, and 88 keys became the common standard only in the late nineteenth century.

title: The Piano Étude: Studies That Became Concert Music
excerpt: An étude is a study piece that focuses on one technical skill. How the genre grew from practice material into concert music, and how to learn one well.

title: Piano Fills Between Vocal Phrases: Small Touches in Accompaniment
excerpt: When accompanying a singer, there is often a gap of a beat or two between phrases. A short, light fill connects the phrases without covering the voice or taking the singer's time.

title: How to Read Fingering Numbers: Four Fingering Techniques
excerpt: Fingering numbers 1 to 5 run from thumb to little finger. This article explains thumb-under, finger-over, finger substitution and extension, plus how to read and mark fingerings yourself.

title: Piano Genie Explained: Improvising on 88 Keys With Eight Buttons
excerpt: Google Magenta’s Piano Genie turns eight buttons into fluent piano music. How the AI works, what it reveals about rhythm and contour, and practice ideas.

title: What Happens When You Press a Key? A Beginner's Guide to Piano Action
excerpt: From key to sound, levers, hammers, escapement and dampers work together inside the piano. This article explains the action in plain language and how it relates to touch practice.

title: Piano Hammers and Felt: How Touch Becomes Tone
excerpt: How felt-covered hammers shape a piano's tone, why firmness changes the sound, and what pianists can listen for when touch and tone seem to disagree.

title: Hand Position Shifts on Piano: Move Between Positions Smoothly
excerpt: How to shift hand positions on piano without gaps: plan the move, look ahead, use pivot fingers and practise the shift as its own small exercise.

title: Piano in the Silent Film Era: Adding Sound to Pictures Without Dialogue
excerpt: Before sound films, cinema pianists played live to the picture, improvising or following cue sheets. Chases, conflicts and tender glances each became different speeds and textures on the piano.

title: Piano Inharmonicity: Why Tuners Stretch the Octaves
excerpt: Why piano strings have slightly sharp partials, why tuners stretch the octaves, and how that tuning affects what you hear at the keyboard.

title: Metal Frames and Cross-Stringing: How Pianos Bear More Tension
excerpt: As the nineteenth century demanded louder, steadier pianos, strings were pulled tighter, and wooden cases gave way to metal frames. Cross-stringing gave bass strings more length in limited space.

title: Simulating Piano Escapement: Recreating the Feel of a Real Key
excerpt: Learn how digital piano manufacturers model escapement, key resistance and mechanical response to reproduce aspects of acoustic piano action.

title: Three-Line Notes After a Piano Lesson: A Summary for Students and Parents
excerpt: After a lesson, students often forget what the teacher said. This article describes the "three-line note": what we learned today, what went well, and what to practise this week, with tips and an example.

title: Lesson Warm-Ups for Piano Teachers: Five-Minute Openers
excerpt: Short warm-up activities piano teachers can use at the start of a lesson to settle students, check technique and connect to the day's main piece.

title: Warming Up Before a Piano Lesson: Three Minutes to Get Your Fingers Ready
excerpt: Before a lesson or practice, three minutes of simple warm-up wakes up your fingers, wrists and ears. A few gentle moves for children and adults, and a reminder to stop if anything feels uncomfortable.

title: Piano Lid Open or Closed: Differences in Sound and Practice Space
excerpt: The lid of a piano changes how loud and bright it sounds. Open, the sound is louder and more spacious; closed, it is softer and more focused. Choose according to your room, the time of day and your neighbours.

title: Piano as a Mindful Hobby: Attention, Flow and Gentle Daily Routines
excerpt: General information on playing piano as a mindful hobby: focused attention, the idea of flow and simple routines that keep practice relaxed.

title: Make a Weekly Mistake Map of the Bars That Trip You
excerpt: Instead of restarting from the top after every slip, mark the bars that keep tripping you and practise them for a week. A simple mistake map for piano.

title: Mordents on Piano: A Short Turn Around the Written Note
excerpt: A mordent is a short ornament that leaves the written note, touches a neighbour, and returns. Learn the usual signs and a slow, clean method.

title: The Piano Nocturne: How a Night Song Took Shape
excerpt: Where the piano nocturne came from, what makes it sound like a night song, and how to practise its singing melody and wide, rolling left hand.

title: Practise With Backing Tracks: Keep Steady Time Like a Band Pianist
excerpt: Playing along with a backing track builds steady time, listening and confidence. How to choose tracks, set tempo and recover when you get lost.

title: Piano Practice Portfolios: Track Student Progress Without Exams
excerpt: A piano portfolio collects recordings, pieces, reflections and goals over time. How teachers and parents build one and use it to show real progress.

title: Practising in Timed Blocks: 25 Minutes of Focus, 5 Minutes of Rest
excerpt: Cutting practice into focused blocks with clear goals and short breaks keeps practice concentrated. This article covers how to plan the blocks, what to practise in each and common adjustments.

title: The Piano Prelude: From Warm-Up to Independent Miniature
excerpt: A prelude began as an introduction played before another piece and became a short, independent form. Its history, its variety and how to approach one.

title: Writing Piano Progress Reports Parents Understand and Use
excerpt: A clear progress report shows parents what their child has learned and what comes next. Learn a simple structure, wording tips and how often to send one.

title: From Low to High: Moving Across the Piano's Wide Range
excerpt: Range is the span from the lowest note to the highest. The piano covers more than seven octaves, and composers use the distance between registers to create a sense of space. Playing such pieces means knowing both ends of the keyboard and staying balanced.

title: Student Recital Programme Order: Making the Programme Sound Better
excerpt: The order of pieces at a student recital affects how much energy the audience has. This article explains how to arrange the programme by length, dynamics and style so the whole concert flows more smoothly.

title: Piano Roll Editors for Learners: Seeing Notes as Blocks
excerpt: How piano roll editors show pitch and time as blocks, and simple review habits that improve practice without heavy quantising.

title: Set Boundaries for Beginner Rubato: Steady First, Then Flexible
excerpt: Rubato can easily turn into unsteadiness for beginners. This article shows how to build a steady beat first, then add limited flexibility in chosen bars, so the playing does not drift apart.

title: Writing a Piano Studio Handbook: Clear Policies Parents Read
excerpt: A short studio handbook sets clear expectations on fees, absences and practice. Learn what to include, how to write it kindly and how to keep it current.

title: Writing a Teaching Philosophy Statement as a Piano Teacher
excerpt: A teaching philosophy statement explains what you believe about learning music and how it shapes lessons. Learn how to write one that is clear and honest.

title: Trills on Piano: How to Play Them Evenly and Musically
excerpt: A trill alternates rapidly between two neighbouring notes. Learn which notes to use, which fingers suit you and drills for an even, controlled trill.

title: Piano Trills: Starting Note, Even Speed and Relaxed Fingers
excerpt: A trill is a quick alternation between two neighbouring notes. Learn where to start, how to build an even speed and how to keep your fingers relaxed.

title: The Gruppetto Turn on Piano: Four Notes Around a Main Pitch
excerpt: A turn weaves four notes around a written pitch: upper neighbour, main note, lower neighbour, then the main note. Learn a slow shape that fits the beat.

title: Bring Out the Melody: Voicing and Balance on Piano
excerpt: Make the melody sing above the chords. Simple voicing exercises to balance melody, bass and inner voices using relaxed arm weight on piano.

title: Piazzolla's Libertango: The New Tango of 1974
excerpt: Argentine composer Astor Piazzolla blended traditional tango with classical music and jazz, a style called nuevo tango. His 1974 Milan recording of Libertango later travelled the world.

title: Piazzolla's Oblivion: A Slow Tango Written for a Film in 1982
excerpt: Oblivion is a slow tango Astor Piazzolla wrote for a film in 1982. It wins not by fast syncopation but by a long, slightly sad melody over a slow, clear tango step, and it has many piano arrangements.

title: The Picardy Third: Ending a Minor Piece on a Major Chord
excerpt: A Picardy third ends a minor-key piece on a major tonic chord. See how the raised third works, where it appears and how to add one at the piano.

title: The Picardy Third at the Piano: A Major Close After a Minor Phrase
excerpt: A Picardy third closes a minor phrase with a major tonic. Find it in the score, prepare the raised third, and make the colour change audible at the piano.

title: Learning a Pop Song: Pick Out the Melody with One Finger First
excerpt: To play a favourite pop song, start with the simplest step: pick out the melody on the piano note by note with one finger. Then add fingering, then left-hand chords, and train your ear along the way.

title: Pickup Notes: Starting a Piece Before the First Full Bar
excerpt: A pickup note, or anacrusis, is a short start before the first full bar. Learn how to count it and how to give it a light, forward-moving feel.

title: Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake: West Lake at Night in Cantonese Music
excerpt: Pinghu Qiuyue is a famous piece of Cantonese music by Lü Wencheng, painting a moonlit autumn night on Hangzhou's West Lake. Originally played on the gaohu, it also has piano arrangements.

title: Pitch Bend and Modulation Wheels: Expressive Keyboard Controls
excerpt: The two wheels beside many keyboards let players slide pitch and add vibrato or movement. Learn what each control does and how to use them musically.

title: Why Middle C Is C4: Pitch Names and Octave Numbers
excerpt: Octave numbers give every piano key a unique name. Learn how C4 became middle C, how to count octaves on the keyboard and why some labels differ.

title: Pivot-Chord Modulation on Piano: One Chord That Belongs to Two Keys
excerpt: A pivot chord belongs to both the old key and the new one. Find it in a piano score, name it both ways, and make the key change audible after it.

title: The Plagal Cadence on Piano: Approaching the Tonic From IV
excerpt: A plagal cadence approaches the tonic from IV. Find the close, voice the two chords, and let the arrival feel finished without copying a perfect cadence.

title: Plain-Language Terms Pages for Music Apps
excerpt: A plain-language terms page helps music app users understand subscriptions, trials, data and cancellation before they agree. How to write one clearly.

title: Finding the Climax of a Piece: Draw a Map of Your Dynamics
excerpt: Many pieces sound flat because every section has similar dynamics. Find the climax, mark it in the score, and plan how the dynamics change on the way up and down, so you do not use up all your strength at the start.

title: Playing a Familiar Major Song in a Minor Key
excerpt: What does Two Tigers sound like in a minor key? Mahler did something similar with Frère Jacques in his First Symphony. Turning a familiar major song into minor is a fun way to hear the difference between the two modes.

title: A Weekly Cold Start: Play the Whole Piece Without Warming Up
excerpt: Once a week, sit down and play your piece straight through with no warm-up and no practising of hard spots first. It shows whether the piece holds up unprepared, as it must in exams and performances.

title: Fugue Practice: Work on Each Voice Separately
excerpt: In fugues and other polyphonic pieces, several melodies run at once. Practise each voice on its own first, then in pairs, and only then all together, so your ears and hands know every line.

title: Play the Same Melody in a Different Octave
excerpt: Once a melody is well learned, try playing it an octave higher or lower. You will hear how each register sounds, get to know the keyboard better, and gain a simple way to vary repeated sections.

title: Try a Different Octave: Make a Familiar Phrase Sound New
excerpt: After many repetitions your ears go numb to a phrase. Moving it eight white keys up or down refreshes your hearing, exposes uneven or unclear spots, and deepens your memory of its shape.

title: Player Pianos: From Punched Paper Rolls to Digital Recording
excerpt: Over a hundred years ago, punched paper rolls made pianos play by themselves; today sensors and digital files carry on the idea. This article covers how player pianos work, their history and what they teach piano learners.

title: Asked to Play at a Holiday Gathering? How to Handle It Calmly
excerpt: When relatives ask a piano learner to play at a holiday gathering, a little preparation helps: pick a short, familiar piece, introduce it, say thank you, and treat it as sharing, not an exam.

title: Playing Over a Drone: Melody, Tension and Release on Piano
excerpt: How to practise melody over a sustained drone on piano: hearing consonance and tension, improvising freely and building stronger listening skills.

title: Playing an Unfamiliar Piano: How to Adjust in Minutes
excerpt: Keys feel heavier, the sound is brighter, the pedal bites early. A short routine for adjusting to an unfamiliar piano before a lesson or performance.

title: Plum Blossom in Three Variations: A Guqin Theme Heard Three Times
excerpt: Plum Blossom in Three Variations is an ancient guqin piece praising the strength and purity of the plum blossom. Its harmonics theme returns three times in different registers of the instrument.

title: Podcasting for Music Teachers: Sharing Expertise in Audio
excerpt: A short podcast lets a music teacher share practical knowledge and build trust with families. How to plan episodes, record simply and stay consistent.

title: The Polka on Piano: A Lively Two-Beat Dance With a Clear Step
excerpt: A piano polka is a lively two-beat dance with a clear step and light accompaniment. Feel the dance pulse, shape the tune, and keep the left hand springy.

title: Polonaise Rhythm for Pianists: A Stately Three-Beat Feel
excerpt: Polonaise rhythm on piano: the decorated first beat, counting tips, left-hand support and a calm practice path for the dance pulse.

title: Polyphonic Aftertouch and Expressive MIDI Controllers
excerpt: Channel versus polyphonic aftertouch, how expressive MIDI controllers shape tone, and simple ways to practise pressure-based articulation.

title: Polytonality: Music in Two Keys at Once
excerpt: Polytonality means two or more keys sounding at the same time, as when the right hand plays in C major and the left in F♯ major. Stravinsky, Milhaud and Bartók all used it.

title: Ponce's Estrellita: A 1912 Song Often Arranged for Piano
excerpt: Estrellita is a song written by the Mexican composer Manuel Ponce around 1912 and later arranged for violin, piano and many other instruments. Its simple, long melody wins by feeling, not technique.

title: Ponchielli's Dance of the Hours: A Day in a 1876 Opera
excerpt: Dance of the Hours is ballet music from Amilcare Ponchielli's opera La Gioconda, premiered in Milan in 1876. Dancers play the hours of dawn, day, evening and night, and it ends in a fast galop.

title: Pop Ballads: Add Chord Tones Under the Right-Hand Melody
excerpt: A single-note melody can sound thin in a pop ballad. Adding one or two chord tones under the melody notes makes the right hand fuller, with the top note kept clear and the lower notes softer.

title: Left Hand in Pop Songs: From Root Notes to Octaves to Fifths
excerpt: In pop accompaniment the left hand plays the bass and gives the song a steady foundation. Start with one root note per chord, then octaves, then alternating root and fifth, then simple rhythm patterns.

title: Portable and Foldable Keyboards: Practising Away from Home
excerpt: Lightweight and foldable keyboards let pianists practise while travelling. Learn their strengths and limits and how to use them alongside a full piano.

title: Portamento and Glissando on Keyboard Instruments
excerpt: How sliding between pitches moved from voice and strings onto keyboards, and what digital controllers add for smooth pitch motion.

title: Dots Under a Slur: How to Play Portato
excerpt: When notes carry dots and are also covered by a slur, the touch lies between legato and staccato, often called portato. Each note is slightly separated but not as short as staccato.

title: Portato: The Gentle In-Between of Legato and Staccato
excerpt: Portato, or mezzo-staccato, asks for notes that are lightly separated but still sing. Here is how to read the markings and practise the touch.

title: Positioning Statements for Music Education Brands: One Clear Sentence
excerpt: A positioning statement says who a music education brand serves, what it offers and why it differs. How to draft, test and use one sentence well.

title: Power Chords: The "Hollow" Chord of Just Root and Fifth
excerpt: A power chord has only a root and a fifth, sometimes with the root doubled an octave higher, such as C, G, C. With no third it sounds neither major nor minor, giving an open, solid sound that works on piano too.

title: Practise piano 15 minutes a day and actually improve: 5 methods that work
excerpt: Practising daily but not improving? The problem is usually where you practise, not how long. Five methods that fit into 15 minutes.

title: Should You Still Practise on a Bad Day?

excerpt: Why a pause option can help music learners and apps alike, how to word it clearly, and what to explain about progress, billing and returning.

excerpt: Play Tchaikovsky’s Sugar Plum Fairy with a bell-like touch: the story of the celesta, pedal and register tips, and a step-by-step learning plan.

excerpt: Superfans buy, share and show up. Why a small committed audience can sustain a musician, and practical ways to welcome and keep devoted listeners.

title: Suspended Chords on Piano: Sus2 and Sus4 Made Simple
excerpt: What sus2 and sus4 chords are, how to build them on piano, how they resolve and how to use them to add an open, unfinished colour to songs.

title: Suspensions on Piano: Holding a Note Into the Next Chord
excerpt: A suspension holds a consonant note into a new chord so it becomes a dissonance, then steps down to resolve. Learn to spot, play and write the pattern.

title: Swing Eighths vs Straight Eighths: Feeling the Difference on Piano
excerpt: Straight eighths divide the beat evenly; swing eighths make the first longer and the second shorter. Learn to hear, count and switch between the two.

title: Symbolic vs Audio AI Music Models: Notes or Sound Waves
excerpt: Symbolic vs audio AI music models for piano learners: notes versus sound waves, and how to experiment without mixing the two.

title: Sync Licensing for Independent Composers: The Basics
excerpt: How sync licensing places music in videos, ads and games, which rights are involved, how independent composers prepare tracks and what to check in a deal.

title: Synthetic Training Data in Music AI: Uses and Limits
excerpt: Some music AI systems learn from generated rather than recorded examples. Learn why synthetic data is used, how it is made and where it falls short.

title: Speak the Rhythm First: Tabla Bols for Tricky Piano Bars
excerpt: Borrow the tabla player's habit of speaking rhythms as syllables. Learn a few bols and use them to fix uneven, rushed or confusing bars on piano.

title: Tablet Music Stands: Page Turns and Digital Scores Explained
excerpt: A plain look at reading sheet music on a tablet: page turns by touch or pedal, annotations, set-up tips and when paper is still a good choice.

title: Silent Table Practice: Rehearsing Piano Fingerings Away From the Keys
excerpt: Silent table practice rehearses fingering and rhythm on a flat surface when a piano is not available. Learn what it can train and a short routine.

title: Tango Rhythm on Piano: Marcato, Síncopa and the 3-3-2 Pulse
excerpt: Learn the core tango rhythms on piano: the four-beat marcato, the síncopa push and the 3-3-2 pattern, with left-hand drills and practice tips.

title: Tap the Rhythm First: A Sight-Reading Habit for Pianists
excerpt: Before playing a new piece, tap its rhythm on your knees. Learn how separating rhythm from pitch makes sight-reading steadier, with a short routine.

title: From Tape Hiss to Spatial Audio: How Listening Technology Evolved
excerpt: How noise reduction, surround sound and spatial audio changed the way we hear music, and what this means for recording and judging piano.

title: The Tarantella on Piano: A Fast Dance in Compound Time
excerpt: A tarantella is a fast dance, often in a compound metre such as six-eight. Learn how to feel the larger beats and how to keep a quick piano dance clear.

title: Teaching Accent Marks Without Banging the Keys
excerpt: An accent is about musical emphasis, not hitting harder. Ways to teach accent marks on piano using arm weight, timing and contrast instead of force.

title: Teach Beginners to Improvise: Question-and-Answer Phrases on Piano
excerpt: Question-and-answer phrases give beginners a safe way to improvise. How teachers use call and response, limited notes and simple rules in lessons.

title: Teacher Cooperatives: Independent Music Teachers Sharing One Studio
excerpt: A teacher cooperative lets independent music teachers share rooms, instruments and admin while keeping their own students. How the model works.

title: Teacher-Student Duets: Making Beginner Pieces Sound Full
excerpt: Why playing simple duets with beginner piano students builds pulse, listening and confidence, plus ideas for creating accompaniments in lessons.

title: Teacher-Student Piano Duets: Making Simple Pieces Sound Full
excerpt: Teacher duet parts let beginners play simple melodies inside a rich musical texture. How to choose, write and use duets in piano lessons.

title: Teaching Adult Beginners: Respecting Their Time and Experience
excerpt: Adults often start piano with busy lives and strong opinions. Teachers can honour their experience, set short goals and keep lessons kind.

title: Teaching Adult Piano Beginners: Planning the First Month
excerpt: Adult beginners bring clear goals, busy schedules and strong opinions. How teachers can plan the first month of piano lessons around real-life music.

title: Teaching Students Who Play by Ear: Building a Bridge to Notation
excerpt: Some students arrive playing songs by ear but cannot read music. How teachers can value that skill while building reading step by step.

title: Teaching Group Piano Classes: Plan Lessons for Many Keyboards at Once
excerpt: Group piano classes need different planning from private lessons. How teachers organise keyboards, pacing, ensemble playing and fair feedback.

title: Teaching Intervals by Distance on the Keys: Seconds, Thirds, Fifths
excerpt: Intervals become simple when learners see them as distances on the keyboard. A step-by-step way to teach seconds, thirds and fifths with hands and ears.

title: Teaching Left-Handed Piano Students: Small Adjustments
excerpt: A left-handed learner uses the same keyboard as everyone else. Here are calm, practical ideas for teachers and parents who want practice to feel natural.

title: Teaching Note: One Clear Sentence of Feedback After Each Run
excerpt: A short teaching note: after a student plays a passage, give one clear, kind sentence that points to one thing to try next, and let them play again.

title: Teaching the Sustain Pedal to Late Beginners: Clear First Steps
excerpt: Late beginners can learn the sustain pedal in small steps: a quiet foot, a simple change, and ears on the sound. A teaching sequence is outlined here.

title: Teaching Piano by Video Call: Camera, Sound and Lesson Flow
excerpt: Online piano lessons need a clear view of hands, good sound and a lesson plan for delay. Practical setup and teaching tips for video-call teachers.

title: Teaching Piano Without Touch: Words, Images and Mirroring
excerpt: How piano teachers can correct hand shape, wrist and posture using words, images and mirroring instead of physical contact, online or in the room.

title: Teaching Rubato on Piano Without Losing the Underlying Pulse
excerpt: Rubato on the piano can move a line without losing the pulse underneath. Learn a teaching order that starts from a steady beat and adds planned time.

title: Teaching Music Theory Through Small Composition Tasks
excerpt: Composition tasks help piano students understand theory by using it. Ideas for short assignments that make scales, chords and form meaningful.

title: The Telharmonium: Early Electric Music by Telephone
excerpt: How the telharmonium sent live electric keyboard music over telephone lines, why the machines were so large, and what that idea still highlights.

title: Tempo Numbers and BPM: Reading the Speed of a Piece
excerpt: A tempo number such as 72 tells you how many beats fit into one minute. Learn how to read it, set a metronome and choose a comfortable speed.

title: Terraced Dynamics: Playing Baroque Contrast on a Modern Piano
excerpt: Terraced dynamics shift suddenly between loud and soft levels instead of gradual swells. Where the idea comes from and how to use it on piano.

title: Text-to-Audio AI: Describing a Sound in Words
excerpt: How text-to-audio AI turns written descriptions into sound, why precise musical vocabulary helps, and what the trend means for piano learners.

title: Theme and Variations on Piano: How One Tune Keeps Changing
excerpt: Theme and variations present a clear tune, then change it in later movements. Learn how to hear the theme in each variation and how to practise the set.

title: Themed Practice Days: A Weekly Rotation for Piano Learners
excerpt: Give each practice day a theme such as reading, technique or playing for fun, so a short daily session still covers every skill across the week.

title: The Theremin: Playing Music Without Touching
excerpt: How the theremin makes pitch and volume from hand movements near two antennas, why it is hard to play in tune, and what keyboard learners can take from it.

title: The Theremin Story: The Instrument You Play Without Touching
excerpt: How Leon Theremin’s touch-free instrument was born, how Clara Rockmore made it sing, and what its story teaches pianists about pitch and touch.

title: Three Against Two on Piano: Feeling a Cross-Rhythm Steadily
excerpt: How to feel three against two on piano: speak the pattern, tap both hands, then move it to simple keys so polyrhythm stops feeling mysterious.

title: Thumb-Under Scale Fingering: Smooth Crossings on Piano
excerpt: Smooth scales depend on passing the thumb under the hand and crossing fingers over it. Learn the motion, common fingerings and drills for even scales.

title: Ticketed Livestream Concerts: How Online Shows Became a Business
excerpt: In 2020 musicians sold tickets to online concerts at scale. How paid livestreams work, what fans pay for and how to plan a small online recital.

title: Ties and Slurs: Two Curved Lines With Different Jobs
excerpt: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound, while a slur joins different notes into a smooth phrase. Learn to tell them apart.

title: Time Signatures Explained: What 3/4, 4/4 and 6/8 Tell You
excerpt: A time signature is the two-number sign at the start of a score. See what the top and bottom numbers mean, and how 3/4, 4/4 and 6/8 feel when you play.

title: Timing Windows: How Practice Software Decides You Played On Time
excerpt: Practice software judges rhythm with timing windows around each beat. Learn how onsets are found, why tolerance matters and how to use the feedback.

title: The Toccata: A Keyboard Piece Built to Show Touch and Speed
excerpt: A toccata is a keyboard piece that shows off touch, speed and brilliance, often with free passages and fast figures. Its history and how to listen.

title: The Tonal Answer in a Piano Fugue: Adjusting the Subject in a New Key
excerpt: A tonal answer adjusts a fugue subject so it can enter in a new key. Find the changed intervals, practise the answer as a true line, and join it on.

title: Tone Clusters on Piano: Pressing Neighbouring Notes Together
excerpt: Tone clusters press several adjacent keys at once with fingers, palm or forearm. Learn how they are notated, why they are used and how to play them.

title: Touch Curve Settings on Digital Pianos: Light, Normal, Heavy
excerpt: A touch curve decides how hard you must press a digital piano key for a given volume. Learn how light, normal and heavy settings change practice.

title: The Toy Piano: A Small Instrument With a Serious Sound
excerpt: The story of the toy piano: how its metal rods make sound, why composers wrote real music for it and what it can teach curious piano learners.

title: Transpose a Melody on Piano: Play the Same Tune in Any Key
excerpt: Transposing moves a melody to a new key while keeping its shape. Learn the interval method, scale-degree thinking and easy practice steps.

title: Trial Lesson Follow-Up: What to Send After the First Visit
excerpt: A calm follow-up message after a trial music lesson: what to include, what to leave out, and how to let families decide in their own time.

title: Tritone Substitution on Piano: Jazz Colour in One Swap
excerpt: Tritone substitution swaps a dominant chord for one a tritone away, giving a smooth chromatic bass. Learn the logic, voicings and drills on piano.

title: Two-Note Slurs for Beginners: The Drop and Roll Touch
excerpt: Two-note slurs sound like a sigh: strong then soft. Learn the drop and roll touch, a simple down-up motion, and avoid common beginner tension at the piano.

title: Two-Part Inventions: Learning to Hear Two Voices at Once
excerpt: Two-part inventions are short contrapuntal pieces where both hands share a motif. Learn how they work and how to practise independent voices.

title: Two Short Practice Sits on the Same Piano Piece
excerpt: Two short sits on the same piano piece, with a break, can settle a passage more clearly than one long sitting. Plan each sit and what to repeat.

title: Una Corda and Soft Pedal: Quiet Colour on Acoustic and Digital
excerpt: Una corda and soft pedal on acoustic and digital pianos: quiet colour, honest tests, and soft control that still uses the fingers.

title: Using a Second Music Stand for Duet Scores at One Piano
excerpt: A second music stand can hold a duet score at one piano. Set both stands so each player can see, turn pages, and keep a shared pulse.

title: Velocity Curves on Digital Pianos: Matching the Keys to Your Touch
excerpt: A velocity curve decides how hard you must press a digital piano key to get each loudness level. How curves work and how to choose one for practice.

title: The Velvet Sundown Case: What an AI-Made Band Taught Music Marketing
excerpt: In 2025 a band with a large streaming audience was revealed as an AI project. What the case teaches about transparency, trust and music marketing.

title: The Vinyl Revival: Why Physical Records Still Sell in a Streaming Age
excerpt: Vinyl came back through collectors, Record Store Day and special pressings. What the revival teaches musicians about physical products and fan rituals.

title: Voicing a Melody Inside Piano Chords: Making the Top Note Speak
excerpt: When a melody sits on or inside piano chords, the top note must speak clearly. Learn a slow method that balances the inner parts without losing the line.

title: Waiting Lists for Piano Lesson Slots: Fair Order and Clear Updates
excerpt: A waiting list for piano lesson slots should keep a fair order and clear updates. Write how names are added, how a slot is offered, and how to reply.

title: The Studio Waiting Room: A Quiet, Useful Space for Families
excerpt: A studio waiting room can be quiet and useful for families. Learn what to provide, what to keep out of the way, and how to share information.

title: Waitlist Emails for Music Studios: Staying Warm While Families Wait
excerpt: A plain guide to waitlist emails for a music studio: what to say at sign-up, how often to write and how to keep families informed honestly.

title: Walking Bass Lines on Piano: Moving the Left Hand Every Beat
excerpt: A walking bass plays one note per beat through chord tones and passing notes. Learn a simple four-beat method to build lines over common progressions.

title: Waltz Left Hand on Piano: Bass, Chord, Chord Without the Bump
excerpt: How to play a smooth waltz left hand on piano: the bass-chord-chord pattern, light offbeats, pedal choices and a weekly plan for steady three-beat flow.

title: The Waterfall Release: Building an Album One Single at a Time
excerpt: A waterfall release groups each new single with the earlier ones, so a growing collection keeps attention on the whole project. How to plan one.

title: Watermarking AI-Generated Audio: Signals, Limits and Studio Policy
excerpt: Watermarking can attach a hidden or visible signal to AI-generated audio. Learn what it can do, what it cannot prove, and how a studio may write a policy.

title: WAV, MP3 and MIDI: Music File Types Explained for Pianists
excerpt: WAV, MP3 and MIDI store music in very different ways. Learn what each holds, when to use it and how pianists can save and share practice recordings.

title: Weekly Practice Goals: One Small Target Per Week
excerpt: Instead of a long to-do list, a learner picks one small target each week. A calm planning method for piano students, parents and teachers to try together.

title: Weekly Practice Notes: How Piano Teachers and Parents Stay in Sync
excerpt: A short weekly note links lessons and home practice. What teachers should include, how parents can use it and how to keep it simple and kind.

title: Should Your Student Enter a Piano Competition? Weighing It Up
excerpt: Competitions can motivate some students and discourage others. Learn how teachers and families can weigh readiness, goals, costs and the right moment.

title: Weighted Keys: How Digital Pianos Imitate Hammer Action
excerpt: How weighted and graded keyboard actions try to copy an acoustic piano's feel, what graded means, and how to choose practice habits that transfer well.

title: Weighted Keys Explained: Hammer Action on Digital Pianos
excerpt: What weighted, semi-weighted and graded hammer action keys mean on a digital piano, and how key feel affects practice and moving to an acoustic.

title: Wekinator Explained: Teaching a Computer to Turn Gestures Into Music
excerpt: Wekinator is free software by Rebecca Fiebrink that lets musicians train machine learning by example. See how it works and what it teaches about AI.

title: A Welcome Pack for New Music Students: What to Include
excerpt: A welcome pack helps new music students and their families settle in. Here is what to include, how long it should be and how to keep it friendly and clear.

title: Welcoming Transfer Students: A Piano Teacher's First Lessons
excerpt: Students who switch teachers bring skills, habits and expectations. Learn how to assess, respect past learning and build trust in the first few lessons.

title: West Coast Synthesis: Touch Plates, Wave Folding and New Sounds
excerpt: What West Coast synthesis means, how complex oscillators, wave folding and low-pass gates differ from classic synths, and why it inspires players.

title: What Is TIGA ALPHA? The AI Piano Teaching App Explained
excerpt: TIGA ALPHA is an AI piano teaching app by a Thai team, teaching in Thai, English and Mandarin. What it does, who it is for, pricing and how to start.

title: The Whole-Tone Scale: A Dreamy Colour on Piano
excerpt: What the whole-tone scale is, why it sounds floating and unresolved, how to find it on the piano, and how composers use its colour in short passages.

title: The Whole-Tone Scale on Piano: Six Notes, No Clear Home
excerpt: The whole-tone scale uses only whole steps, giving six notes and a floating, unresolved sound. Learn its two forms, fingering ideas and creative uses.

title: Why Piano Learners Stop, and What Studios Can Do About It
excerpt: Learners leave piano lessons for many reasons, some outside a studio's control. Learn the common patterns and practical steps that help students stay.

title: Writing Teacher Bio Pages for a Music Studio
excerpt: Teacher bio pages help families choose a music teacher with confidence. How to write them warmly and factually, with consent and no overstated claims.

title: Pedalling for Young Pianists When Feet Do Not Reach
excerpt: How teachers and parents can help young piano learners whose feet do not reach the floor or pedals: footrests, posture and first pedal steps.

title: A cappella: de "al estilo de la capilla" a la música vocal sin acompañamiento
excerpt: A cappella viene del italiano y significa literalmente "al estilo de la capilla". En el Renacimiento, muchas obras corales de iglesia se cantaban sin instrumentos, o con instrumentos que solo duplicaban las voces, y el término pasó a designar el canto coral sin acompañamiento.

title: Después de un ritardando, vuelve al tempo: entiende el a tempo
excerpt: Rit. es la abreviatura de ritardando, que indica ir frenando poco a poco; a tempo significa volver a la velocidad original. Al ver a tempo, recupera el tempo anterior al ritardando y no te quedes en el pulso lento.

title: Accelerando: la indicación de tempo que acelera poco a poco
excerpt: Accelerando es italiano y significa "acelerando gradualmente"; en la partitura suele abreviarse accel. Al verlo, el tempo debe subir poco a poco, no de golpe. Se practica con metrónomo, fijando el tempo inicial y el final.

title: Acento, tenuto y marcato: los pequeños signos sobre las notas
excerpt: Los pequeños signos sobre o bajo una nota indican cómo tocarla: ">" es el acento, la raya corta es el tenuto y la "^" es el marcato, más fuerte que el acento. Ajusta la intensidad al estilo de la pieza.

title: Caso ficticio: un estudio de piano hace su web más accesible para las familias
excerpt: Caso ficticio: un pequeño estudio de piano revisa su web con textos alternativos, subtítulos, buen contraste y lenguaje claro para que todos la usen.

title: Sostenido, bemol y becuadro: cuánto dura una alteración
excerpt: Una alteración es un sostenido, un bemol o un becuadro escrito delante de una nota que cambia su altura de forma temporal. Su efecto dura hasta el final del compás y solo afecta a esa misma altura; en el compás siguiente todo vuelve a lo que marca la armadura.

title: Acompañar a un cantante al piano: sigue su respiración, no solo el pulso
excerpt: Al acompañar a un cantante, el piano apoya la voz en lugar de competir con ella. Conoce la letra y la melodía, toca más suave que en solo y sigue la respiración y los cambios de tempo del cantante.

title: Cómo suena el acordeón: fuelle, lengüetas y botones de bajos
excerpt: En el acordeón la mano derecha se parece al piano, pero la izquierda tiene filas de botones; el sonido nace del aire del fuelle que hace vibrar las lengüetas. Veamos cómo suena, por qué los bajos van en quintas y qué puede aprender un pianista.

title: Ad libitum: qué tan libre es el "a voluntad" en una partitura
excerpt: Ad libitum es una expresión latina que significa "a voluntad" y en las partituras se abrevia ad lib. Puede indicar tempo libre, una parte opcional, repeticiones a discreción o improvisación, según el contexto.

title: Notas largas en el adagio: pulsa cada tiempo con paciencia
excerpt: El adagio pide paciencia: cada nota larga necesita su tiempo completo para cantar. Imagina el adagio como esperar a que una flor se abra poco a poco: no se puede apurar, pero cada instante cambia.

title: Cada niño aprende a su ritmo: cómo adaptar las clases de piano
excerpt: Unos niños aprenden rápido y otros necesitan más tiempo. Este artículo reúne métodos generales para profesores de piano: dividir los objetivos, explicar con varios sentidos, organizar la clase con flexibilidad y comunicarse con las familias.

title: Música adaptativa en videojuegos: por qué cambia con el jugador
excerpt: La música de un videojuego se tensa o se relaja según las acciones del jugador: es la música adaptativa. Conoce las técnicas de capas y secciones y lo que un pianista puede aprender de ellas.

title: Metrónomo adaptativo: los límites de un metrónomo que sigue tu tempo
excerpt: El metrónomo adaptativo escucha el tempo del intérprete y se ajusta, mientras que el tradicional mantiene un pulso estable. Este artículo compara ambos, explica cuándo conviene el adaptativo y qué límites suelen pasarse por alto.

title: Añade una línea de armonía en terceras bajo la melodía
excerpt: Si tocas la melodía con una sola nota en la mano derecha, el sonido puede resultar delgado. Una forma sencilla y bonita de enriquecerla es añadir debajo una línea de armonía a distancia de tercera, que la vuelve cálida y plena.

title: Añade la dinámica desde la primera semana, sin esperar a dominar las notas
excerpt: Mucha gente aprende primero las notas y el ritmo y deja la dinámica para el final. Pero tocar semanas con un solo volumen crea un hábito difícil de cambiar; conviene aprender la dinámica junto con las notas desde la primera semana.

title: Añade una nota cada vez: construye poco a poco una frase difícil
excerpt: Si tocas una frase difícil de principio a fin de golpe, suele salir cada vez peor. Un método sencillo es tocar la primera nota, luego las dos primeras, luego las tres primeras, añadiendo solo una nota cada vez hasta completar la frase.

title: Primero el esqueleto, después los adornos
excerpt: En la música barroca y clásica abundan los adornos: trinos, mordentes, apoyaturas. Un método más seguro es tocar primero solo las notas principales, el esqueleto de la melodía, y añadir los adornos uno a uno cuando el ritmo y la digitación estén claros.

title: El acorde add9: un toque de brillo sobre la tríada
excerpt: El acorde add9 añade a una tríada la novena, la nota situada una octava y una segunda por encima de la fundamental. Cadd9 son C, E, G y D; al no llevar séptima suena fresco y abierto, y es habitual en el pop, el folk y la música de cine.

title: Acorde con sexta añadida C6: una sexta sobre la tríada mayor
excerpt: Si a una tríada mayor le sumas la sexta mayor sobre la fundamental, obtienes un acorde con sexta añadida. C6 suena cálido, luminoso y relajado, y es habitual en el jazz y el pop.

title: Ritmo aditivo: ocho corcheas agrupadas como 3+3+2
excerpt: En un compás de 4/4, las ocho corcheas suelen agruparse de dos en dos. Si las agrupas como 3+3+2, las mismas notas suenan muy distintas, con un pulso asimétrico que parece saltar hacia delante.

title: Cómo ajustar la altura del banco: guíate por codos y antebrazos
excerpt: Para ajustar la altura del banco, siéntate, apoya las manos en las teclas y observa codos y antebrazos: deben quedar casi a la altura del teclado. Con la altura adecuada, los dedos trabajan sin esfuerzo.

title: ¿Qué es la envolvente ADSR? Cómo nace, se sostiene y muere una nota
